May there be auspiciousness! May there be freedom from obstacles! Victory to Śrī Rāma! Salutations to Śrī Mahāgaṇapati! Salutations to Śrī Śāradāmbā! (.................. Salutations to the venerable Gurus! Hariḥ Om! [Now begins the procedure for the Great Festival].
The Ritual for the Great Festival (Mahotsavavidhi)
[The Ritual for Collecting Wood and Installing the Staff]
First is the bull-sacrifice (*vṛṣayāga*), and second is the hoisting of the banner (*dhvajāroha*).
Third is the *bahattāla* rite, and fourth is the offering of sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*).
Following that is the worship of the sacrificial hall (*yāgaśālārcana*) and then the weapon-sacrifice (*astrayāga*).
The seventh is the offering of bali, and the eighth is the sequence of the vehicles.
The ninth is the *pariveṣa*, and the tenth is known as the *nīrāñjana*. The eleventh is named *kautuka*, and the twelfth is the *tīrthasaṃgraha*.
[In the] thirteenth [is] the *āsava*, and in the fourteenth is the *tīrthaka*.
The descent (*avarohaṇa*) is the fifteenth, and the sixteenth is the *snapana* itself;
the wedding ceremony (*vaivāhika*) is the seventeenth, and after that comes the festival of food (*bhaktotsava*).
Having understood the festival through such distinctions as these...
In the Śānti-bha [nakṣatra],
[the rite] is performed for the joy of the newly married couple.
One should begin the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) during the first part of the night.
[The rites of] the ascent and descent, etc., [should be performed].
At the end, having eaten, one who avoids oil-anointing, contact with women, [excessive] eating, and so forth, and who bathes three times a day, should have his hair shaved and...

Having first formed this intention and paid homage to one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), one should perform the following: starting from the first day until the end of the ninth day, the *bali* offering should be performed twice daily. On the tenth day, having offered the morning *bali*, one should on that same day commence the full festival and the pilgrimage (*tīrtha*).
Prior to the raising of the banner during the nine-day festival, it should already have been prepared; in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, under the asterism Ārdrā... (text fragment).

In the month of Māgha, [the moon] culminates in Puṣyā; in Phālguṇa, it culminates in Makhā (Maghā); in Caitra, it culminates in Uttaraphalgunī; in Vaiśākha, it culminates in Citrā; in Jyeṣṭha, it culminates in Jyeṣṭhā;
in Āṣāḍha, it culminates in Uttarāṣāḍhā; in Śrāvaṇa, it culminates in Śravaṇā; in Bhādrapada, it culminates in Pūrvabhādrapadā; and in Āśvayuja, it culminates in Aśvinī; in Kārttika... (fifth line).

One should cause a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) to be constructed at the edge of the ocean during the full-moon festival (*parvan*), or at the mouth of a river during a festival—whether the moon is in conjunction with or separated from the asterisms beginning with Kṛttikā; or on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, or at the time of the new moon; or under the asterisms of the preceptor, the patron, the deity, or the rest-house; or under the asterism desired by the builder. At the ocean, it should be made in the forenoon during a festival; at a lotus pond (*puṣkara*) and the like, in the afternoon; and at a river, at midday.

(... One should perform the *tīrtha* rite when there is an excess of lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), or one should perform the *tīrtha* in the evening; or when two lunar days (*tithi*) coincide in a single month, or when a fortnight has arrived, or when it is joined with the solstices (*viṣu-ayana*), the transits (*saṃkrānti*), and so forth. If such a conjunction occurs, the festival day (*parvan*) should be accepted. From the *ārohaṇa* rite up to the end of the *tīrtha*, within a single month, the period ending with the solstice, the end of the transit, or an eclipse is most excellent; thus one should perform the *tīrtha*. When there is an abundance of Śaiva rites, during the festival of Śiva, it should be performed in the morning.

At the concluding bath (*avabhṛtha*) at night... [the rite] called "the Banner" (*dhvaja*); indeed, it should be performed either in the evening or in the morning. One should cause the hoisting of the banner to take place.
On the banner, one should not depict a banner; rather, the bull-banner (*vṛṣabhadhvaja*) should be depicted.
But for others, a great calamity arises from [erecting] a banner... (5th line).
In a single location such as a village or the like, it would be auspicious for the offering of oblations and so forth;
however, one should not perform a festival for a deity in the center, nor should one cause auspicious rites to be performed there.

And there arises a fault for the kingdom. Having renovated everything from the commencement of the festival and the primary vehicles up to the chariots, and having decorated [the area] according to the rules for the temple of the Goddess and so forth— up to the banana pillars, clusters of areca palms, *nālikera* fruits, and *keralikucaka* [fruits], as well as the fruits, sprouts, flowers, garlands, door-arches, gateways, canopies, banners, and so on, ending with the water-stalls and rest pavilions— (1) *The portion in parentheses indicates that the text is partially illegible or lost.* (2) *The portion in parentheses indicates that the text is partially illegible or lost.* (6th line) Having renovated everything from the commencement of the festival and the primary vehicles up to the chariots, and having decorated [the area] according to the rules for the temple of the Goddess and so forth— up to the banana pillars, clusters of areca palms, *nālikera* fruits, and *keralikucaka* [fruits], as well as the fruits, sprouts, flowers, garlands, door-arches, gateways, canopies, banners, and so on, ending with the water-stalls and rest pavilions— (2nd line)

Having caused the sweeping, sprinkling with water, and other such rites to be performed, one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*). At the conclusion of the festival of Bhadrakālī, one should conduct a festival for Vighneśvara lasting nine days, seven days, five days, three days, or one day. It is as follows: Vināyaka, Skanda, Devī, Vīraśāstā, the twenty-five forms of Śiva, the weapons, the devotees, and Caṇḍa.

Having specifically worshipped the [images of] Vigraha and the others, preceded by the offering of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and having adorned them with all ornaments, the Preceptor (*ācārya*), the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the king, and the patron (*yajamāna*), together with those Brahmins and the ritual diagrams (*yantra*), at an auspicious moment for the festival, shall perform the recitation of the *puṇyāha* preceded by the worship of Vighneśa. Then, having performed the ceremonial bath (*snāna*) and worshipped Vighneśa, they shall honor the sixfold throne (*ṣaḍutthāsana*) with: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Vighnavināyaka; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Vighnavināyaka."

May the red-colored Vināyaka, who holds a noose and a goad, possesses his own teeth and a mango fruit, and has a rat as his vehicle, swiftly destroy all obstacles! *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vighnavināyaka.* Having thus meditated, and having worshipped him with all the services beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*), one should offer sweetmeats (*modaka*), hard foods, soft foods, and other offerings such as betel-leaf; then, having fed the Brahmins...
Having prayed, "May there be no obstacle," he should satisfy all those present in the temple— whether divine, ignorant, or wretched— with food and clothing as they deserve;

then, having placed the King of Weapons, Caṇḍeśvara, upon the chariot of Vināyaka or in a palanquin and so forth, accompanied by mirrors, umbrellas, chowries, various banners, perfumes, and flowers...

Accompanied by incense, lamps, various musical instruments, and the chanting of the Vedas, one should circumambulate the city and install [the image] in the pavilion of the assembly hall (*āsthānamaṇḍapa*). Then, one should perform the collection of the eight winds (*aṣṭamarut*) as previously described for the collection of the stone. One should select one from among trees such as the *bilva*, *khadira*, *devadāru*, *campaka*, *ajara*, *nāśo*, *śirīṣa*, and *veṇu*.

Having examined the base of the peak and worshipped Śiva with the following: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Śiva; Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Śiva; Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva," and having thus performed the worship and offered the sacrificial oblation (*bali*), one should obstruct [the tree] and cut it with an axe. If it falls toward the east, north, or northeast, it is auspicious; otherwise, however, [it is inauspicious]. One should then fashion it into a square.

Having taken the image along with the artisan, [having brought it] and bathed it with cow’s products, having tied the *kautuka* (protective thread) on the hand, and having caused the *puṇyāha* (declaration of an auspicious day) to be recited, one should place it in the assembly pavilion (*āsthānamaṇḍapa*),

wipe it with oil and other substances, and cause betel-leaf, etc., and the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to be offered. There, having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) and drawn an eight-petaled lotus, one should place the staff (*daṇḍa*) in its center.

Having adorned [it] with garlands and other ornaments, having decorated it with flowers and so forth, and having offered incense and lamps, [one should place] the three principles (*tattva*) beginning with the Śiva-portion upon the corners of the square or one’s own [mandala], etc.:

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Self-principle (*ātmatattva*). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā, the lord of the Self-principle. Oṃ hīṃ, obeisance to the Knowledge-principle (*vidyātattva*). Oṃ hīṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu, the lord of the Knowledge-principle.

"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Śiva-tattva. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śiva, the lord of the Śiva-tattva. Having thus worshipped, one should raise [the image] with the Praṇava, place it in its respective position, and—following the procedure for general consecration—consecrate it together with the eight [accessories]. This applies whether it extends to the pinnacle (*sthūpī*), the crest (*cūlikā*), or the *śukanāsa* (frontal projection), including the three shafts, the three planks, the two secondary staffs, and the bell. Eight...

One should have it fashioned with a hundred thousand darbha-grass tufts (*darbhakūrca*) wrapped around darbha-ropes and provided with rings; this is the procedure for the collection of wood and the installation of the staff.
[The Procedure for the Collection of Clay:

Having gone to another such site accompanied by the images of Vighneśvara and others, and accompanied by various musical instruments and the chanting of the Vedas, one should collect clay as previously described, and with that clay—

Having been carried by attendants of Maheśvara, by the *rudragaṇikās*, and by elephants and other mounts, and having circumambulated the city, he entered the palace; then, having placed [the image] upon the altar for the offering of sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*), he [worshipped] Vighneśa with sweetmeats (*modaka*), cakes (*apūpa*), sugarcane, coconut,
wood-apple (*kapittha*), citron (*mātuluṅga*), plantain, and other items appropriate for that occasion.
Having offered chickpeas (*caṇaka*), *mudga* beans, betel leaves (*tāmbūla*), and so forth, one should worship with all the ritual services (*upacāra*). This is the procedure for collecting the clay.
[Now follows] the procedure for the consecration (*adhivāsana*) of the bull.

The sprout of the banner (*dhvajāṅkura*) is the first, the sprout of the festival (*utsavāṅkura*) is the second, and the sprout of the sacred ford (*tīrthāṅkura*) is the third; thus the sprout is said to be threefold. One should perform the rite of offering the sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) as previously described. On the eve of the hoisting of the banner, one should perform the ritual of consecration (*adhivāsana*) during the night. Then: *Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the seat of Śiva* (*śivāsana*). *Oṃ hāṃ haṃ*.

Having worshipped with "Hāṃ, [he] by whom [it was] taken," and having made the formal request, one should decorate the site of the bull (*vṛṣasthāna*) with canopies and other ornaments. Having caused the Guru to face north, and having established a firm seat (*sthirāsana*), one should accomplish the ritual of the offering (*ārpya*) and worship the Lord of the Bull (*vṛṣeśa*). Then, having offered mung-bean rice (*mudgānna*), one should prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with rice and other grains in front of him.

In the middle of that [area], having strewn it with *kuśa* grass and flowers, and having established nine jars, one should worship a bull in the central jar, preceded by the sixfold arising seat (*ṣaḍutthāsanapūrva*). [Oṃ] *hāṃ*, obeisance to the seat; *oṃ hāṃ*, obeisance to the form of the Bull. [He is] whose feet are the Vedas, whose breath is the wind, who is radiant, whose eyes are the moon, and whose lotus-face is the Creator; whose ears are the Aśvins... [4th line].

[................... adorned with golden garlands and anklets, possessing divine jewels and a body as white as crystal, [I bow] to the Imperishable One... Having meditated thus: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Gopati," and having worshipped him with all the ritual offerings beginning with the invocation, one should worship in the directions from the East to the Northeast: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ukṣā; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Gopati; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śṛṅgin."
*Namaḥ*. *Oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to Nandin; *oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to Vṛṣapati; *oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to Viṣāṇin; *oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to Śaṅkukarṇa; *oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to Mahodara.

Having thus worshipped [the deities] beginning with those of the seat (*āsana*) using the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), and having worshipped the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) in their proper order: *oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to Indra; *oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to Agni; *oṃ hāṃ*... [Yama].
Salutation to Yama. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Nirṛti. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Varuṇa. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Vāyu. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Kubera. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Īśāna.

(Second line) Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Brahmā. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu. Having thus worshipped, [one should prepare] the banner-cloth, which is the best, with its length [measured] from the hand of Nala and so forth, and its width being one-fifth [of that]. (Third line) Width...
One should take wool that is even, soft, white, fine, smooth, and derived from cotton or similar materials; having divided it into three parts, one should draw a bull in the middle portion—
[occupying] one-third of a third [of the total area]— and, having colored the horns, ears, and hooves with red, and the tail and the smooth [body] with white and black, one should have it fashioned.

After that [having drawn] ... after that, a lamp, a bell, the *śrīvatsa* and other *svastikas*, and the remaining auspicious forms, one should begin the ritual of the flag (*dhvajayāga*). (6th line) Having performed [the rites] on the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) according to the previously mentioned procedure up to the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), and after the purification of the image (*beraśuddhi*), having prepared two sacrificial mounds elsewhere and having placed the flag-cloth (*dhvajapaṭa*) in the center— (F5b, 1st line)

Having filled a small vessel (*matūlikā*) with Soma-water and performed the opening of the eyes with the *Vṛṣagāyatrī*—namely, "Oṃ, let us know Him who has sharp horns; let us meditate upon Him whose feet are the Vedas; may He, the Bull (*vṛṣa*), inspire us"—or having done so with the root mantra, and having performed all the rites beginning with the beholding of the cow, one should sprinkle [the image] with earth, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and auspicious water (*śivāmbhas*). [Then] in a mirror, the products of the cow...

[The deity] should be propitiated with the [mantras] beginning with *dibhiḥ*. Having emerged from the water and brought the banner-cloth (*dhvajapaṭa*) into the sacrificial hall (*yāgaśālā*), one should again sprinkle it with cow-products (*gavya*) and so forth using the Vṛṣabha-gāyatrī.

Having placed it upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) and worshipped the sixfold seat (*ṣaḍutthāsana*), one should worship the form (*mūrti*) preceded by meditation. Afterwards, having covered it with cloth and performed the placement of the Brahmans (*brahmavinyāsa*), one should offer incense and lamps, and [place] the sleep-vessel (*nidrākumbha*).

Having established [the image], one should worship the bull and the others on all sides. Standing at the base of the bull, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the thirty-four principles (*tattva*) together with their presiding deities, from the head down to the feet. It is as follows: *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of Sadāśiva*; *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā, the presiding deity of the principle of Sadāśiva*; *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of Īśvara*; *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ananta, the presiding deity of the principle of Īśvara*.

Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā-tattva). Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Śambara, the lord of the principle of Pure Knowledge. In the portion belonging to Viṣṇu: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of Māyā. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Gahaneśa, the lord of the principle of Māyā. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of Time (kāla-tattva). Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Kālanāman, the lord of the principle of Time. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of Limited Agency (kalā-tattva).

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Lord of the principle of Kalā, the drop of gnosis. (Third line) Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of Niyati. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Lord of the principle of Niyati, the Restrainer. In the portion of Brahmā: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of Vidyā. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Lord of the principle of Vidyā, the Knowledge of the Vedas. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of Rāga. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Lord of the principle of Rāga, the Bestower of Desire.

Salutation! Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Puruṣa-tattva. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Sūkṣmanāda, the lord of the Puruṣa-tattva. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Prakṛti-tattva. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Pradhānaka, the lord of the Prakṛti-tattva. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Guṇa-tattva. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Trideha, the lord of the Guṇa-tattva. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Buddhi-tattva. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the lord of the Buddhi-tattva.

Homage to the Buddha! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of ego-consciousness (*ahaṃkāra-tattva*). Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the creator of ego-consciousness (*ahaṃkṛti*), the sovereign of the principle of ego-consciousness. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of the mind (*manas-tattva*). Oṃ hāṃ, homage to conceptualization (*saṃkalpa*), the sovereign of the principle of the mind. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of the ear (*śrotra-tattva*). Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the sky-walker (*vyomacārin*), the sovereign of the principle of the ear.

Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of the skin. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the lord of the principle of the skin, the All-Limbed One. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of the eye. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the lord of the principle of the eye, the Illuminator. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of the tongue. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the lord of the principle of the tongue, the Great-Mouthed One. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of the nose. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the lord of the principle of the nose.

Salutation to Vilambakāya. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of speech (vāk-tattva). (4th line) Salutation to Dundubhi, the lord of the principle of speech. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of the hand (pāṇi-tattva). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Sāma, the lord of the principle of the hand. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of the foot (pāda-tattva).

(5th line) Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Ramaṇa, the lord of the principle of the foot. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of the anus (pāyu-tattva). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the lord of the principle of the anus.

Salutation to Tūrṇakṛta. Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to the principle of the generative organ (upastha-tattva). Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to Ghanānanda, the lord of the principle of the generative organ. Salutation to the principle of sound (śabda-tattva). Salutation to Sūkṣmanāda, the lord of the principle of sound. Salutation to the principle of touch (sparśa-tattva). Salutation to Balavattara, the lord of the principle of touch. Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to the principle of form (rūpa-tattva). Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to Bhānumat, the lord of the principle of form.

Homage! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the element of taste. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Jalada, the lord of the element of taste. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the element of smell. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Gandhāṅga, the lord of the element of smell. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the element of space. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Sūkṣmanāda, the lord of the element of space. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the element of wind. Oṃ hāṃ, [homage to] Vāyu...

Salutation to Mātariśvan, the presiding lord of the element of fire (tattva). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the element of fire. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Tviṣāṃnidhi, the presiding lord of the element of fire. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the element of water. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Jaleśa, the presiding lord of the element of water. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the element of earth. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Śrīkaṇṭha, the presiding lord of the element of earth. [In the portion belonging to Rudra].
Up to the end of the *Sadāśiva-tattva*:

*Oṃ hāṃ śivatattvāya namaḥ | Oṃ hāṃ śivatattvādhipataye rudrāya namaḥ*. In the portion belonging to Viṣṇu, up to the end of the *Vidyā-tattva*: *Oṃ hīṃ vidyātattvāya namaḥ | Oṃ hīṃ vidyātattvādhipataye viṣṇave namaḥ*. In the portion belonging to Brahmā, up to the end of the *Māyā-tattva*: *Oṃ hāṃ ātmatattvāya namaḥ | Oṃ hāṃ ātmatattvādhipataye*.

Having performed the placement [of mantras] with "Obeisance to Brahmā" (7th line), and having offered a flower garland and a protective cord (*pratisara*) for the purpose of showing the three parts, one should conceive of it as divided into three sections. To each section, in order from the east to the northeast, one should recite: *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Subtle Form (Sūkṣmamūrti).* *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Mistress of the Subtle Form (...kṣāyai).* *Oṃ hāṃ hrūṃ, obeisance to the Fire Form (Vahnimūrti).* *Oṃ hrāṃ hrūṃ, obeisance to the Lord of the Fire Form...*

Salutation to Gopati. Oṃ hāṃ śrīṃ, salutation to the embodiment of the sacrificer (yajamāna-mūrti). Oṃ haṃ śrīṃ, salutation to Śṛṅgin, the presiding lord of the embodiment of the sacrificer. Oṃ hāṃ ṣūṃ, salutation to the embodiment of the Sun (arka-mūrti). Oṃ hāṃ [....], salutation to Nandin, the presiding lord of the embodiment of the Sun. Oṃ hāṃ hrūṃ (vrūṃ), salutation to the embodiment of Water (jala-mūrti). Oṃ hāṃ vrūṃ, salutation to Vṛṣapati, the presiding lord of the embodiment of Water. Oṃ gāṃ, salutation to the embodiment of Wind (vāyu-mūrti).
*Namaḥ*. *Oṃ hāṃ yūṃ*, obeisance to Vāyu, the lord of the Vāyu-form (*vaṣaṭ-kāriṇe*). *Oṃ hāṃ sūm*, obeisance to Indu-form.

*Oṃ hāṃ sūm*, obeisance to Śaṅkukarṇa, the lord of the Indu-form. *Oṃ hāṃ hūṃ*, obeisance to Kha-form. *Oṃ hāṃ hūṃ*, obeisance to Mahodara, the lord of the Kha-form. Having thus worshipped the forms and the lords of the forms, here indeed, according to the instruction of the Guru, [one should perform] the mantra from the *kanda*...

One should slowly utter a subtle sound consisting of *śakti*, spreading like the resonance of a bell; by means of the yoga of abandoning the causal source, it emerges from the *brahmarandhra*, possessing the brilliance of a thousand suns and equal to ten million flashes of lightning, illuminating the quarters and trees with a canopy of rays. With the mind, one should pierce the mantra, which has reached the outpouring of the essence of bliss; having drawn it back from the *dvādaśānta* [to the heart], one should contemplate the bull (*vṛṣa*) endowed with thirty-four *kalās*.

Having meditated upon the orb of light—blazing with a thousand rays, consisting of all powers, complete with its limbs, and joined in *añjali*—situated on the forehead, one should bring it to the door of the uvula (*ghaṇṭikā*). Having brought it out through the *suṣumnā* [channel]... (3rd line)... having meditated upon it entering through the aperture of Brahma (*brahmarandhra*) like a stream of clarified butter from a vessel of fine jewels, one should install the all-pervading *sakala* [form]. Thus indeed is the installation of the living soul (*jīvanyāsa*), which accomplishes all aims in the Vṛṣa [system]... (4th line)... it is... (5th line)... (Note: The ellipses indicate portions of the original text that were illegible or missing in the provided fragment.)

Having worshipped with yak-tail whisks (*cāmara*), one should go to the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) or to the vicinity of the altar (*sthaṇḍila*). Then, having placed [the fire] in the fire-pit with the mantra "Salutation to Ādhāraśakti" (*ādhāraśaktaye namaḥ*) and offered three oblations (*āhuti*), [one should proceed].

Having performed the placement of the *ātmatattva* (the principle of the self), and having worshipped the principles [of *vidyātattva* and *śivatattva*] with "Salutation to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra" (*brahmaviṣṇurudrebhyo namaḥ*), one should offer three oblations to each. Having worshipped the forms (*mūrti*) and the lords of the forms (*mūrtīśvara*), one should offer three oblations to each.

Having offered one hundred or fifty oblations each for the root-mantras and the limbs (*aṅga*), and having performed the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), the Guru, holding the *śāntikumbha* (peace-pitcher) in his hand, approaches the bull.

(7th line) Having sprinkled [it] with the water from the *śāntikumbha*, touched it with the roots, middles, and tips of *kuśa* grass while reciting the root-mantra, and having offered oblations and performed the concealment (*avakuṇṭhana*) with the armor-mantra (*varma*), he should restrain [the breath] and proclaim the command of the Lord of the Principles (*tattvādhipa*). Having projected the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) and restrained [the breath], [he should proceed].

With oblations, recitations from the Vedas and other scriptures, and great festivals of song and dance, one should perform this with devotion for at least one night. The Guru should perform the consecration of the bull (*vṛṣādhivāsana*) and the binding of the directions (*dikbandhana*)... [as before]. He should sleep as previously described. This is the procedure for the consecration of the bull. [The Procedure for the Hoisting of the Banner (*dhvajārohaṇa*) follows.]

On the following day, having performed the ritual bathing and other preliminaries, having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), and having performed the rite of personification (*sakalīkaraṇa*), one should prepare the general water-offering (*sāmānyārghya*). Having completed the entire procedure for the daily self-worship (*ātmapūjāvidhi*) and having worshipped the western jar and the others in their proper order, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations of fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge (*caru*) into the fire. Having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) and withdrawn the fire, one should draw three mandalas within the pavilion and other areas, and having summoned the attendants, [one should empower them] with the Weapon-mantra (*astra*).

(5th line) Having sprinkled [the image] and donned the turban and upper garment, one should lift up the cloth [icon] together with the jar and other [vessels], accompanied by all musical instruments from the *astra* mantra up to Caṇḍeśa;

(6th line) having performed the circumambulation of the hermitage (*śrama*) to the right along with the sounds of conchs and drums and the chanting of the Vedas, one should enter the sanctuary (*laya*), placing the cloth [icon] in one [vessel] and the King of Weapons (*astrarāja*) in another jar. (F9a, 1st line)

Having placed three sacrificial mounds (*sthaṇḍila*) upon which site, having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, having sprinkled [the area] with the *pañcagavya* and the water for the guest-offering (*arghya*), having sprinkled it with the water from the bull-pitcher (*vṛṣakumbha*), having consecrated [the deity] in order starting from the west with the jars of the bull and so forth, having adorned [him] with perfumes and other offerings, having presented the sacrificial food such as chickpeas and the like, and having also consecrated the King of Weapons (*astrarāja*) with the water from that pitcher—

Having adorned [the site] and offered [oblations], and having completed the recitation (*japa*), one should worship [the deity]. Having caused the powder of *rajanī* to be given to the King of Weapons (*astrarāja*) and having applied it oneself, one should cause the powder of *rajanī* to be given to all—the kings, the devotees, the retinues, and everyone else. Then, having adorned the flagstaff (*dhvajadaṇḍa*), one should worship the staff with the *Gāyatrī*. Having mounted the Deity upon a chariot or similar vehicle—

Having been consecrated by the preceptor, the sacrificer Vṛṣatoya, together with all the people, having circumambulated the city— equipped with all musical instruments, accompanied by auspicious sprouts, joined with various [ornaments], umbrellas, chowries, and lamps, provided with processions and gifts, and accompanied by song, dance, and offerings of oblations in the cardinal and intermediate directions— (F9b, 1st line)

Having entered the *ālaya*, having brought [the image] to the place of worship, having recited the *puṇyāha* formula, and having sprinkled the altar (*vedikā*), one should worship [the deities] from Śakti up to Īśāna-Śakti. (Second line) The meditation:
[one should visualize the deity] with one leg, two arms, three eyes, adorned with a line of body hair, and possessing beautiful thighs.

Having meditated thus: "His body is white, his nose is like that of a parrot, and he is seated upon a lotus throne... (3rd line). Having worshipped with: *oṃ hāṃ sadāśivamūrtaye namaḥ* and *oṃ hāṃ sadāśivāya namaḥ*, [one should place] three blades of grass on the staff with: *oṃ hāṃ ādhāraśaktaye namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ jñānaśaktaye namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ icchāśaktaye namaḥ*. On the shoulder-blades: *oṃ hāṃ sadāśivāya namaḥ*. (5th line)

*Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Soma.* *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Agni.* On the side-poles: *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Anila.* On the rope: *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Takṣaka.* [In the... *Kṣaṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vāyu.* On the banner: *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vṛṣa.* Having worshipped them in this sequence and having honored them with all the ritual services beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*), one should offer green-gram rice or milk-rice (*pāyasa*) to the bull, present incense and lamps, and [offer] gold to the Brahmins.
Having offered betel nuts, betel leaves, and other gifts, and having wrapped the cloth with a cord,

one should inform [the deities] that the festival to be performed is now being commenced; then, having uttered "May it be auspicious" (*śivaṃ*) and having sounded large cymbals (*bṛhattāla*), and for the purpose of removing obstacles, having offered a coconut oblation (*nālikerabali*), at an auspicious moment accompanied by various musical instruments, the *teśika* stands at the base of the staff, while the attendants have been stationed [above].

Having first touched the base of the flagpole with his hand, he should quickly raise it together with the image-keepers (*mūrtipāḥ*) by means of a rope in a clockwise direction. Having wrapped it around and secured the base of the staff, he should dismiss the fire of the bull-sacrifice (*vṛṣayāgāgni*). Pure dance should be performed in the cardinal and intermediate directions. This is the procedure for the raising of the banner (*dhvajārohaṇavidhiḥ*).

One should cause the woman to eat that bolus... she shall obtain... it destroys disease, it destroys all defects; for Vṛṣocchiṣṭa and Śivadhvaja, this is performed upon a leaf in the kingdom. When the banner... the subduing of [enemies]...
there is no untimely death there, nor is there fear of misfortune, sin, or the lowly who approach; there is no illness, nor confusion. Those with perverted minds... yoga...

Furthermore, when the rain-god showers at the proper time, there is abundance of food and the king is victorious; all beings are peaceful, and the land becomes rich in milk. One who is ungrateful is purified by the sight of the Brahmabhāga-oghna [tirtha]. Having seen the installation of the banner, one attains liberation from sin—what need is there to mention the three families? When the great banner is raised, the fruit is multiplied ten millionfold. *Salutations to me, the sole Lord of the Mango Tree (Ekāmranātha).*
[The Procedure for the Great Tāla]

It has been stated in the *Utsavapaddhati*: "At the end of the protection of the [image] of Sarvadoṣapriyā... if the drum (*bherī*) is struck before the deity or at the top of the banner, one should act as if toward the deity itself. Having consecrated three sacrificial mounds (*sthaṇḍila*), one should place the trident (*triśūla*) on one [mound] with the *Tatpuruṣa* [mantra], the cloth-painting (*paṭa*) in front of that, and the drum (*bherī*) at its tip; on the right, the *ghoṣadaṇḍa* [should be placed]... just as in the case of the reality (*tattva*) of the trident."
Having performed the placement of the nine solar-pada mantras as follows:

on the central petal—*oṃ hrīṃ śivatattvāya namaḥ*, *oṃ hrūṃ śivatattvādhipataye rudrāya namaḥ*, and so forth, together with the seed-mantras; on the left petal—*oṃ hāṃ vidyātattvāya namaḥ*, *oṃ hīṃ vidyātattvādhipataye viṣṇave namaḥ*; and on the right petal—*oṃ hām ātmatattvāya namaḥ*.

Oṃ hāām, salutation to Brahmā, the lord of the principle of the self (ātmatattva). (4th line) On the blade: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Pārvatī. At the base of the vessel: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Senānī. At its mouth: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Vighnarāja. At the tip of the staff: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Madana. In the middle of the staff: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Bhāskara. At the base of the staff: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Caṇḍeśvara.

In the seven petals beginning with the southeast: *oṃ hāṃ* [6th line] *brāhmyai namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ māheśvaryai namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ kaumāryai namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ vaiṣṇavyai namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ vārāhyai namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ indrāṇyai namaḥ* [F 11b, 1st line]; *oṃ hāṃ cāmuṇḍāyai namaḥ*. In the middle of the western petal: *jyeṣṭhāyai namaḥ*. In the middle of the northern petal: *kātyāyanyai namaḥ*.
At the base of the trident: *oṃ hāṃ* (second line) *mahādevāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ śivāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ rudrāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ śaṅkarāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ nīlalohitāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ īśānāya namaḥ*;
*oṃ hāṃ* (third line) *(vijayāya)* *namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ bhīmāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ devadevāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ*.

Salutation to the source of existence. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Kapālīśa. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Vaikartana. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Vivasvat. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Mārtāṇḍa. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Bhāskara. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Ravi. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Lokaprakāśaka. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Lokasākṣin. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Trivikrama.

Oṃ hām, obeisance to Āditya. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Sūrya. Oṃ hām, obeisance to Aṃśumālin. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Divākara. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Dhara. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Dhruva. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Soma. Oṃ hām, obeisance to Āpa. Oṃ hām, obeisance to Apāya. Oṃ hām, obeisance to Agnilocana.

Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Pratyuṣa. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Prabhāsa. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Nāsatya. (Second line) Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Aśvin. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Deva. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Daityajana. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the host of Dānavas. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Sarpa. (Third line) Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Rākṣasa. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Bhūta. Oṃ hāṃ...

Homage to the preta! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the piśāca! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the kinnara! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the nāga! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the vidyādhara! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the gandharva! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the uraga! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the guhyaka! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the [vi...]! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the yakṣa! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the kiṃpuruṣa!

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Siddha. Having invoked and worshipped the eleven Rudras, the twelve Ādityas, the [Aśvin] deities, and the eighteen Gaṇas—and having uttered the various benedictions—one should cause the drum to be struck. Then, having wrapped the drum with a variegated cloth, one should [place] "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Rudra" in the center; on the seven pegs, "Oṃ hāṃ..."

Salutation to Brāhmī. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Māheśvarī. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Kaumārī. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Vaiṣṇavī. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Vārāhī. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Indrāṇī. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Cāmuṇḍā. In the *kīla*: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Āditya. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Soma. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Aṅgāraka. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Budha.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Bṛhaspati. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śukra. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śanaiścara. (Fourth line) Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Rāhu. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ketu. On the shields: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vāsuki. At the strikes: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ṣaṇmukha. Having thus worshipped with [the appropriate] ritual action and adorned them with perfumes and other offerings, one should strike the drum. The Preceptor...

Having meditated upon the weapon (*śastra*) in the form of a drop, one should strike it three times with *darbha* grass. If that sound reaches the range of hearing of living beings, they become freed from sin. Afterwards, the preceptor (*deśika*), having summoned the drummer and sprinkled him with the general *arghya* water, and having caused him to wear the sacrificial thread (*yajñasūtra*), the upper garment (*uttarīya*), and perfumes, garlands, and so forth, and having placed a flower in his hand, he [the drummer], by the permission of the preceptor, [places] the flower on the drum.

Having set aside the musical instrument and placed it upon his shoulder, he should strike it with the *Nanditāla* mantra. Then, having summoned Śiva and all the other deities, the eighteen *gaṇas*, the lords of the directions beginning with Indra, the oceans, the subterranean realms (*pātālas*), and all others, he should strike it. Subsequently, for the purpose of invoking the deities of the center and so forth, [he should invoke] the King of Weapons (*Astrarāja*), the Goddess, Vināyaka, and...

Accompanied by Skanda, Nandin, Caṇḍa, Bhakta, Vigraha, and the others, together with all auspicious deities, he arrives at the site of the bull (*vṛṣasthāna*). Having offered worship and a sacrificial oblation (*balin*), and having gratified [the deity] with dance, handfuls of flowers, melodies, pure songs, and so forth, he subsequently takes recourse in the station of Brahmā (*brahmasthāna*). Having performed everything there in the location of that mandala, such as the sprinkling for the auspicious day (*puṇyāha-prokṣaṇa*), he worships the seat with the root-mantra of the form: *oṃ hāṃ śivāsanāya namaḥ*.

"Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Śiva. Having thus worshipped, and having taken parched grain (*lāja*) and flowers in his hand with the *mukula-mudrā*, he should meditate upon Brahmā. Then: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Brahmā; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Brahmā; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā. Having thus invoked and worshipped him, and having offered perfume, flowers, incense, lamps, [and other offerings], he should give an oblation (*bali*) for the sake of the sacrificial ground (*vedi*). Immediately thereafter, [he should perform] the *tāla* [gesture].

Having performed the *brahmatāla* rhythm, the *vakula* melody, the *samapāda* dance, and the *pañcamavādya* musical instrument, as well as the *śacca-puṭa* [drum], together with dance, song, instrumental music, and so forth,

and immediately thereafter having resorted to the Indra-night [rite], one should perform in that maṇḍala— as before— the sequence beginning with the seat and ending with the *bali* offering. Then, having performed the *samatāla* rhythm, the *bhairavī* melody, the *bhujaṅga* dance, and the *śāciuṭa* instrumental music, one should proceed in the same manner for the Āgneya [quarter].

In the [eastern] direction, having performed the rites from worship up to the offering of bali, one should satisfy [the deity] with the *tāla* called *mattāvaraṇa*, the *rāga* [called] *varāla* (or *varāli*), and instrumental music such as the *paṇvakaulliva* and the *udghaṭita*. Then, in the southern direction, having performed the rites from worship up to the offering of bali for Yama, one should satisfy [him] with the *tāla* called *bhṛṅgi*, the *śrīnṛtta*, the *maṇḍapādī*, the *paśvakaushi* (or *paśvakaushika*), and the *militamaṭṭaya* instrumental music.

Having performed [the rites] beginning with these, and having completed the worship of Nairṛti and so forth up to the *bali* offering in the southwest (*naiṛta*), one should satisfy [the deity] with the following: the rhythm (*tāla*) is [as prescribed], the melody (*rāga*) is Bhairavī, the dance (*nṛtta*) is the Terrifying of Serpents (*bhujaṅgatrāsa*), the language is Paṇvanaṭṭa, and the instrumental music is [as prescribed]. Having thus satisfied [him], and having performed the worship of Varuṇa and so forth up to the *bali* offering in the west (*vāruṇa*), the rhythm is the Nine Rhythms (*navatāla*), the melody is Deśika, and the dance is the Kuñcita. Paṇva...
The musical instrument for Śrīkāmarāja is the *siṃhanāda* [drum], and so forth...

Having performed the worship and offerings up to the *bali* for Vāyu in the northwest, [one should employ] the *tāla* as the *balidāla*, the *rāga* as *makuṭarāgagiri*, and the dance as the *bhujaṅgalalita*... having performed the *jaṃpuṭa* [mudrā], one should perform the worship and offerings up to the *bali* for Kubera in the north, [employing] the *tāla* as the *koṭṭaratāla*, the *rāga*...

(... Having pleased [the deity] with that merchandise, the *tarkarāga* melody, the instrumental music, and the five *tālas*, and having performed the worship of Īśāna in the northeast— from the initial offerings up to the concluding *bali*— one should please [him] with the *tāla* (...), the *deśākṣi* melody, the dance with raised feet, the *paṇvaśālā*, hand-clapping, the *kumbhavādya* drum, and so forth, following the sequence beginning with Indra.

Having performed the rite of *dakṣiṇā* and entered the temple, one should cast the remainder [of the offerings] at the base of the banner or upon the sacrificial pedestal (*balipīṭha*). This is the procedure for the Great Tāla ritual (*bṛhattālavidhi*). Thus ends the venerable [text].
Then, following the previously mentioned method, after the completion of the auspicious sprouts (*maṅgalāṅkura*), follows the worship of the sacrificial hall (*yāgaśālā*).
[The Worship of the Sacrificial Hall]

In front of the deity, or in the northeast, southeast, north, or west, one should construct a pavilion measuring five cubits or more; having provided a western entrance, one should fashion in its center a main altar resembling the surface of a mirror, accompanied by subsidiary altars, and outside of it, one should prepare sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in order from the east to the northeast.
[The Characteristics of the Fire-pit]
In the eastern quarter, the fire-pit is square;
in the southeastern, it is in the shape of a vulva; in the southern, it is bow-shaped; and in the southwestern, it is triangular.
In the west, there should be a circular pit; in the northwest, a hexagonal one;
in the north, a lotus-shaped pit; and in the northeast, an eight-cornered one.
Between Purandara and Īśa, the primary [fire-pit] is circular;
according to the five-fold system, it is square, with circular pits in the four directions as the primary ones.
Alternatively, [one may construct] a single fire-altar site, with a circular sacrificial pit (*vṛttakuṇḍa*) as the primary feature.

Having thus smeared the sacrificial hall (*yāgaśālā*) with cow dung, one should provide it with a canopy, banners, a parasol, garlands of *darbha* grass, and other such items, along with door-arches, auspicious symbols, and the eight auspicious objects (*maṅgalāṣṭaka*), as well as a mirror, a full water-jar (*pūrṇakumbha*), and a bull.

And the *ca* [is the first], then the *śrīvatsa*, the *svastika*, the conch, the lamp— the eight auspicious signs of the gods. [Then] the thunderbolt (*vajra*), the spear (*śakti*), the staff (*daṇḍa*), the sword (*khaḍga*), the discus (*cakra*), and likewise the goad (*aṅkuśa*).
Having fashioned the trident, the lotus, and the wheel— these being the ten weapons—

together with the collection of implements such as the *sṛṣṭi* [spoon] and so forth, and having performed the mounting [of the deity], one should initiate the festival in the evening; this is the procedure for the worship of the sacrificial hall (*yāgaśālā*).
The preceptor, together with the officiating priests, having performed the evening twilight ritual (*sāyaṃ-sandhyā*) and the special twilight ritual (*viśeṣa-sandhyā*),

and having returned to the temple, prepares a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) before the deity. Having drawn an eight-petaled lotus and sprinkled it with water while reciting the *astra-mantra*, he places within its center jars that are very smooth,
stainless, made of gold or clay, provided with *kūrca*-grass tufts, lids, cloths, fruits, and lotuses.

Having washed with water consecrated by the Astra-mantra those [vessels] which are provided with threads, endowed with [mantras], and possess the characteristics as described, and having fumigated them; having filled [the central vessel] with scented water ending in *vauṣaṭ* by means of the Hṛdaya-mantra;

and having placed the Śiva-vessel in the center upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) and the Vardhanī-vessel to the north, and having arranged eight jars all around starting from the east; one should [worship] the jar with the Mūrti-mantra and with Śakti.

Having worshipped [the deities] from Vardhanī up to Śikhaṇḍin within the jars, and having summoned the attendants from Nandī to Ādhāra around them, and having sequentially placed the auspicious jar (śubhakumbha), the Vardhanī, and the deities beginning with Ananta, one should [proceed with] the Vimāna [procession] accompanied by the sounds of the conch and drum, and the chanting of the Vedas, starting from the Vajra and ending with the Cakra.
Having circumambulated [the site] and entered the sacrificial hall (*yāgaśālā*), one should spread out eight *droṇas* of *śāli* rice,

half that amount of husked rice (*taṇḍula*), along with sesame seeds, parched grain (*lāja*), and the seven types of grain (*saptadhānya*) in the center of the altar (*vedikā*). In the middle of that, together with the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), one should establish the *śivakumbha* and the *vardhanī*, as well as the jars for the *vidyeśvaras*.

The Guru, together with the *yammānas*, having first performed the worship of Vināyaka and requested a declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), and having performed the worship of the Sun as usual and then dismissed Him,

[performs] the application of ashes (*bhasmadhāraṇa*) and the ritual of empowering the limbs (*sakalīkṛti*). Having prepared the general water-offering (*sāmānyārghya*) and worshipped the doors starting from the east, he places two [officiants] at each door.

Having worshipped [the mandala] ending with the *ṇaṇḍānta* as before, and having propitiated the gatekeepers as described for the western [direction], one should worship Vāstunātha in the southwest. Then, sitting to the south of the Brahma-position facing north, one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and so forth, as well as the special water offering (*viśeṣārghya*). Having [worshipped] oneself with perfumes and so forth, along with the *uṣṇīṣa* and the other [deities] together with the *lokapālas*...

Having prepared the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) according to the rules, and having performed the consecration of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) with the *arghya* water of the five products, one should worship the *śivakumbha* and the *vardhanī* as before up to the end of the recitation (*japa*).

Then, having meditated upon and worshipped the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) together with their vehicles and weapons, and having honored Mahālakṣmī, Gaṇapati, and the preceptor’s wife in succession, [one should worship] all...

He should cause [the mantra] to be recited. Then, having sat down to the south of the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), he should worship the seat in the *śivakumbha* vessel, beginning with Śakti and ending with Śakti. Having performed the *daṇḍabhaṅgi*, *muṇḍabhaṅgi*, *vaktrabhaṅgi*, and *kalābhaṅgi* [mudrās], and having meditated upon Śiva as endowed with all the paths (*adhvan*) according to the previously stated method, he should invoke Him. Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of Śrīkaṇṭha in the *vardhanī* vessel, [he should worship] the two-armed [deity].
She had a beautiful face, fine breasts, and was in the full bloom of youth;
she wore silken garments, was serene, and her face bore a slight smile.
One should meditate upon the Goddess, adorned with all ornaments, seated upon a throne, accompanied by Sarasvatī, and wearing a crown and a jeweled casket, following the prescribed sequence.

Having meditated thus, having invoked [the deities] with their root-mantras, having worshipped them with the five enclosures (*pañcāvaraṇa*) and the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*), having presented the food offering (*naivedya*) and the recitation (*japa*), and having praised and made supplication, they should worship Dharma and the others in the corners beginning with the southeast, announce the command of Śiva, and proceed to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
Having performed the rites from the consecration of the pit up to the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), they should divide the fire into nine or five parts.

Having cast [the materials] into the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) starting from the east and having worshipped each respective Śiva along with His limbs, they should perform the oblations together with the guardians of the images (mūrtipās), concluding with the expiatory rite (prāyaścitta). Having especially worshipped Śiva in each of those respective pits, [they should offer fuel-sticks of] Aśvattha, Udumbara, Plakṣa, and Vaṭa in the directions starting from the east; Śamī, Khadira, Māyūra, and Śrīparṇī in the corners starting from the southeast; and Palāśa in the principal pit, for that is approved everywhere.

Having offered *caru*, parched rice (*lāja*), barley, sesame, mung beans, black gram, peas, *āḍhaka* beans, chickpeas, horse-gram, and mustard seeds, and having offered oblations with the *vyāhṛtis* at the conclusion of the substances, one should offer one hundred and eight, one thousand, or five hundred oblations with the root mantra, followed by the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). Having performed the salutation to the ears and extracted the fire, and having caused the protection of the sacrifice and the installation of the root mantra upon the liṅga, image, and so forth to be performed, one [should do so] oneself together with the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) because of the [requirement for] a thousand [oblations].

In that regard, having brought a trident and installed it in either the northeast or the northwest, one should perform this very same rite every day at evening and morning; such is the procedure for the weapon-sacrifice (*astrayāga*).
[The binding of the protective thread (*rakṣābandhana*)].

Then, having worshipped a cotton [thread] fashioned from gold, one should prepare another protective thread (*rakṣāsūtra*) consisting of nine fierce lunar days (*raudra-tithi*). [Dividing it into] sixteen parts, one should wrap [it] around the neck of the *liṅga* [with a portion] equal to its circumference, and [another] equal to the stalk upon the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*). Having filled the base (*sthalikā*) with rice, parched grain, and flowers, one should draw a lotus in its center.
Placing [the deity] upon that, one should arrange [offerings] all around: ashes, turmeric, *dūrvā* grass, perfumes, flowers, fruits, gold, betel, and so forth.
Having offered that thread, having wiped it with *bhasma* while reciting the *Tryambaka* mantra, having caused the proclamation of *puṇyāha*,

and having worshipped [the deity] preceded by the six-fold rite of rising from the seat (*ṣaḍutthāsanapūrva*), having offered incense and lamps, and having circumambulated the temple, he enters within. Having fully worshipped Śiva and offered incense and lamps, he meditates upon Vāsuki, holds [the thread] in the middle of the *liṅga* with its root-mantra (*tanmūla*), and binds it to the *nāla* portion of the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) with its root-mantra, [reciting] the *Tryambaka* mantra.

Having offered ashes and placed a *rajani* leaf upon them, having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, and having bound it to the middle petal within the King of Weapons (*astrarāja*), one should bind it to the right hand— along with the *triyaṃbaka* mantra— of the consecrated images (*bhakta-bera*) starting from the seat;

and for the female images (*strī-bera*) such as Gaurī and others, one should bind it to the hand with the root-mantra of Gaurī, as well as for oneself, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), and the bearer of the sacrificial offering (*balivāhaka*).

Having tied the protective cord (*kautuka*) for Raṭāḍaka and the ten weapons, one should apply ashes and turmeric powder over it; then, having placed the cord upon the middle of the flagstaff, one should bind it very firmly with a rope along with flower-garlands. One should cause turmeric powder, gold, betel nuts, betel leaves, and so forth to be given to all. This is the procedure for the binding of the protective cord (*rakṣābandhana-vidhi*).
Thus: *Obeisance to the glorious Ekāmranātha*. Then follows the offering (*bali*).

[The Bali Offering: At a great festival, the *bali* offering should be performed in the evening or in the morning, extending either from the station of Brahmā (*brahmasthāna*) up to the flagpole (*dhvaja*), or from the bull and other deities up to the *balipīṭha*. It is as follows:

in the stations beginning with that of Brahmā, one should prepare a square measuring one cubit in width, half a cubit in height, and twelve or eight finger-breadths in thickness, provided with three girdles (*mekhalā*). One hundred... [the rest of the line is illegible].

Having fashioned a pedestal (*pīṭha*) made of stone, or else made of brick or fine wood, endowed with the characteristics of a *kaika-pīṭha* consisting of a pericarp and eight petals; having constructed the pedestals with their respective marks and having smeared them [with plaster], and having adorned the cardinal directions accordingly, one should worship it with a *droṇa* or half of that [measure] of [grain], and taking a vessel for the oblation (*balipātra*), having sprinkled it with the *astra-mantra*, [one should place it] in another pot.

Having brought half of that [measure], one should fashion an image of the food (*annaliṅga*) endowed with the proper characteristics: twelve finger-breadths in height, its circumference being four finger-breadths, and its pedestal (*pīṭha*) two finger-breadths; having prepared it thus, and having smeared it and installed it according to the rules, one should perform meditation (*dhyāna*).
The three-eyed, four-armed deity, wearing a crown of matted hair,
with hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and holding a rosary in his left hand;
(fourth line) joined with a trident in the right, fierce, and endowed with a piercing gaze.
Adorned with serpent ornaments, with hair standing erect and eyes cast downward.

One should worship this divine cloth-painting (*paṭa*) in the center of the *liṅga*. Alternatively, having worshipped Śiva as before, the preceptor (*ācārya*), together with the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), accompanied by the ten weapons and the king of missiles,

adorned from the sacred ash up to the turban (*uṣṇīṣa*), accompanied by attendants, and provided with various banners, parasols, chowries, and so forth, along with the sounds of various musical instruments, bells, [offerings of] clarified butter, and the chanting of the Vedas (*brahmaghoṣa*), together with the chief dancers and their singers— [should perform the rite].
One should offer the *bali* at the festival of the new [initiation].
The specific *bali* offerings for the deities are stated in sequence: on the first day, *oṃ hāṃ vighnarājāya svāhā*; on the second, *bhūtebhyaḥ svāhā*;
on the third, *ṛṣibhyaḥ svāhā*; on the fourth, *indrāya svāhā*; on the fifth, *brahmaṇe svāhā*; on the sixth, *viṣṇave svāhā*; on the seventh, *indrāya svāhā*.

On the eighth day, [one offers] "Svāhā to Īśvara"; on the ninth, "Svāhā to Sadāśiva. During these days, at the conclusion of the worship of the *liṅga* with the oblation (*havir-liṅga-pūjā*), one should perform the following: one should cast [into the fire] an offering of pure rice mixed with clarified butter (*ājya*), soaked in that [butter], and the size of a hen's egg. As for the special oblation (*viśeṣa-bali*) in the cow-pen: "Oṃ hāṃ, Svāhā to Indra; Svāhā to Kumbhodara. [The offering] is made upon *kuśa* grass.
(... *svāhā* to Kāyī; in the rivers, *svāhā* to Gaṅgā; in the pond, *svāhā* to Kṣetramūrti; in the assembly hall, *svāhā* to Sarasvatī;

*svāhā* to Durgā; in the treasury, *svāhā* to Mahālakṣmī; at the gate-tower, *svāhā* to Bhīma. In this manner, one should offer the bali-oblation in the evening and in the morning. Or, [one may offer] from the station of Brahmā down to the end of the bali-altar. Having entered [the temple], one should cast the remainder upon the bali-altar. Having discarded the food-offering into water, washed one's feet, sipped water for purification (*ācamana*), and smeared oneself with pure ashes, one should enter.
[Thus ends the procedure for the circumambulation with offerings. Homage to the illustrious Ekāmranātha. Now begins the procedure for the processional rite (*yānakramavidhi*).
The procedure is as previously described; having fully adorned [the deity], [he is placed] upon the chariot on the stage... (4th line).

Or else, having brought the deity together with Śakti— adorned with various ornaments and joined with flowers— to the location of the primary *liṅga*, and having invoked and worshipped [the deity], offered incense and lamps, and worshipped with a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), one should begin the circumambulation accompanied by the devotee’s image (*bhakta-bera*) such as Śakti and others. In front [of the deity] is gathered a collection of various ornaments.

The preceptor, accompanied by the sounds of drums and other instruments, should perform the rites for Śiva and the others in the intervals between them; in the center, Nandin, Vināyaka, and Subrahmaṇya; in the middle, Somāskanda together with the Goddess; in front, [the image of] Soma; behind, the images of the devotees; and after that, Caṇḍeśvara. Standing on his left side, he should recite the Mūla-mantra or the Aghora-mantra the prescribed number of times. In front stands the King, and behind... [the rest of the line].

The sacrificer’s servants for the deity, male and female dancers, flute-players, singers, and drummers [are stationed] on both sides; [in front are] the Rudra-prostitutes adorned with garlands; in the foreground is the Great [Deity]; behind them follow the Māheśvaras born of the four castes, accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas and other hymns. They obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Having thus gratified the God, on the first day, [they perform] the *raṅga* in the morning and the *haṃsa* at night.

On the second day, [he should perform] the Sūryasoma-yantra. On the third day, in the morning, the Bhūta-yantra; at night, the Siṃha. On the fourth day, in the morning, the Nāga; at night, he should perform the serving of food in the interval following the circumambulation of the Bull. For example: in a courtyard or open space within a garden, accompanied by Vedic hymns, the Vedas, lutes, flutes, singers, dancers, and the Rudra-prostitutes, with offerings of fruits and other gifts.

Having gratified the Lord at every step with betel leaves and other offerings, one should lead Him into the temple. On the fifth day, [the image] should be placed upon a palanquin equipped with a Rāvaṇa-machine on its top. On the sixth day, having mounted [the image] upon a palanquin or a chariot, one should perform the powder festival as will be described, and [bathe] the deities with water infused with saffron, safflower, turmeric, and so forth.

Having sprinkled [the elephant] with water and smeared all the deities with saffron paste, one should sprinkle [them again]. At night, [one should perform this for] the elephant; on the seventh day, for the chariot;

on the eighth day, having performed the mounting ceremony (*sāropaṇa*), at the time of departure, those mounted on horses—equipped with cruel weapons such as bows, shields, and so forth—and the Rudra-attendants (*rudragaṇikā*) adorned with all ornaments, [should surround it] on all sides.

They should proceed. In the meantime, having suppressed the wicked and protected the righteous, and having caused all the *dharmas* to be heard, he should cause [the image] to enter the temple. On the ninth day, at night, [he should place] black incense on a palanquin (*dolaka*) equipped with a human-machine (*puruṣayantra*). On the tenth day, having seated the deity upon a jeweled lion-throne (*ratnasiṃhāsana*), [he should lead him] into the city...

Having circumambulated [the deity], one should carry the prepared food around the top of the palace or the top of the flagstaff and cast it at a crossroads. Immediately thereafter, the preceptor, along with married women (*suvāsinī*) or female attendants of Rudra (*rudragaṇikā*), should perform the *nīrāñjana* rite. Then, having offered a lamp in a water-pot (*ghaṭadīpa*) to the deity, one should subsequently perform the *ārātrika* and *nīrāñjana* rites while holding the lamp-vessel in one's hands.

The attendants of Rudra, accompanied by dancing, singing, and all types of musical instruments, shall perform circumambulations in due order; then, together with Śailādi, Nandin, Vināyaka, Skanda, Devī, Bhakta, and Caṇḍeśvara, they should circumambulate [the deity] in the morning and proceed to the temple.
Thereafter, accompanied by those singing auspicious songs and all musical instruments, they should go to the temple of Somāskanda.

Having caused [them] to enter and established them in the pavilion for the [deity's] abode and other locations, having drawn a curtain, and having offered a great oblation, one should worship with all ritual services. To remove their fatigue, one should offer coconuts, sugarcane juice, mung beans, and fruits appropriate to the season, and having worshipped with all ritual services, [one should honor] the Brahmins.

Having adorned [the image] with perfumes and flowers, one should feed it. One should feed those devoted to Śiva and others, as well as the blind and so forth, with due consideration. Alternatively, one may perform the procession in another manner; such is the procedure for the rite of the procession. Now follows the procedure for the *nīrājana* rite.
[The Procedure for the *Nīrājana* Rite]

For the purpose of *nīrājana*, one should take vessels made of gold, silver, or bell-metal, which are five finger-breadths in width and height and have a rim of one finger-breadth; having placed them upon the mandala and worshipped them with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, as well as with the fire-seed syllable (*agnibīja*) and the Brahma-mantras, one should worship them thus:

"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Brahmā (*brahmāsana*); Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Brahmā (*brahmamūrti*); Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā. Having worshipped them in this manner, [one should perform] the four purificatory rites (*catuḥ-saṃskāra*).

(4th line) Having consecrated [the deity], having displayed the *triśūla-mudrā* and the *dhenu-mudrā*, and taking a lamp with vessels of clarified butter (*sarpis*) accompanied by auspicious hymns (*svasti-sūkta*),

(5th line) placing it upon his head, circumambulating [the deity], and establishing it within the mandala before the deity, [he should perform the rite] three times from the head down to the feet of the deity. (6th line)

Having circumambulated three times with the [three] forms, and having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) to Śiva with the root mantra while holding a mirror, umbrella, chowrie, fan, and ashes... having prostrated, and having had [the deity] escorted as before by courtesans accompanied by musical instruments and the like, one should cast [the deity] into the water along the bank... having performed the washing of the feet and other rites.
"One should not enter the *liṅga*," thus concludes the procedure for the lustration (*nīrājana*). Now follows the procedure for collecting the sacred waters (*tīrtha-saṃgrahaṇa-vidhi*).
[The Procedure for Collecting Sacred Waters] Now, on the day prior to the pilgrimage site, one should collect the sacred waters. [The protective mantras for the waters... (3rd line)

Having performed [the rites] as before and caused the benedictions to be recited, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) in the center of the pavilion. Having drawn an eight-petaled lotus in its center, one should place the "mind-transcending" (*manonmanikara*) [deity] upon it, and arrange eight water-jars (*karkarī*) around it. In the center, [one should offer]: *Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the seat of Manonmanī*. *Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the form of Manonmanī*.

She is absorbed in meditation, possessing the luster of a distant river, three-eyed, with the digit of the nectar-moon as her crest-ornament, clad in red garments, weary from the weight of her full, high, and swelling breasts, and established in the bloom of youth.

Having meditated thus: "I worship that Ambikā, who is adorned with various ornaments, whose abode is the lotus, whose form is transferred from the seed-syllable, who is the God [Śiva] endowed with the noose and goad, and whose hands grant the gestures of fearlessness and boons"—[one should worship her with:
*Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Manonmanī*. Having worshipped [her], [one should worship] in the eight jars starting from the east: *Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Gaṅgā*; *Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Yamunā*.

Salutation! Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Narmadā; oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Sarasvatī; oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Sindhu; oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Godāvarī; oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Kāverī; oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Tāmraparṇī.

Having thus worshipped with the mantras of the forms beginning with the seat (*āsana*) and so forth, and with the ritual services (*upacāra*) such as invocation (*āvāhana*), one should carry [the deity] upon the head.

Having circumambulated the city together with the pitchers equipped with missiles and accompanied by all musical instruments, one should proceed for the purpose of bathing at river-banks and other holy sites (tīrthas). This is the procedure for the collection of holy sites (tīrthasaṃgrahaṇavidhiḥ). Now follows the procedure for the powder festival (cūrṇotsavavidhiḥ).
On the days for the collection of the sacred sites (*tīrtha*), one should begin the powder preparation after midday.

Having drawn an eight-petaled lotus upon two sacrificial mounds (*sthaṇḍila*) at the front of the temple, and having caused the declaration of the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, and having strewn it around with *darbha* grass and flowers, one should place a trident on one of them.

Then, having fashioned the *ugra-khala* and pestle from trees such as *plakṣa*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, and *vaṭa*, and the [pestle] from *khadira* wood according to the prescribed characteristics, they should be installed by others.

Having sprinkled [the items] with the Astra-mantra and consecrated them with the four purificatory rites (saṃskāras), one should wrap the mortar (ulūkhala) and pestle (musala) in a cloth. Then, thinking "Brahmā is the presiding deity," one should worship the Rudra-vessel (rudrakumbha) between the two, as well as the eight jars of the world-protectors (lokapāla) all around; or alternatively, having worshipped Śiva, one should place dūrvā grass together with [other materials] upon the petals starting from the east, all around the mortar.

Having placed the Devīkoṣṭha, turmeric oil, ghee, betel nut, fruit, incense, flowers, and ashes, and having consecrated it with the four purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), one should worship the mortar (*ulūkhala*) with "Oṃ Hāṃ,

obeisance to Pṛthivī" (*pṛthivyai namaḥ*). Then, having worshipped the pestle (*musala*) with "Oṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to Mount Meru" (*meruparvatāya namaḥ*), one should cast [the substances] into that mortar while reciting the *pada-mantra*.

The preceptor, having taken that powder— which has been ground by courtesans using a pestle and mortar, brought in a vessel along with turmeric and other ingredients, and mixed with oil, fragrance, and water for the *arghya* offering— along with gold, and having consecrated it, should cause it to be applied together with ashes to the primary *liṅga*. Then, having placed a turban of saffron upon it and smeared it with its paste...

Having caused [the offerings] to be given to the Brahmins, having adorned them with flowers, and having presented the food offering (*naivedya*) and so forth, one should display the lotus mudrā; then, holding it oneself and causing it to be given to all, and having offered the *uṣṇīṣa*, *rajanīphala*, betel, and so on, and having given these to the Brahmins and the *ichas*, one should circumambulate the city and so forth together with the trident and enter the temple.

Then, having installed the weapon-vessel (*astrakumbha*) and the vessels for the thunderbolt (*vajra*) and other [emblems], having sprinkled them with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), and having consecrated them with the four purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), [one should worship them with]: Oṃ hāṃ vajrāya namaḥ | Oṃ hāṃ śaktaye namaḥ | Oṃ hāṃ daṇḍāya namaḥ | Oṃ hāṃ khaḍgāya namaḥ | Oṃ hāṃ pāśāya namaḥ | Oṃ hāṃ dhvajāya namaḥ | Oṃ hāṃ gadāya namaḥ | Oṃ hāṃ...

*Oṃ, salutation to the trident; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the lotus; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the discus.* Having worshipped with these and other [mantras], one should cause the powder to be reduced to ash. This is the procedure for the festival of the powder (*cūrṇotsava*).

Thereafter, having performed the rite of the sprouts (*aṅkura*) as before, one should perform the ritual bath at a sacred ford (*tīrthasnāna*). This is for the sake of removing the fault of being touched by all those who are untouchable (*aspṛśya*).

For the sake of accomplishing the grace of the sacred ford (*tīrtha*), for the sake of bringing pleasure to all the gods, for the sake of attaining the fruits of dharma and so forth, and for the sake of reaching the state of *sāloka* and other realms, [he] established a water-station (*prapā*) on the bank of the sacred ford according to his ability, accompanied by the King of Mantras (*astrarāja*), Soma, Skanda, and others, along with sprouts, parasols, chowries, various musical instruments, the chanting of the Vedas, and hymns of praise, together with the ritual jars of the sacred ford and its attendants.

Having established the deities upon the altar (sthaṇḍila) at that site, having placed the eight pitchers beginning with Gaṅgā in the center of Manonmani, and having specifically arranged a thousand *pālikā* vessels and worshipped them, [one should worship] in the northeast: "Om Hrīṃ, obeisance to the seat of Durgā.
[One should meditate on her] as resembling thousands of millions of rising suns, with a gentle smile upon a single fang.

One should meditate upon the Great Bhairavī Durgā, who bestows the fruits of the practitioner’s desired aims; she wears a crown with the luster of a moon adorned with red [gems], her ears are radiant with earrings, and she holds a sword, a shield, a shining discus, and a conch— the destroyer of the Daityas.

Having worshipped with "Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to the form of Durgā; Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to Durgā," one should perform the invocation of the thirty-three crores of deities, the eighteen Gaṇas, and the world-protectors (lokapālas) in the vicinity of the trident. Having released the *kautuka* (protective thread) of the deities beginning with the Weapon-mantra (*astra*), and having cast it into the midst of the holy water (*tīrtha*), one should perform the ritual bath together with all [the participants], from Śiva down to the Weapon-mantra, using those jars along with the *pālikās*.

Then the preceptor, having dismissed the deities of the sacred sites (*tīrthadeva*) and entered the sanctuary, consecrated the respective water-pots (*kumbha*) of all the deities with offerings of food, incense, lamps, and so forth.

Having entered [the hall], while all [the participants] stand in the assembly area accompanied by the chanting of the *brahmaghoṣa*, they place auspicious parched grains (*āślakṣata*) into the hands of the preceptor; the instructor, preceded by a blessing, [bestows them].
One should cause [the deity] to enter its respective place; this is the procedure for bathing at a sacred ford (tīrtha-snāna-vidhi). Now follows the procedure for the jar-bath (ghaṭa-snāna-vidhi).
[The Procedure for the Jar-Bath]

For the fulfillment of the festival of Hara, for the stabilization of the people, for the attainment of divine grace, and for the attainment of proximity to the deities such as Indra, one should perform the ritual bathing of the jar (*ghaṭasnāna*). Having specifically performed the fire-oblation (*homa*) in the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*), they should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) in the principal pit with the root mantra. Having joined the respective Lord into the principal [deity] and having worshipped Śiva—

Again, having offered the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), having especially worshipped the Śiva-pitcher (*śivakumbha*) and the others, having joined [the ritual fires] and offered incense and lamps, having given the prescribed sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor (*ācārya*) and others,
and having given garments, gold, and so forth to the attendants and others, one should lift the pitchers as before and [enter] the temple.

Having circumambulated [the shrine] and entered the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*), one should install [the deity] upon the primary *liṅga* (*mūlaliṅga*) after first performing the deposition of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvanyāsa*). Having consecrated the *vardhanī* vessel on the pedestal and the jars of the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśakalaśa*) in their respective places, one should consecrate the Goddess with a jar while preceded by the *śrīkaṇṭhanyāsa*. After offering the great sacrificial oblation (*mahāhavis*) and presenting incense, lamps, and so forth, one should proceed to the fire-sanctuary. In the Śiva-fire, having offered more than a hundred oblations with the head-mantra (*śiras*), the root-mantra (*mūla*), and the *aghora-āsinā*, and having given the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), [one should attend to] the fire.

Having joined [the deity] with the Lord of Sacrifice (*yāgeśa*) according to the method taught by the Guru, and having joined the deities of the five enclosures (*pañcāvaraṇa*), such as those of the water-pot (*kumbha*) and the ewer (*vardhanī*), in their respective places, one should also dismiss him. Having offered abundant sacrificial food (*havir*), one should perform the ceremonial bath (*snapana*) for the image. This is the procedure for the pot-bath (*ghaṭasnāna*). Homage to the venerable Gurus.
[The Ritual for Descent]
For the purpose of suppressing the wicked and protecting the virtuous, on a holy day during the forenoon and so forth— or at night— after the recitation of the *tāla* [instrumental music] (line 4),

one should first perform the descent (*avarohaṇa*) of the deity in the most excellent manner; thus, for the sake of the banner, having yoked the bull to the [chariot], one should also place the bull before Śiva (line 5).

Having mounted [the deity] upon the bull and having joined the deities of the enclosure to their respective enclosures, one should worship them according to the prescribed rite. On that day, there is the silent offering (*maunabali*).

Since it has been stated that at the conclusion of the *homa* an oblation portion is for the deities, one should commence that supreme silent offering. The Preceptor, having gone near Soma and Skanda, and having worshipped [the deities] from Śakti down to Śaktiparyanta, should perform the deposition of the thirty-six principles (*ṣaṭtriṃśatkalānyāsa*)—namely the *daṇḍabhaṅgi*, *muṇḍabhaṅgi*, and [others]—as well as the *Śrīkaṇṭhanyāsa*.
One should meditate upon Kṛṣṇa, whose left foot is bent and resting upon his right leg which is tucked up in sleep, and who holds a deer, the gesture of fearlessness,
an axe, and a bracelet in his left hands.

I worship the Lord of Soma and Guha, who is joined by the Goddess whose other two feet are asleep, leaning upon his left [arm], and who is accompanied by Skanda holding two lotuses in his hands. (5th line) Having thus meditated and worshipped him along with his limbs and the fivefold enclosure (*pañcāvaraṇa*), and having meditated upon and worshipped the God and Goddess who will be described hereafter, [one recites]: *Oṃ Hrīṃ*.
Salutation to Manonmanī for the seat.
She stands in the *ardhaparyaṅka* posture with her left foot hanging down,
endowed with the splendor of the moon, possessing two arms and three eyes.
With her hands resting upon the pedestal, holding a lotus in her hand, she stands to the left of the Lord, positioned beside the celestial woman.

"Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the form of Manonmanī; Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Manonmanī. Having thus invoked and worshipped [the deity], and having prayed to Śambhu, the Lord of the World, and received permission from him, one should assume the vow of silence with palms joined in *añjali*.

Then, having placed upon the vehicle the weapons and deities beginning with Astra—equipped with food as their *liṅga* and accompanied by perfumes, flowers, and so forth, as well as swords, shields, and other weapons—one should [place them] many times in the heart.

Recalling [the deities], observing a vow of silence, and without the sound of musical instruments, [they should offer] at the joints beginning with the Brahma-sthāna, in the *pīṭhas*, or in their respective locations, an oblation (*bali*) the size of a hen’s egg, accompanied by the sounding of musical instruments and preceded by the hoisting of the banner. Having performed this, they should dismiss the deities of the joints in due order as before; then, having circumambulated the temple, entered it, descended, and placed [the banner] in the previously designated spot.

One should dismiss all [the deities] into the water of the *liṅga*; this is the procedure for the *avarohaṇa* (descent). Homage to the venerable Gurus. Now follows the procedure for the *Caṇḍotsava* (festival of Caṇḍa).
[The Procedure for the Caṇḍotsava]
