Then, having invited Caṇḍamūrti into the sacrificial hall and consecrated him with the water from that [cauldron], preceded by the worship of the seat arising from the six syllables: *oṃ hāṃ caṇḍāsanāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*.
[He is] one-faced, with his right hand resembling a makara and holding a battle-axe, and his left hand resting upon his thigh.
[He saw] Śiva, who wears white garments, carries sacred ash, and possesses a fierce devotion consisting of meditation upon the feet of the Lord.
*Oṃ hāṃ caṇḍamūrtaye huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*.

*Oṃ hāṃ caṇḍāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*. Having worshipped with all the ritual offerings (*upacāra*) consisting of the invocation (*āvāhana*), and having discarded the remains of the offerings (*nirmālya*) and so forth, one should offer a hundred, a thousand, or half that number of oblations into the expiatory fire (*prāyaścittāgni*). Then, having led [the deity] back into the temple (*ālaya*) by means of the three [mantras], one should circumambulate together with the devotees and [re-establish the deity] in its place.
"One should cause [the deity] to enter"—this is the procedure for the festival of Caṇḍa. Homage to the venerable Gurus.
[The Procedure for the Festival of the Ācārya]
Thereafter, one should worship the preceptor and cause him to receive a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā);
one should cause to be given cows, land, gold, jewels, and so forth, as well as clothing.
"The preceptor is satisfaction through the mind; therefore, Śiva is the supreme satisfaction.

Having thus worshipped him along with the officiating priests (ṛtvij) like Śiva himself, and having placed him upon a chariot or a palanquin, he should, accompanied by various musical instruments, dances, songs, the chanting of the Vedas, hymns of devotion, umbrellas, chowries, and various kinds of lamps, circumambulate the city together with the patron, the king, and all the people, and enter his own home at the time of departure. This is the festival of the preceptor (ācāryotsava).
The ritual procedure.
Salutations to the venerable gurus.
[The Ritual for Ascending the Chariot]

On the seventh or ninth day, the mounting of the chariot (*rathārohaṇa*) should be performed. On the preceding night, having performed the binding of the protection cord (*rakṣābandhana*), and in the morning, having completed everything such as the ritual bathing (*snāna*) and so forth, and having performed [the rites] at the conclusion of the daily worship (*nityapūjā*) according to the rules, one should worship [the deity] duly. Following the path prescribed for the noble fire (*agnirārya*), one should perform everything up to the oblation of the *caru* and the expiatory rite (*prāyaścitta*) using *dūrvā* grass; then, with the root mantra, one offers clarified butter (*ājya*), and with the *Īśa* mantra, the ritual action is performed with the *Ghora-hṛdaya* mantra.

Having offered parched grain with the *vāmā* mantra, sesame with the *kavaca*, molasses with the *netra*, and the *bali* offering with the *mūla* mantra; having offered substances and grains in the northeast (*īśāna*) along with the oblation (*āhuti*) known as the *hṛdaya*;

having performed the *pūrṇāhuti*; having bound the Lord of Sacrifice (*yāgeśa*); and having entrusted him to protection—one should present a full water-pot and a cow with its calf to the Brahmins. Having fully worshipped Vighneśa, one should offer sweetmeats (*modaka*) and offer milk-rice (*pāyasa*).

Afterwards, having prepared [the offering] in a silver cauldron with saffron, agallochum, camphor, sandalwood, turmeric, and so forth— or having placed flowers such as *pāṭala*, blue lotus, and jasmine, along with fresh mud from a *campaka* tree and the like into the cauldron— one should wrap the cauldron with saffron-colored cloth and other materials, place it upon a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) before Śiva, worship it in the cauldron with the Kāma-bīja, worship the fresh [mud] with the root mantra, perform the consecration, and offer incense and lamps.

(5th line) Having likewise given [the offerings] to the primary liṅga and the others, the preceptor himself, together with the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), should don a turban moistened with mud and saffron; then he should give turbans moistened with mud to the king, the patron (*yajamāna*), the devotees, and all other people. Afterwards, having sprinkled the chariot with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and the water of the *puṇyāha* rite, [he should perform] the four purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) upon the chariot.

Having consecrated [the deity] and having placed a god upon it, one should remain there and worship all the gods on the chariot. On the wheels: *oṃ hāṃ sūryāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ candramase namaḥ*. Around [the chariot]: *namaḥ haraye*, *namaḥ vajriṇe*, *namaḥ etāṅghraye*, *namaḥ dvidaṇḍakāya*. Having thus worshipped, [one should worship] on the banners...

Having worshipped the hundred Rudras, and having worshipped Dharma and the others upon the limbs, one should worship with "Oṃ Sadāśivāya namaḥ" in the cooking vessel; with "Oṃ Dakṣiṇāmūrtaye namaḥ" at the joints; (5th line) with "Oṃ Viṣṇave namaḥ," "Oṃ Brahmaṇe namaḥ," and "Oṃ Skandāya namaḥ," thus having performed the worship, one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) at the edge of the chariot; with "Oṃ Ūrubhyāṃ namaḥ" and "Oṃ Vedhase namaḥ" on the ropes; and on the four [corners]. (F31b, 1st line)
Having worshipped in this manner in the various directions in sequence,

and having made the banner highly beautiful with variegated cloth, clusters of *saṃhaga*, *dalī*, and *pūga* fruits, coconuts, and so forth, one should meditate upon the Brahmāṇḍa [as the pedestal] and invoke the Lord of the Gods (Śiva), together with his weapons, into the banner.
Having worshipped the Bull, one should meditate upon him:
five-colored, very subtle, bestowing fearlessness and the boon of granting wishes,
six-footed, with a single belly, four-armed, and holding a trident and a noose.
Jāṅghikā has one face, three eyes, six spots, is endowed with auspiciousness,
is joined with the *palāśa* tree and the discus, and is the support of all beings.
The mature region is called *sujānu*; the pelvic region consists of the thighs.
The abdominal region is declared to be the seat of the gods (*devāsana*), while the heart region belongs to the class of pillars (*stambhavargaka*).
The peak is said to be the two shoulders, and the throat is called the axle.
The head is the top of the pole, and the crest is ordained as the charioteer.
This meditation on the chariot is proclaimed as the cause of all auspiciousness.
Having meditated thus, one should perform worship. In this manner,
having mounted the Goddess, Skanda, Vināyaka, and Caṇḍeśvara upon their respective chariots, having smeared them with fresh mud and saffron, having donned the *uṣṇīṣa* and *kavaca* mantras,

having offered fruits, cakes, and other edibles, having honored them with red flowers, and having given gifts of gold and so forth, [one should bestow] garments and gold upon the preceptor and other devotees.

Having given fruits, betel leaves, and other offerings, and having satisfied everyone, at an auspicious moment during the favorable portion of a movable *lagna*, he circumambulated the city—which was accompanied by all manner of musical instruments—preceded by benedictions.

Then, descending from his chariot and entering the temple, he performed the ceremonial bath (*abhiṣeka*) for the deity. Having bestowed garments and other gifts upon the artisans and those who controlled the chariot, he held a great [festival].

Having offered the oblation (*havis*) to all, one should cause it to be given; such is the procedure for mounting the chariot (*rathārohaṇavidhi*). Salutations to the glorious Ekāmranātha. Hereafter follows the procedure for the black ointment (*kṛṣṇagandhavidhi*). [The Procedure for the Black Ointment] (second line).

Whoever— be they anyone at all— beholds the form of the Dancing One, attains the fruit [of their desire]: the accomplishment of desired objects, the cause for obtaining a virtuous son, the destruction of faults such as the killing of a Brahmin, and the total eradication of all enemies.

Thereafter, having brought the image of Nṛtta-Mūrti to the assembly hall (*āsthānamaṇṭapa*), and having performed the protection ritual (*rakṣā*) as before on the night following the eighth day, one should place fruits, betel, and other offerings in both hands, adorn both [the image and the officiant] with variegated garments and so forth, and bind a protective thread (*rakṣā*) on the left hand with the *Gaurī-mūla-mantra*. Having offered the food offering (*naivedya*) and so forth, and having circumambulated the temple, one should install [the image] in the assembly hall.

One should pass the remainder of the night by means of diversions. On the following day, having concluded the festival, one should prepare two sacrificial mounds (*sthaṇḍila*) before the deity in the evening;

having drawn a lotus and strewn it with *darbha* grass and flowers, one should place black aloe-wood (*kālāguru*) in its center, perform the worship of Vināyaka, and cause the proclamation of the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited.

Having prepared the *śāntikumbha* according to the rules and having worshipped it, and having performed the rites beginning with the consecration of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) up to the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) by the path prescribed for the fire-ritual, and having worshipped Maheśa therein, one should offer fuel-sticks, parched grain, mustard seeds, barley, sesame seeds, and so forth, each one hundred and eight times with their respective root-mantras; and likewise [offer] wood-apple, lotus, plantain, jackfruit, and so forth.

Having offered the three types of honey and, at the conclusion of the substances, having offered with the *vyāhṛtis* and given the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should worship and adorn the deity. Then,

having placed black fragrant paste into a vessel filled with rice, wrapped it with cloth, sprinkled it with water from the *śāntikumbha*, mixed it with camphor and other perfumes, and purified it with the *astra-mantra*:

Having covered [the deity] with the *varman* [armor-mantra], consecrated it with the *brahmāṅga* [limb-mantras], and worshipped it with the root mantra (*mūla*), one should display the *dhenumudrā* with the root mantra. Having offered water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), the guest-offering (*arghya*), incense (*dhūpa*), lamps (*dīpa*), and so forth, and having performed the *saṃpātābhihuta* oblations and the *pūrṇāhuti*, one should dismiss the fire. Then, accompanied by the sounding of conchs, drums, and musical instruments, one should circumambulate the temple, enter the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*), and unite [the deity] with the primary *liṅga*. Immediately thereafter, having established [the deity] before Maheśa on the seat beginning with Śakti and ending with Śakti, [one should proceed].
And by means of the sequence of the breaking of the staff and the breaking of the head, one should meditate upon Śrīkaṇṭha, who consists of thirty-one kalās and who bears the matted locks,
the moon, the golden *kurari* bird, the severed heads, the bones, the celestial river, the white sun, the tree, and the five kings.

He possesses supreme Vaiya-tya, holding a serpent in his right hand and displaying the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) along with a *ḍamaru* drum; he holds fire in his left hand. Reclining upon a bed of green ashes, he stands with his right foot bent and his left foot raised. Situated in the midst of radiance, he is adorned with a banner, small bells, and jewels; on his left ear, he wears a sacrificial earring (*kratukuṇḍala*) encircled by millions of [rays] and decorated with leaves.

Therefore, one should worship the three-eyed Naṭeśa, who is smeared [with ashes] and joined with Umā. Having performed the ritual invocation (*āvāhana*) of the Lord, who consists of twenty-five principles (*kalā*), and having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of Śrīkaṇṭha, one should meditate.
*Oṃ hrīṃ māyāyai namaḥ*—on the head. [................... *namaḥ*—on the face. *Oṃ hrīṃ* [...................]—on the heart. *Oṃ hrīṃ* (F34b, 1st line).

*Śuddhāyai namaḥ* (—) at the throat; *oṃ hrīṃ jarāyai namaḥ* (—) at the belly; [at the right] arm; *oṃ hrīṃ medhāyai namaḥ* (—) at the left arm; *sthūlāyai namaḥ* (—) at the abdomen; *svastyai namaḥ* (—) at the navel; *pālinyai namaḥ* (—) at the womb; [at the] secret place; *tṛṣṇāyai namaḥ* (—) at the right thigh; *smṛtyai namaḥ* (—) at the left thigh. (Third line)

Salutation to Kṣamā on the right knee; salutation to Manonmanī on the two knees; salutation to Prajā on the right shank; salutation to Cintā on the left shank; salutation to Dhṛti on the back; salutation to Kriyā on the right side;
salutation to Kṣānti on the left side; salutation to Śānti on the left foot; salutation to Bhrānti on the right foot. (Fifth line)

Salutation to Dayā (Compassion)—on the right hand; salutation to Smṛti (Memory)—on the left hand; salutation to Dviraṣṭavarṣā (the Eight-year-old)—on the right breast; salutation to Sādhyā—on the left breast; Oṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to the Body of Knowledge (vidyādeha)—at the heart; Oṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to the Three Eyes—at the eyes; salutation to the Heart—at the heart;
salutation to the Head—at the head; salutation to Śivā—at the waist; salutation to the Armor (kavaca)—at the armor.

"Astrāyai namaḥ"—with this, one performs the cleaving of the hands (*karasphāṭana*). Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of Śrīkaṇṭha according to the method described in the aforementioned section, one should meditate upon the Supreme Goddess as follows:
she is dark-complexioned, two-eyed, two-armed, and in a triple-bent posture (*tribhaṅgī*); her right and left feet are placed with the toes tucked in.
She may hold a blue lotus in her right hand, or she may be adorned with bracelets, or she may have her hand resting [on her thigh]. Thus is the Supreme Goddess.

Having thus honored both [deities], and having offered incense and lamps, one should present an offering of flour-cakes (*paiṣṭya*) and milk-rice (*pāyasa*) along with [other items], give betel-leaf (*tāmbūla*), and apply an ointment of black fragrance (*kṛṣṇagandha*). On the forehead, with the *ghora* [mantra], on the crest, on the arm, and on the cloth—[one should cause] the forms of Sadāśiva to be bestowed. For the female images (*strībera*), [this should be done] on the forehead.
One should hold that [substance] at the throat and heart with its root-mantra;

thereafter, one should cause the preceptor and others, ending with the [final] person, to apply black ointment. Having placed the Deity upon a jeweled lion-throne, with Gaurī to His left and the Preceptor to His right, [the performers], whether women or men, should perform both types of dance and movement according to the [prescribed] sequence.

Having performed singing and dancing on both sides accompanied by musical instruments, and having danced as far as the seven-peaked mountain before entering the temple, one should perform the lustration ceremony (*nīrājanā*) and other rites as previously described. (4th line) Thereafter, having established [the deity] in the assembly pavilion (*āsthānamaṇṭapa*), having offered the eight-limbed respectful offering (*sāṣṭāṅga-arghya*), and having presented food offerings (*naivedya*) such as fruit and so forth, one should worship with the lustration ceremony and other rites. (5th line)

Thereafter, having bathed [the image] with cow-products such as milk and so forth, and having consecrated pure camphor as before, one should adorn it by placing fruits and other items on all its limbs, decorating it with very white *jāti* flowers and white garments, offering milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and presenting incense and lamps.
At the time of the procession, the palanquin should be carried very slowly; therein, as before, [one should proceed] with Vedic recitations, dance, song, and so forth.

Having arranged the rows [of deities] and performed the rites beginning with the *nīrājana* as before, he should enter the temple and worship [the deity] with all ritual offerings (*sarvopacāra*). He should pass the remainder of the night by means of viewing various entertainments. At dawn, having worshipped the Lord of Dance (*Nṛtteśa*) and adorned him, he should perform the *tīrtha* rite at a river or similar location as before, and [perform] the *kautuka*.

Having dismissed the city and other [attendants], having performed a circumambulation, and having caused [the king] to hear the proclamation concerning the suppression of the wicked, the protection of the virtuous, and all legal affairs in a pure place; having removed any quarrel regarding the consecrated water (*praṇītā*) of the Goddess; and having entered the palace without [other] retinue, one should establish him in his own place, consecrate him with ablutions and other rites, and have a pure dance performed.
[This is the ritual for the black ointment.]

Immediately thereafter, on the tenth or seventh day, one should perform the auspicious vow festival (kalyāṇavrata-utsava) for the marriage ceremony with the secondary ritual (aupacārika). Next is the procedure for the Goddess festival.
[End of the Procedure for the Goddess Festival]

One should hold a festival for nine days, seven days, three days, or one day. On the eleventh day and night, having decorated everything such as Indra’s celestial chariot (*vimāna*) and having consecrated it with sprinkling (*saṃprokṣya*), and after first performing the ritual bathing (*snāpana*), one should adorn the Lord and his consort. Having placed all the deities upon their respective celestial chariots, at the time of circumambulating the city, one should decorate a water-shed (*prapā*) in the northeast direction with flowers and so forth up to the banners; in its center, [one should place] Śiva residing in the celestial chariot.

Having honored that [image] preceded by the Goddess, and having performed three circumambulations together with Caṇḍeśa, the end of the [procession], the king, the sacrificer, and the musicians, one should cause the display of the "diversion" (*vinoda*)—[the resolution of] the quarrel of love—at the front of the *gopura* or on top of the palace at the time of entering the temple, and then cause it to enter according to the prescribed rite. This is the procedure for the festival of the Goddess. Now follows the procedure for the festival of the devotees (*bhakta*).

[The Ritual for the Festival of the Devotee’s Image] Now, having established the devotee’s image, the *bhera* drum, and so forth, either before the [central] Śiva or in the pavilion (*maṇṭapa*), and having performed the preliminary ablution and consecrated both the mobile and immobile images, one should perform the powder festival (*cūrṇotsava*) as previously described.
Then, the Preceptor (*ācārya*), taking up the devotee’s image, should cause the initiated practitioners (*sādhaka*) and other devotees to receive the powder.

Having offered saffron, the *uṣṇīṣa*, sacred threads, garlands, and so forth, and having praised [the deity] with the hymns of devotees; having given betel-leaf and other offerings to the devotees of Śiva;

having circumambulated the city and entered the temple; having stationed everyone in their respective places; having presented the offerings and given incense and lamps; one should cause [them] to perform the art of singing the praises of Śiva (*śivagānavidyā*) and so forth—this is the procedure for the festival of devotees. On the following day...

Having performed, in due order, the great ablution (*mahāsnāna*) preceded by the *śāntihoma*, *mūrtihoma*, *diśāhoma*, and so forth, and having consecrated [the deity], one should cause the completion of the ritual sequence.

The festival (*utsava*) is said to be fivefold, consisting of maintenance (*sthiti*), emanation (*utpatti*), dissolution (*laya*), concealment (*tirobhāva*), and grace (*anugraha*). This fivefold activity, beginning with creation (*sṛṣṭi*), includes the planting of the sprout (*aṅkurārpaṇa*), the auspicious rite (*kalyāṇa*), and the banner (*dhvaja*).
The act of planting [the tree] is indeed called the "Binding of Protection" (*rakṣābandhana*); it is declared to be the ritual of creation (*sṛṣṭikarman*).
It is joined with the festival of the vehicle (*vāhanotsava*), consisting of fire-offerings (*homakarman*) accompanied by oblations (*balibhṛt*).
The rite of stabilization has been declared; now the rite of withdrawal is described:
it consists of the application of night-powder and the mounting of the chariot.
The festival of black aloe-wood is well-known in the Āgamas;
likewise, the festival of silence is the concealment [of the deity], while grace is bestowed by the Lord of Power.
The affection and dispute at the beginning and end of the day of the *tīrtha* are called *praṇaya* and *kalaha*.
The fivefold activity (*pañcakṛtya*), beginning with creation, is joined to the seed-field (*bījakṣetra*).
[Thus ends the work] composed by the venerable Aghoraśivācārya, whose supreme name is the Supreme Lord (*Parameśvara*).

In the *Kriyākramadyotikā*, the ritual procedure beginning with the festival of the [image] installation (*naijāyakotsava*) and ending with the festival of the [divine] portion (*bhaktotsava*) is completed. Homage to the glorious Ekāmranātha.
[The extensive ritual for the hand-drum (*bṛhattālavidhi*)].

"O best of elephants," and so forth, is the invocation for the twilight rites (*sandhyāvāhana*). "Īśāna" concludes the juncture (*sandhi*). This is the invocation of the deity (*devatāvāhana*). "That which is the Veda of Brahman," and so forth—may he grant his presence upon the divine trident-seat. I proclaim the resounding beat of the drums of the illustrious gods and demons.
[The Monthly Festival].

The moment of transition (*saṃkrānti*) is subtle and difficult to perceive even for those with the eyes of a seer (*piśitekṣaṇa*). At that time, there are thirty *nāḍīs* [of breath] in the form of the zodiacal signs (*rāśimūrti*), beginning from Aries (*meṣa*). This will occur in the meritorious [northern course]; likewise, there are thirty in the southern [course]. In the north, the *nāḍīs* are as previously stated. The transition (*saṃkrānti*) and the equinox (*viṣuva*) are specifically [defined] in that pair within Taurus, Scorpio, Aquarius, and Leo. [This is] the so-called "Viṣṇupada" (*viṣṇupada*).
The fruit beginning with the equinoxes:

O twice-born ones, when the sun’s motion is in Virgo, Gemini, Pisces, and Sagittarius, the six-aśīti sacrifices are most meritorious. There are sixteen nāḍīs before the transit and fifteen after it; in Libra and Aries, however, there are ten on both sides. Now, regarding the sacrificial oblation for Viṣṇu, listen... [end of fragment].
Likewise, during the *māna*, the *viśeṣa-ṣaḍaśītimukha*, and when the *uttarāyaṇa* has passed; at the *rāstu-darśana-saṃkrānti*, the end of a marriage, and during times of increase (*vṛddhi*);

one should perform bathing, giving, and other rites, as well as optional vows (*kāmyavrata*) at night. Furthermore, one should perform the festival of the gods and the worship of Śiva at that very time. As for those *nāḍīs* (moments) that are joined together—those [are the auspicious ones].

These are remembered as most meritorious. Then, at the time of the transit of the sun (*saṃkrānti*), having likewise performed the bathing and other rites as before, one should consecrate the deity; having adorned the primary *liṅga* and other icons with all ornaments, accompanied by all musical instruments, and together with the images of Vināyaka, Soma, Skanda, and other deities of the devotees, [one should proceed] to the village or—

Having led [the bull] clockwise around its former dwelling, one should place it in the Brahma-position, perform the [ritual] beginning with the Vṛṣa... and so forth, and then settle it in its own place. Thus, when this is performed in the kingdom, no monthly defects arise; therefore, with every effort, one should celebrate the festival... This is the procedure for the festival.
Now, the procedure for the fortnightly festival (*pakṣotsava-vidhi*). On the fourteenth day of the waning moon, when the moon has descended to its eighth part, it becomes a subtle *kīla* once again.

When the moon is half-visible, it is known as Vālī; when the moon has vanished, it is considered Kuhū. [In the middle... having invoked Amāvāsya, that which subsequently proceeds is to be known as Bhūtasiddhā;

she constitutes the fifteenth *nāḍī*. Even if there is but one *ghaṭikā* of Amāvāsya and the first day (*pratipat*) follows immediately, Bhūtasiddhā must be employed for rites directed toward the gods (*daiva*).

Regarding rites for the ancestors (*pitṛ-karma*), if the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*) or the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) extends into the forenoon (*pūrvāhna*), it should be performed as if it were the [preceding] fourteenth day (*bhūta-siddha*). For rites for the gods (*daiva-karma*), [the time is] always [during the sun's northern course] when [the sun is] in Capricorn or Pisces; likewise, even if it is the fourteenth day, the new moon in Virgo or Gemini [is suitable].

One should diligently honor the full fourteenth day here; however, even if the festival falls on the fourteenth, it should be celebrated on the fifteenth (bhūtā). One should perform the pilgrimage on the new moon (amā); indeed, the new moon serves as a barrier against the Vedas.

If the seventh lunar day falls on a Sunday, or the fourth on a Tuesday, the fruit is equal to that of the equinox. If the new moon falls on a Monday, it becomes equal to Śivarātri; one should perform a vigil during the night.
Then one should perform the festival of the deity when the new moon (amāvāsyā) falls on the lunar mansion Ārdrā;
if it also coincides with a Monday, it is equal to ten million sacrifices, ascetic penances, and gifts.

One obtains the fruit from that vow. (4th line) Now, on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), having performed the great consecration (*mahābhiṣeka*) preceded by the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) for the installation and removal of the primary lingas and so forth, and having adorned them with all ornaments; having offered the great sacrificial oblation (*mahāhavis*); and without the procession of offerings (*balibhramaṇa*) in villages, market towns, and the like—[the rite is performed] together with an umbrella and chowries, accompanied by many various lamps. (F40b, 1st line)

Having led the deity, accompanied by various musical instruments, in a circumambulation and brought him to the station of Brahmā, one should perform the *nīrājana* and other rites as before and then install him in his own place. The mortal who acts in this manner shall attain a meritorious state. One desiring sons obtains sons; one desiring a wife obtains a beautiful maiden; one desiring wealth obtains abundant riches; and one desiring liberation attains liberation. [He ensures that] there is no untimely rain...

"Parjanya shall be free from disease and free from calamity; by means of the New Moon festival alone, one shall obtain all desires. Thus ends the procedure for the New Moon festival. Now follows the procedure for the Full Moon festival.
[The Procedure for the Full Moon Festival]

Rākā and Anumati are considered to be the two Paurṇamāsīs; that which is the earlier Paurṇamāsī is Anumati, and the latter is Rākā. The end of the fortnight, known as the fifteenth day, is traditionally called Paurṇamāsī.
On the sixteenth day it is called *abhīṣṭā* (desired); on the fifteenth it is *madhyā* (middling);

on the fourteenth it is *jaghanyā* (lowest). On the seventeenth day, all the lunar days (*pratipad*) and the *bhūta*s are for the purpose of offering (*samarpaṇā*) from sunrise to sunrise; they are renowned in divine rites as *pāvanī* (purifying).
The Yamāgni (third), Yamabhūta (fourth), and the two [tithis] of the six Munis (fifth and sixth); the twelfth joined with the eleventh (Rudra), and the full moon joined with the fourteenth;
the Bhūtasiddha (fourteenth) joined with the new moon—this pair of lunar days yields great fruit.

There too, as before, having performed the ritual up to the offering of food (*naivedya*), preceded by the worship of Vighneśa, one should lead Vighneśa and all the other deities, adorned with every ornament, in a circumambulation starting from the *curā* [the threshold], and install them in their respective places as before. By this, any defect resulting from the omission of any part of the rite shall perish by the command of Śiva. This is the procedure for the Full Moon Festival (*paurṇamāsy-utsava*). Now follows the procedure for the Nakṣatra Festival (*ṛkṣotsava*).

[The Ritual for the Festival of the Constellations; The Ritual for the Great Tāla and Other Festivals Ending with the Constellation Festival] Now, O twice-born ones, I shall declare here the worship of all the constellations, which is dear to Śiva, and its corresponding fruit, which is equal [for all].

One other [factor] is said to possess a single quality; the lunar day (tithi) possesses ten qualities. Ten times more than that is the astrological conjunction (yoga); the karana is said to be ten times more than that. The ascendant (lagna) is ten times more than that, and the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) yields even greater fruit than that.
Wherever, through the setting of two [stellar] utterances, one should lead the sun to rise with the moon—
at that very asterism one should fast, except for the asterism Śravaṇa.
If the asterism arises for two or three nāḍīs after sunset, one should observe the fast right there;
the ritual bath and worship should likewise be performed at that time.
Alternatively, if a lunar mansion is reached during the day within half a watch (yāma),
then there indeed [should be] fasting, worship, giving of food, and charity at that time. If two lunar mansions occur in a single month, the former should be accepted and not the latter.
If it is the northern course, joined with yoga, or likewise the equinox or solstice;
There may also be a solar or lunar eclipse, or it may be accompanied by hardships;
[one should avoid] the formal reception at the rites of the gods or at festivals, O best of sages.
In the evening when the constellation of the Bears (Ursa Major) prevails and is expansive, one should perform the pilgrimage;
having worshipped Śiva under the Kṛttikās, one shall be endowed with wealth, grain, and other riches.
Having enjoyed supreme happiness here, one attains union [with the Divine] at the end;
for the sake of destroying untimely death, one should worship Śaṅkara under Rohiṇī.
And having worshipped Īśvara under Saumya, one is endowed with great strength and prowess.
He shall become vigorous and endowed with spiritual luster (*brahmavarcas*), that most excellent practitioner.
(4th line) Under Ārdrā, the worshiper of [the deity] shall seize all prosperity.
Having worshipped Bhava under Punarvasu, he slays his enemies along with their followers. (5th line)
Under Puṣya, one obtains a body that brings nourishment, and under Śleṣā, one obtains excellent sons;
O Lord of Gods, the worshipper there indeed obtains many sons.
Having worshipped Śiva under the asterism Makhā, one shall become possessed of the most excellent [attainments];
under Pūrvaphalgunī, one is endowed with good fortune and the fivefold [group] beginning with cattle.
(…) grains, essences, and jewels are not found outside of the supreme gift.
(2nd line) But by worshipping Hara, one shall attain preeminence among one's own kin.
The worshiper of Hara, endowed with the wonderful qualities of beauty and virtue,
immediately attains his heart's desire under the constellation Svāti;
likewise, the worshiper [of Śiva] becomes possessed of abundant gain under the constellation Bahula.
Through trade, one acquires great wealth; living in Vātsa, one dwells happily for a long time.
By worshipping Śiva during Viśākhā, one attains many desires.
And for those performing rites under Anurādhā, a most magnificent wheel shall appear.
Having performed a sacrifice on the ninth lunar day under Jyeṣṭhā, one certainly attains wealth;
by worshipping Śiva under Mūla, the wise person shall obtain bodily health.
By worshipping Mahādeva under Pūrvāṣāḍhā, one attains fame;
by worshipping Śambhu under Uttarāṣāḍhā, the worshipper shall become a conqueror of enemies.
If there is worship of Hara under Śravaṇā, one will obtain an excellent and auspicious daughter-in-law.
Under Dhaniṣṭhā, one who worships Śiva obtains great and abundant clothing;
having obtained wealth and enjoyed pleasures, he should always be of a charitable disposition.
Under Abhijit, the worshipper of the God becomes a knower of all truths and half [of the divine power].
One who is endowed with these six limbs obtains the Veda along with its phonemes;
and in the rite of worship to Śiva under the constellation Vāruṇa, a physician attains success and medicinal herbs.

If Śiva is worshipped during the asterism known as Proṣṭhapadā, then Aja shall conquer and one obtains cattle; there is no doubt about this. Furthermore, the wise man should propitiate Śiva during the Uttaraproṣṭhapadā.
O twice-born ones, by the command of the Lord, there shall be liberation from all diseases for all men,
women, and kings, even the most exalted.
Great anger at all times shall perish through the worship of Śaṅkara.
Furthermore, a man who performs worship under the asterism Aśvinī shall obtain elephants and horses.
By worshipping Śiva under the asterism Bharaṇī, one obtains long life;
therefore, with every effort, one should perform worship during these asterisms.
Whether one intends to perform it oneself or not, worship should be conducted by others as well.

Having caused [this] to be made, the wise man certainly obtains its fruit. When the moon is in those respective fixed asterisms, one should perform worship and festivals for Śambhu; by fasting on the day of Ārdrā, the merit is multiplied ten million times ten million.
Or even one who causes the worship to be performed shall obtain steadfast sons and grandsons;
whether he be a son of a regular initiate (*samayin*), a spiritual son (*putraka*), a practitioner (*sādhaka*), or even one who is uninitiated (*adīkṣita*).
But he who does not observe the Śarva constellation shall go to hell as a sinner.
Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and those related to the twice-born—
Whether she be a maiden, a widow, a woman of virtuous mind, or one observing the vows of an ascetic,
she should perform this practice in every month, under every constellation, and at every auspicious moment.
Having bathed in the evening and performed the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyopāsana*), she should proceed.
Then, having performed the worship of Śiva, and having caused the worship of the Svāyambhuva and other [liṅgas] to be conducted according to the rules up until the festival,
one should circumambulate the Lord and praise the auspicious Śiva with hymns.
Having bowed down many times with devotion and returned to his own home, he should feed [the guests];
and in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, he should offer drākṣā fruits in the presence of Śiva.
Having then formed a resolve, one should practice for one year;
whatever desire the practitioner longs for, that he shall obtain.
At the end of the year, however, the wise man should perform the rite of dismissal (*udvāsana*).
Having performed [the rites] and honored the Brāhmaṇas, he should give sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) according to his capacity.
[This is equal to] a thousand horse-sacrifices and a hundred million other sacrifices.
By that vow, one obtains the fruit of giving away ten million maidens in marriage.
His portents shall perish, as well as his terrible afflictions from enemies;
he will be liberated from all diseases and endowed with sons, grandsons, and wealth.
Having enjoyed great pleasures, he prospers with long life and happiness;
this is the supreme secret, the most excellent among all vows.
Whatever fruit a man obtains on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, at twilight, on a Monday, during the *vyatīpāta* yoga, or at the time of a solar eclipse—
that same fruit, indeed that unsurpassed fruit, who can obtain for them?
Whether one be a slayer of a Brahmin, a drinker of liquor, a killer of a cow, or one who violates the teacher's bed.
[It is] bestowed from that supreme vow [only] upon one who is free from the multitude of sins arising from [the failure to perform] the *grahaṇa* rites,
who is a devotee of Śiva, tranquil, a learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), and a householder.
One should bestow the vow upon one who is impoverished and afflicted by a great disease.
[Thus ends the procedure beginning with the Bṛhattāla and ending with the Ṛkṣotsava, composed in the Kriyākramadyotikā by the venerable Aghoraśivācārya, whose supreme name is Parameśvara.]
Now follows the procedure for expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
It is said that *prāya* means destruction, and *citta* is called rejoining.
Furthermore, the re-establishment of what has been lost is traditionally held to be expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
By the neglect of one's own proper conduct, a human being goes to hell;
therefore, the teacher should prescribe expiation for the purification of one whose conduct has lapsed.
One who acts for one suffering from a severe illness, or during times of fear caused by kings or thieves,
or for the sake of duties toward a guru, fire, or the gods, or when there is constant loss [of livelihood], incurs no sin.
The penance prescribed for both the celibate student and the householder is declared to be twofold;
and each of those two is further proclaimed to be of two kinds, according to whether it is committed intentionally or unintentionally.
But for one who acts with desire toward another who is without desire, the atonement is declared to be double;
for a student (*naiṣṭhika*) it shall be double that [of a householder];
for a forest-dweller (*vanastha*) it is triple, but for ascetics (*yati*) it is fourfold.

Before sixteen years of age, [the initiation] is not auspicious; after that year, it is indeed [permissible]. For that one who is old or a child, one should prescribe [the rite] for the sake of expiation.
And for women, when they are afflicted by disease, this is declared for the sake of expiation.
For one who is unable to perform it himself, the merit is doubled when performed by another;
for one who is incapable, his son, brother, wife, and so forth, or paternal kinsmen [may act].
When it has been thus analyzed, the expiation should then be performed accordingly; that is equal.
[The Procedure for the Ritual Bath]
I shall describe the procedure for the ritual ablution as enjoined in the Śiva-siddhānta;
it is declared to be threefold: daily (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*).
Each of these is said to be further divided into three types: inferior, middling, and superior.
It is deficient by five *nābhis* and consists of twenty-five *kumbhakas*.
In the middle [grade], there are forty-nine and likewise eighty-one *ghaṭas*;
the best [grade] has one hundred and eight, and two hundred and sixteen.
The thousand [repetitions] for the purpose of one thousand plus eight is not described in that way.
It is considered a triad according to the sequence of daily (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*) rites.
The *taptakṛcchra* and others have been proclaimed; the first among them is known by the name *tapta*.
There are two types of *atikṛcchra* penances, followed by the procedure for the *cāndrāyaṇa*.
For one who eats a single meal every third day, there should be fasting for three days.
Thus is the *kṛcchra* fully described; it is remembered as the *prājāpatya*.
One should drink warm water for three days and subsist on milk for three days;
then one should consume warm clarified butter for three days, and finally, when one subsists on nothing at all for three days,
that is known as the *taptakṛcchra* penance, while the *atikṛcchra* is described as follows:
Therein, for twenty-one days, one should subsist on milk and the three myrobalans (*triphalā*);
this is known as the *atikṛcchra*. Now, the *parāka* is described here: abstaining from food for twelve days is traditionally remembered as the *parāka*.
For half a month there should be an increase [of morsels] during the bright fortnight, and one should decrease them during the dark fortnight;
this is declared as the rule for the Cāndrāyaṇa, which is performed with water alone when no water is available.
As before, in the pavilion, [one should place] those of auspicious intent... (2nd line).

Having prepared a circular *kuṇḍa* with three *hāsa*s in its center, and having established four jars (*ghaṭa*) or four *vardhanī*s in the northeast or the west, filled with heaps of grain (3rd line), and having performed the worship of Vighneśa and caused the declaration of the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, one should [perform] the meditation on Śivāstra as it will be described in one of the primary jars (4th line).
Having worshipped *Rassara*, one should worship [the weapon] in a single southern jar as previously described, preceded by the meditation (*dhyāna*) on the *Aghorāstra*; or else,

having worshipped the *Aghorāstra* according to what will be explained below, one should worship the *Pāśupatāstra* in the western jar according to what will be explained below, and likewise worship *Pratyaṅgirā* itself in the northern jar.

Those initiated in the five directions—beginning with [the letter] *ka* and so forth—who have been born from the various quarters of the reality of Śiva-knowledge, shall recite the *Tatpuruṣa* and other mantras in the east and other directions innumerable times.

They should perform the study of the *Ṛgveda* and other Vedas, as well as the recitation of the *Śānti*, innumerable times, as prescribed for the consecration pavilion (*pratiṣṭhā-maṇṭapa*). Having worshipped these [deities] in sequence up to the end of the recitation, [they should proceed to] the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*)...

Having performed the rites beginning with the consecration of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa-saṃskāra*) and ending with the expiation for the offering of the sacrificial porridge (*caru-havana-prāyaścitta*) as previously described, one should worship each *mūrti* in succession and offer oblations.

(4th line) In the four pits, together with the guardians of the *mūrtis*, they should invoke the respective deities and offer oblations. [The materials include] the three sweets (*madhutraya*), sesame seeds, *dūrvā* grass, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and so forth, as well as milk-rice (*pāyasa*). (5th line)

Or they should offer *kṛsara*—consisting of three *kuḍuba* measures, three fruits, and mustard seeds—either a hundred, a thousand, or fifty times daily at dawn and dusk, together with the *pūrṇā* offering, ending with "svāhā. [At the end of each mantra,] one should append the phrase "O you who cause all agitation, give the corpse again! Do it! Do it! at the conclusion of every ten mantras. In the case of a multi-day rite, having restrained Śiva right there, [one should proceed].

Having gone into the presence of the deity, having announced the performance of the *homa*, and having performed the protection (*rakṣā*), one should pray for the removal of misfortune (*durita*)... [as desired]. Whether on the first, third, fifth, seventh, ninth, or tenth day, or on the new moon, or under any lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), [one should perform it] so that it may be uninterrupted. Thus is the peace (*śānti*). Now follows the procedure for the *śāntihoma*.
[The Procedure for the Śāntihoma]

As before, in the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), having placed a single water-pot (*kumbha*) adorned with all ornaments upon all kinds of grain, and having arranged eight pots around it, one should worship the seat (*āsana*) in the central sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and meditate upon the *Pāśupatāstra*: seated upon the seat of the *Praṇava*, invincible, of great power, five-faced, [with ears like those of] a bull... (F48a, 1st line).

[He] whose fangs are formidable, who is exceedingly fierce, who has released a roar that is difficult to overcome, who is adorned with a garland of skulls, who has the crescent moon as his crest-ornament, [who is] adorned with peacock feathers, who laughs while licking [his lips], who possesses the splendor of ten million times ten thousand suns, and who crushes the hosts of obstacles— with these ten arms, he is thus described... (3rd line)

One should meditate upon the god Mahāpāśupata, who is endowed with all [auspicious] marks, holding in his right hands a sword, a bow, a great trident, and the gesture of fearlessness along with a noose, and in his left hands a shield, an arrow, and a skull-cup, while granting boons; he is joined with a face possessing a beard and hair of a reddish-brown hue, and is the source of the accomplishment of all aims.

Having performed the worship beginning with "Oṃ ślīṃkāra-samāyuktaṃ puṃ śuṃ huṃ phaṇṇama svāhā" and so forth, up to the end of the worship of the vehicles and other enjoyments (*bhogāṅga*), and having worshipped [the deities] starting from the east as before, and having offered various food offerings (*naivedya*) and the like, and having offered the recitation (*japa*), one should go to the vicinity of the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) and sit down to perform the purification of the pit (*kuṇḍasaṃskāra*).

Having performed the rites up to the end of the *prāyaścitta*, and having worshipped the King of Weapons (*astrarāja*) within that interval as before, one should offer oblations— consisting of sacrificial wood (*samit*), clarified butter (*ājya*), sesame seeds (*tila*), and parched grain flour (*saktu*), preceded by the three sweets (*madhutraya*) and honey— either one hundred, one thousand, five hundred, or one hundred and eight times with the respective mantras for the removal of those specific defects, performing the offerings until the conclusion of the *pūrṇāhuti*. Having performed the offerings until the conclusion of the *pūrṇāhuti*...

Having offered incense and lamps, having placed [the vessel] upon the pitcher, and having dismissed the fire, one should consecrate [the recipient] with the water remaining in that pitcher. In the case of many days, on the day prescribed for the rite of pacification (*śānti*), one should have the recitation of the *Kāmika* and other scriptures performed according to the required number, as well as the recitation of the *Śānti*, and so forth, as previously described;
then one should feed the Brahmins. This is the procedure for the *Śāntihoma*.
[The Ritual Procedure for the Directional Fire Offering]

The other [rite] is an ancillary part of the expiation (*prāyaścitta*), while this is an ancillary part of the ceremonial bathing (*snāna*). Having installed the *liṅga*, the image (*bera*), the water-jars (*ghaṭa*), and so forth upon the altar (*vedikā*) in the center of the previously described pavilion, one should place eight jars around this central jar of Śiva’s weapon (*śivāstra*). Then, having adorned the central jar with all manner of splendor, one should worship Śiva’s weapon therein. Having prepared the seat as before, [one should meditate on the deity] who has four faces, flaming hair, and a luster equal to lightning arising from its pedestal.

Having meditated thus: "I bow to the divine Śivāstra, whose head is adorned with [the crescent moon], whose four sprout-like hands are joined with lightning and fire, who is unbearable and of terrifying prowess, endowed with twelve eyes, holding a spear, a trident, and the gesture of fearlessness, the crusher of bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and wicked rākṣasas, with blood-red eyes, most fierce"— and having worshipped it with all the ritual offerings (*sarvopacāra*).

Having prepared a water-pot (*kumbha*) on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), one should satisfy [the deities] therein through the rites ending with the *caru* oblation and expiation (*prāyaścitta*), and then make a petition for one's desired object. Alternatively, they say that in the center is the *śivakumbha* and *vardhanī*; in the eastern direction, the *śivāstra*; in the south, the *aghorāstra*; in the west, the *pāśupatāstra*; and in the north, the *pratyaṅgirā*. Oṃ hrīṃ kā...

*Raṃ*, then *kṛṣṇavāsase*, and from that [the word] *siṃhavadane*, and also *mahāvadane*, and *mahābhairavivarṇāśca*, then one should extract the word *sarvaśabdam* in the middle; afterwards, *dinī*, and also *bhṛtidamanī*. Then one should extract the words *sarvabhūtāntato bandha bandha*; [and] *sarvavighneti chindi chindi*.

The word *sarvavyādhini nikṛnta*, and the word *nikṛnta*; then at the end of all the wicked ones, the word *bhakṣa bhakṣa* in the subsequent [verse]; *jvālāmālakarāle* for the crookedly wicked; then the word *pratyaṅgira*; and after that, the word *donnamastu*. Then *sa vāha*—this is the mantra consisting of *pratyaṅgirā* which possesses all splendor.
Having worshipped the supreme goddess Pratyaṅgirā upon a firm seat in the center of the *vardhanī* vessel, one should meditate [upon her] as follows:
she possesses a lion’s face, fierce fangs, and fire-like upward-pointing crests;
she is endowed with three eyes whose form is like black collyrium and the sky.
With her two left hands, she carries a severed head, a plowshare, and a sprout;
wearing black garments and shedding tears, she holds a trident, a *ḍamaru* drum, and a lotus.
With her two right hands, she likewise carries a severed head, a skull, and a sprout.
Wearing black garments, tearful, with a face intent on dancing,
adorned with suitable ornaments of pearls, possessing auspicious marks on all her limbs,
filled with the passion for loud laughter, and clad in a black antelope skin.
"One should meditate upon Pratyaṅgirā, the destroyer of diseases, obstacles, and enemies.

Having thus meditated, one should worship her with all the ritual services (*upacāra*), beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*), using the root mantra. Then, having worshipped the Vajra and other deities of the surrounding enclosure (*āvaraṇa*) and the ritual jars (*kalaśa*), one should [worship] Pratyaṅgirā in the center of a lotus-shaped sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) or a womb-shaped pit (*yonikuṇḍa*).

Having performed worship with [the aforementioned materials], one should offer oblations— one hundred each, or fifty, or twenty-eight— of fuel-sticks (*samidh*), products of the cow (*gavya*), sesame (*tila*), *dūrvā* grass, milk, sacrificial porridge (*caru*), the three sweets (*madhutraya*), the three sweet substances (*madhuratrāya*), the three *kuḍuba* measures, white mustard seeds (*gaurasarṣapa*), cloves (*lavaṅga*), nutmeg leaves (*jātipatra*), sacred sandalwood (*śrīgandha*), saffron (*kuṅkuma*), yellow pigment (*gorocanā*), and so forth; and having offered these along with the expiatory full-oblation (*prāyaścitta-pūrṇāhuti*), one should do so for the sake of pacifying the sins of that [person] before the Goddess.

Having prayed for victory among the gods, or while they are being victorious, one should bathe [the deity] with the water contained in that jar and perform the protection with ashes (*bhasmarakṣā*). Alternatively, as before, one should worship the four weapons in the center and Pratyaṅgirā; thus they say—this is the procedure for the fire-offering (*diśāhoma*) according to the directions.

[|| Saṃhitā-homa ||] Whether in the perpetual fire (*nityāgni*) or the special fire (*viśeṣāgni*), having worshipped Śiva together with his limbs (*brahmāṅga*) in the center of that [fire], one should perform an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) and so forth by offering oblations—such as fuel-sticks (*samid*) and other materials—with the mantras of the limbs of Brahmā, numbering one hundred, one thousand, or half [of those], in order to remove any defects incurred therein. (... "Excluding the [letter] ṭa. (6th line)
The Saṃhitā-homa. Now follows the Mūrti-homa. [The Mūrti-homa]

On the roof of a palace or elsewhere on a prepared sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), in the center of the *āpadama*, one should place the *śivakumbha* and the *vardhanī*. In the eight directions, one should establish eight jars known as *vajra* and *agni*, provided with threads and lids, and filled with cloth, gold, gems, medicinal herbs, and scented water. Having performed the purification of the pavilion and other rites as before, one should worship Śiva in the center and recite the *aghora-astra* mantra over the *vardhanī*. Alternatively, [The text continues: ...on the roof of a palace or elsewhere on a prepared sacrificial mound, in the center of the *āpadama*, one should place the *śivakumbha* and the *vardhanī*. In the eight directions, one should establish eight jars known as *vajra* and *agni*, provided with threads and lids, and filled with cloth, gold, gems, medicinal herbs, and scented water. Having performed the purification of the pavilion and other rites as before, one should worship Śiva in the center and recite the *aghora-astra* mantra over the *vardhanī*. Alternatively,
Having established the Śiva-kumbha and the vardhanī in the center, one should worship the Aghora-weapon within it;
around that, one should worship the Vajra and other [weapons]. For the seat of the weapon: *huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*. For the form of the weapon: *huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*. The meditation (*dhyāna*):
possessing the luster of thousands of millions of suns, with a roar like the clouds at the time of universal dissolution.
With his face and neck illuminated by the light from the edges of his blazing eyes.

Three-eyed, with a tongue [protruding from] the mouth of a woman, blazing brows, and hair standing erect; wearing a serpent as a sacred thread (*upavīta*), and bearing a trident, sword, spear, and mallet;
four-armed and four-faced, with the crescent of the autumn moon as his crest-ornament.
He was dancing, possessed of a massive body, and adorned with ornaments of serpents.
"Having meditated thus upon the crushing of the arrogant gods, *dānavas*, and *daityas*, [one recites]:
*oṃ sphura sphura*—this pair of words; then the word for the two trembling bodies, *rūpa*; followed by the word *caṭacaṭa*;
then the second *pracaṭa*; then the word *kaha kaha*; then the word *vama vama*; then the second *bandha*; then the second *ghātaya*; and finally, *aghorāstra*."

Having understood the mantra ending with *ṛtaṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā*, one should perform the practice, beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*) and concluding with the recitation (*japa*). Having performed the worship in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) or on the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), one should invoke the King of Weapons (*astrarāja*).

Then, with the Aghora-Astra mantra, one should offer into the fire one hundred, one thousand, half of those, or one hundred and eight oblations of each—namely, fuel-sticks (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), sesame seeds (*tila*), milk (*kṣīra*), dūrvā grass, the three sweets (*madhuratrika*), and sacrificial food (*haviṣya*).

To remove those defects, one should perform oblations accompanied by the *pūrṇāhuti*. Alternatively, having established the *śivakumbha* in the center and the *vardhanī* in the eight directions—starting from the east and so forth—one should worship them according to the eight-fold system; however, in the five-fold system, one should establish and worship the forms (*mūrtis*) beginning with Earth. Then, having performed the oblations up to the end of the expiation (*prāyaścitta*), [one should offer fuel-sticks of] *pālāśa*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, *vaṭa*, and *śamī*.

Having offered one hundred and eight or fifty oblations separately with fuel sticks of *khadira*, *mayūra*, *plakṣa*, and so forth, each with its own mantra, and having given the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should sprinkle the *liṅga* or the *bera* image— or the patron— with that water, apply the sacred ash (*bhasma*), and perform everything according to the number of days [prescribed] for the *ayanādi-śānti*. In this regard, those [mantras] recited in the *ayanādi-śānti* [are to be used].

The patron, having adorned the reciters of the *Kāmika* and other Tantras—headed by the preceptor—with perfumes, flowers, garments, and so forth, and having given the prescribed sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), should bow down and pray for the pacification of misfortunes. Together with his mother and father, the preceptor should offer unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*). Having satisfied the poor, the blind, the wretched, and the helpless with food and clothing, [the rite is concluded]. Thus ends the Mūrtihoma.
[The Procedure for Expiation] Having touched one who has not been initiated into his own caste, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on.
Upon touching a Śūdra, one should immediately perform a bath with one's clothes on.
Upon touching any of the intermediate spaces, one should bathe twice;
at the time of seeing a Caṇḍāla, one should always meditate upon Sadāśiva.
Having heard his speech, one should recite the root mantra one hundred times;
if it is near the staff, two ablutions must be performed.
In the event of contact through negligence, one should know that bathing in water must first be performed;
having then performed a bath with ashes, one should recite the Śiva-mantra a hundred times.
If the contact occurs intentionally, one should perform the aforementioned rites twice.
Having seen that, at the time of eating, the wise man should discard the remainder of it.
Then, having performed the two ablutions and recited the root mantra one hundred and eight times,
if a foul odor should reach him by way of the wind while it remains at the tip of his nose, [he should proceed].
Having resorted to cow dung, one should immediately recite the five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣara*).
And for those who have not been initiated into their own caste, [the rule applies] regarding eating the first portion in the village... [of you].
If one recites the *Vyomavyāpin* mantra once out of desire, one should recite it a hundred times;
if a Brahmin eats the food of a king, he should recite the *Aghora* mantra a hundred times.
Having eaten the food of a Vaiśya, he should recite it a thousand times in sequence.
Having eaten the food of a Śūdra out of desire, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
For eating it out of desire, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa; for eating it unintentionally, the Kṛcchra or Atikṛcchra.
But having eaten it for more than one day, one should perform both the Kṛcchra and the Cāndrāyaṇa.
By eating [this] continuously for a month, one attains the state of Rudra;
however, if it is eaten by a Śūdra alone, he shall undergo the constant descent into the state of a Śūdra.
Having had sexual intercourse with a Śūdra woman, one should then perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance;
for one who approaches her for half a month, the *taptakṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* [should be performed] for a month.
For six months or even for a year, one should perform the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances;
however, when the union occurs after a full year has passed, no expiation is prescribed.
His conduct and his killing of that [creature] must be treated with particular severity.
If one should feed [the deity] upon leaves of the castor-oil plant, the sun-plant, the banyan, or the holy fig tree—
whether out of desire or even by chance— one should recite the Śiva-mantra a hundred times.
This should be done while observing the vow of eating only the remnants [of the offering], with milk that is free from salt.
And having recited his heart-mantra, which cuts through all defects,
[he should do so] when hair, bones, or even nine insects and the like are seen.
Having abandoned what was left over from the meal and having washed one's hands,
one becomes pure by touching ashes, recollecting the lords of the gods, and drinking water from the joined palms (*añjali*).
One should avoid garlic, fish, meat, and the remains of offerings (*nirmālya*).
But having consumed [forbidden food] through negligence, one should recite the Śiva-mantra while remaining pure.
If one should eat while desiring [sensual pleasure], one should recite the Śiva-mantra a hundred times;
[the sins of] killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, and stealing gold [are thereby purified].
Approaching the wife of one's guru, and through association with her, the fifth [offense] occurs;
along with drinking liquor and killing a Brahmin—these three [are the mortal sins].
These are declared to end in death; now hear of their execution.
He who, out of greed, steals silver shall undergo a punishment equal to that [of stealing gold].
Beyond ten *gadyāṇas*, one shall pay double the amount as a fine.
But the procedure for gold on the head is recorded as being double that of the thousand-fold rite.
One should perform the purification of gold by striking it with the finest gems;
however, for all other metals and ores, one should perform the *parāka* penance.
For the theft of grains, the Kṛcchra and Tilārdraka penances are prescribed;
for the theft of base metals and gems, the Ghorakṛcchra lasting twenty-one thousand days is ordained.

For stealing clothing, bedding, seats, and the like, one should perform the *baindava* penance for one hundred thousand repetitions accompanied by the *gāyatrī*; this is equal to violating the teacher’s bed (*gurutalpa*). Likewise, [the penances for] killing a cow, being a *vrātya*, [stealing] a horse, and the acquisition of wealth through usury [are prescribed].
Not maintaining the sacred fires, superseding a younger brother in marriage, abandoning the duties of a vow, likewise the non-performance of the duties of a vow,
adultery with another's wife, and acts of deception in trade.
Living off a woman, a Śūdra, or a Kṣatriya; censuring [others] for one's livelihood; hypocrisy; greed regarding religious observances; and the selling of one's own daughters.

Stealing livestock, abandoning one's father, mother, or son, selling a tank or a grove, defiling a maiden, and [the act of] a younger brother marrying before his elder—these are [forfeiture]. The sale of a Vedic student's skin-cloak; |||
Giving away a daughter in marriage to him alone, crookedness, violation of vows, [the undertaking of] the beginning of a trade, the prohibition against drinking liquor or associating with women,
the abandonment of the sacred fire and the gods under the asterism Svāti, and likewise the abandonment of kinsmen.
Cutting down trees for fuel and killing women constitute six ways of losing one's livelihood.
The ritual application of mantras for violence, the various transformations of the self,
and the authority over the forms and names derived from false scriptures [are all abandoned].
The sale of a wife is likewise a minor offense (*upapātaka*);
one purified from a minor offense may be cleansed by a divine vow,
or by subsisting on milk for a month, or even by the *parāka* penance.
Or even from one marked by Aghora; now the distinction is proclaimed.

One should perform [the penance] for the murder of a Brahmin; for the killing of a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, one should perform it for two-thirds [of the duration]; but for the sake of killing a Śūdra, one should perform one-eighth [of the penance].

Upon striking living beings, one should recite [the Aghora mantra] a hundred times; from the sin consisting of harming living beings, one becomes pure by reciting the Aghora mantra a hundred times. When a collection of breath-beings (prāṇas) that lack bones has been struck, or when a sweat-born being has been killed, one should recite [the mantra] a hundred times for the sake of the unborn [being], from the sin consisting of harming living beings.
One becomes pure by reciting the hundred-fold *aghora* mantra after killing a boneless creature or a swarm of living beings born from sweat;
however, if one kills an unborn creature (*ajātasya*), the recitation is half that amount when done unintentionally.
Having killed many boneless creatures such as wild flowers and the like, [one is purified by the same].
Having seen both the desirable and the undesirable, one becomes pure through the remembrance of Śiva.
By the very same [penance] one becomes pure for killing a cat or a mongoose;
for killing a dog or a jackal, it is the same; and for a monkey or a cock, it is double.
In the case of all egg-born creatures, including birds such as swans,
and in the killing of beasts of prey such as lions, as well as the slaughter of domestic animals such as goats,
one becomes pure by reciting the *Bahurūpa* mantra one hundred times up to four hundred times.
Having killed a cow through negligence, one becomes pure by reciting the Aghora mantra one hundred thousand times.
Having committed the murder of a woman or a child, one is purified by one hundred thousand recitations of the Aghora mantra.
Out of lust, a wise man should recite it one hundred thousand times [for killing] a brahmin woman, as well as for causing an abortion.
One should recite the third [mantra]...
even one bitten by a dog shall be purified by the eight hundred repetitions of the Gāyatrī.

One bitten by a cat or a mouse is purified by reciting [the mantra] one hundred times; or one bitten by a jackal or a deer, the wise man should recite it one hundred thousand times. One bitten by a potter-fish (*kumbhīra*) or a crocodile (*makara*) is purified by reciting it just once.

If one has been bitten by a snake through negligence, one should recite the *ghora* mantra one thousand times. If one has been bitten by a dog or similar creature out of desire, one should recite it ten thousand times while standing in water.
One should also [counteract] poison-science and the shifting illusions of sorcery (*indrajāla*).
But for the expulsion of spirits, *bhūtas*, *śṛṅgins*, *piśācas*, and the like, [the recitation] is two hundred times;
however, one should not perform killing even mentally or by means of a mantra.
Having performed rites such as *uccāṭana* (expulsion), or having caused suffering to others through the actions of speech, mind, and body by means of various forms,
one should— recognizing this through negligence— recite the Śiva-mantra a hundred times.
Whoever has uttered a falsehood by deed, mind, or speech;
By [the recitation of] the *vāmabhaṃ* [mantra], one is released from the sin born of this [life].
Having been freed a hundred times, or having reached the end, one should mutter the *ghoṣa* twice as many times.
The mental [unwholesome action] is fourfold: the intention regarding another’s wife or wealth, thinking of what is undesirable with the mind, engaging in what should not be done, and fear (*bhīti*).
[The verbal unwholesome action] is that which consists of idle chatter day and night, as well as that which is untrue and unpleasant.
And vocal action is of four kinds, being free from slander of others.
The consumption of what is not to be eaten, violence, and the practice of falsehood;
the appropriation of another's property—these constitute the fourth type of physical action.
In the case of verbal [offense], there should be silence for three days, as well as fire-rituals, worship, and recitation;
having completed [the penance], she should offer it to her teacher, the deity, and the [other] elders.
He is said to be liberated from verbal bonds and from the bonds of karma;
[he who] remains without food for three nights, [performs] ablutions at the three junctions of the day,
[and is] a reciter of the *brahma-mantra* while observing silence, is not yet released from the bonds of karma.
But for mental sin, when one is devoted to the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma), [it is purified].
By means of the *śivagāyatrī* mantra, one is released from mental [impurities];
for the removal of all defects, one should drink the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) once.

One is liberated from all sins arising from one’s mother and father. Whatever innate sin has entered into the bones and marrow, even that which was committed unintentionally while asleep, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) shall burn away in an instant.
When [the body] is seen to be impure, one should bathe again with one's clothes on;
then, whether it occurs during the day or in a dream, one should recite the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*) one hundred times.
He who has dwelt among cows out of lustful desire should perform double the penance for the sake of the Great Soul, the *praṇava*.
By restraining the fluctuations of the *praṇava*, he should repeat it one hundred thousand times.
This is the rule concerning ascetics; preceded by the lifting of the vow, this is the intended path.
One should take a wife; otherwise, downfall is certain.
(3rd line) Or else, there would be as many matted locks, braids, or particles of ash as there are [years].
The one who, blinded by desire, should again entertain such thoughts after having once [renounced them], shall dwell for that same duration in the most terrible Raurava hell;
yet he is purified by a thousand recitations of the Vāmadeva hymn— of this there is no doubt.
Having involuntarily discharged semen,
one should recite [the mantra] two hundred times at night, and if one has fallen asleep during the day, one should recite it one hundred times.
Whenever one sees a drop of semen, even unintentionally, one should recite it one hundred times.

When she has bathed after her menses and [approaches him]... then for a period of five days, she should remain faithful for the sake of obtaining a son; otherwise, he would become a killer of an embryo (*bhrūṇahā*).
O you who are valiant in performing austerities, she should perform recitations, fire-oblations, and other such rites.
That brahmin who constantly practices sexual intercourse, deluded by desire, should be known as being like a donkey; for him, the mantras are turned away.
There is a fault in approaching a Kṣatriya woman and others; one who commits the act on a festival day by day incurs the full penalty.
This [penalty] applies to the physical act, not merely to speech; one must never engage in intercourse with another’s wife.
If one should perform such an act unintentionally, purification is achieved by the quarter-penalty for killing a cow.

In the case of a maiden, [the penance] is double; likewise for those of other castes. Having engaged in sexual intercourse on the junctions of the lunar phases (*parvan*), on the eighth day, or ever during the daytime, a wise man established in the vow of the *praṇava* should recite it ten thousand times.
Having performed half of ten thousand [recitations] at night, one should recite ten thousand during the twilight;
having heard [the sound] produced by sexual intercourse, one should recite a hundred for the sake of the one who has shed blood.
When the vow of celibacy has been maintained, the wise man should [recite] the *pra...* with a focused mind;
O Śūdrī, he should recite ten thousand of the *sāmānya* [mantras], and double that number.

One born of the Vaiśya or other castes, having heard [the mantra], should recite the four [verses] by which one becomes free from sin, whether it be a serpent or whatever else may be [hostile]. He who desires the maiden Mahāvratarī again...
Especially one whose nose and lips are severed... (............................. ||
Having performed a journey on a clean chariot, one who has been initiated should recite the *Grahī* mantra one hundred times.
A Brahmin who approaches a Brahmin woman or another [woman] is liberated from that sin by reciting it one hundred and eight times.
A Kṣatriya, having recited [the Vāmadevya] two hundred times, and Vaiśyas three hundred times,
and Śūdras four hundred times, [attain] Śiva through the Vāmadevya.
Having stayed there for even one night, he is liberated from that sin;
even if he has eaten for a long time, he should perform a hundred *vāma* penances.
Having gone from the *homā* to the *vivarṇāvitāt*, the Blessed One, desiring [to dwell] in a cave... (4th line)...
remained for three days without agitation, standing in water reaching up to his chest.

By means of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and recitation (*japa*), one is purified from secret sins (*guhyapāpa*). Having approached a menstruating woman (*udakyā*) once unintentionally, one must fast; however, if done intentionally, one must perform [the penance] for two or three days for a secret sin.
When that Caṇḍāla woman was stationed in the hall of knowledge, [the king said:]...
One should immediately abandon earthen vessels, bathe, and purify that house;
having recited the *Narāyaṇa* mantra five thousand times, one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance.
Having eaten [the food], she shall, if it was done unintentionally, perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance first,
and then purify herself by reciting the *Vāmadeva* mantra ten thousand times along with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
If she has eaten it intentionally, she should likewise recite the *Vāmadeva*.
Having understood that the vow is fulfilled when the [period of] separation has passed, and having eaten for a long time, he then becomes equal to her—
whether she be a Rajakī or a Karmakārī. Or,
having touched her while staying in the temple, he becomes pure by discarding his vessels, as is the case with goats.
If one eats without having touched [the food] for five thousand three days, one should recite the *ghora* mantra for three days; if it was done intentionally, that [penance] should be doubled.

From a single instance of union, there is [a single] desire; from many instances of union, [many desires] arise. Since both of these have occurred, the performance of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance is required.
Otherwise, a yoga lasting many days is not purified at all;
if it has arisen through intentional desire, then the Cāndrāyaṇa penance must be performed.

O venerable one, by accepting from us only water, one is released from the suffering of a difficult initiation; even a base person becomes consecrated. Having accepted clarified butter, oil, and sugar, one may indulge in desire.
Salt, molasses, pungent substances, fire, and various fragrant materials.
Milk, curd, ghee, oil, honey, meats, and grains; silk cloth, cotton, wool, linen, and hempen fabric.
Having gone to the place where the hide is kept, one should mutter three hundred times the *Ghora* mantra;
[it is] a collection of jewels beginning with diamond (*vajra*), like a mass of gold and pure crystal.
Minerals such as yellow orpiment, collections of other precious substances like gold,
a bull, an elephant, a vehicle, a kṣatriya, and likewise the interval between the twilights—
having purified these many forms with effort in temples and other sacred places...
One becomes pure by hundreds of times for stealing wood, stones, leaves, and the like.
I [gave] a horse, a woman, or a thousand or a hundred men;
land with many tens of thousands of crops, and a thousand grains in the house.
A wise man, having taken away whatever belongs to another, whether it be a dwelling or anything else of many forms, should recite [the mantra] one hundred times;
likewise, for the theft of clothing, bedding, seats, and so forth, he should recite the Gāyatrī one hundred times.
A wise person should recite the thousand-fold mantra of the Face for the recovery of lost knowledge;
he who, having abandoned his own proper livelihood, conducts himself otherwise.
One who has been initiated but has fallen from his own duty through action, yet has been readmitted,
is liberated from that sin by constantly reciting the Aghora mantra for one month before Śiva and by offering oblations appropriately into the Śiva-fire.
One should perform ten times the severe penance for stepping over three or four footprints.
Even for many evils, when [the situation] has arisen, one should perform [the rite] with dust...;
if he does not become appeased, the Aghora mantra should be recited.

He who studies the *Śivasaṃhitā* according to the prescribed rule day after day— he is a hand [of protection], he is a destroyer of sin, and he is the illuminator of the *nirāmiṣa* (unmixed) state. During the morning, evening, and twilight sandhyās, one should mutter the *Sadyojāta* mantra a hundred times.
The sin committed during a day and night perishes at that very moment.
When a woman who has reached her menses does not worship Śiva, she is not pure;
on the first day she is a Cāṇḍālī, and on the second she is a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa.
In the third [chapter] Rajagī is mentioned; in the fourth, the bath [is described].
Having performed the bath with (... and having consumed the products of the cow (*gavya*), one should worship Śiva.

Having recited the terrible mantra one hundred times during greed (*lobha*), one should worship Śiva. Then follows the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*), the mounting of the *vardhanī* vessel, and the offering on the previous day. One should give a third part to the voice (*vāk*) at night, excluding the third part [of the ritual].
If it is desired that "I" here [be understood] as beginning with the morning and so forth, while remaining unperceived.

In the house of a woman who has miscarried or is menstruating, that which is seen [there] is not defiled for one who is plowing. A *caṇḍāla*, a woman who has recently given birth, and a menstruating woman are called "impure" (*sūtakān*).
Upon hearing of the death of a kinsman, one should bathe in a river or similar body of water.
Having eaten [food] from one who has been approached [for sexual intercourse], one should perform the Prājāpatya penance.
If an ascetic should touch a Brāhmaṇa, Śūdra, Vaiśya, or Kṣatriya woman who is in her courses (udakyā), [he must likewise perform penance].

Having committed [the offense] with a quarter [of the body], one becomes pure by performing the Kṛcchra penance; having committed it with half [the body], one becomes pure by performing the Atikṛcchra. He who eats without having bathed should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.

If one should touch a jackal, a dog, a donkey, a *kādi*, a moth, a fallen person, or an outcaste, or if one should touch livestock, [having performed the prescribed rite], one should perform the *atikṛcchra* penance.
For Śūdras and others, the penance is respectively a gift, a quarter-*kṛcchra*, and fasting.

A Vaiśya or a Śūdra woman, having touched a Kṣatriya man, becomes pure by performing half a Pādakṛcchra penance. Upon touching women of the Vaiśya, Kṣatriya, or Śūdra castes, one is purified by a Pādakṛcchra.
A Śūdra woman, having been touched by a man of a higher caste, is purified by a gift alone.
But a menstruating woman who, while eating, sees a corpse or similar [impurity] through delusion,
shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance once three days have elapsed.
If one who is menstruating eats during the day and her food should be touched by a person of ill repute,
she should observe three days of fasting and is purified by the *pañcagavya*.
If a woman in her menses enters while defiled by the remnants of food from a *caṇḍāla*, [she must likewise purify herself].

If one touches a woman who has not bathed after her menses, one should fast; if one eats with her, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. If a woman of the same lineage (*sagotra*) who is menstruating is touched, one should likewise fast for three days.
If a woman in her courses is touched by another woman in her courses, she becomes pure by bathing and fasting.
If one converses with, eats with, or sees a menstruating woman while in a state of ritual purity,
