he should eat only at the end of the period of impurity for an *āsnātaka* and consume the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).

One should drink from this [vessel] even while a corpse is present or during a period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*). If she experiences menstruation (*rajas*) or is touched by a corpse, she should eat only after [the impurity has passed]; having done so, she should fast for a day in the case of impurity from a corpse or from a woman in her courses (*udakyā*).

If one should eat after being consecrated in the midst of *sūtaka* (impurity due to birth), [he becomes pure]; likewise for touching or eating the remnants [of food]... [in the case of] a menstruating woman or death. Having eaten or drunk during *sūtaka*, and having acted thus when it has arisen, one must perform the rite without delay.
Women who have had their menses shall attain purification through the ritual sprinkling.
Otherwise, one should bathe with clay and water at this place;
on the fourth day, one whose head is covered in impurity should bathe during the six *nāḍīs* of the morning.
Upon the disappearance [of the body], clothing [is offered] with ashes from the cremation ground;
purity is attained by smearing [the body] three times seven times with ash after the consumption of food.
One should wash bronze, fire-vessels, and beds with water;
that which is used for lying down or sleeping is purified by scraping and so forth, as prescribed in the scriptures.
By the trampling of cows, it is purified; and from the power of the ritual bath after menstruation, one is freed from impurity.

Wherever one sees another woman without her husband, on ground where not even a blade of grass exists— (5th line)— there a bath is prescribed for the *vaidhavya* woman along with a cow's tail-fan; the cow's tail-fan serves as the staff.
Or else, according to human measurement, when there is an obstruction by grass or leaves... [in those various substances] or with a cow-tail fan (*govālavyajana*).
No ritual bathing is prescribed there; however, upon seeing her in the midst [of the assembly], a householder should mutter the *praṇava* and subsequently gaze at the sun.
Having performed the practice of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and having also beheld [the deity],
one should recite the root mantra one hundred times.
A Caṇḍāla who has climbed onto the same tree as [a Brahmin], or a woman in her menses,
becomes pure by staying for one night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
For women, purification is prescribed to be like that for urine until the twelfth day.
Alternatively, the bath may take eighteen days; beyond that, one is pure after three nights.
But a woman who has become menstruating again while already menstruating shall remain impure for three nights after the twentieth day.
Having scrubbed away the impurities of the teeth and so forth with clay repeatedly, one should bathe;

or else, having consumed the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) or clarified butter, one should worship Śiva. An inner sacrifice (*antaryāga*) must be performed by oneself during the three preceding days.
Or else, at the end, one should recite the terrible mantra a thousand times.
If one is touched by a woman of one's own caste who is in her menses, one should worship Śiva with desire and other [motives];
at that time, one should recite the mantra of the Lord of one's own caste one thousand times.
If one worships her out of ignorance, purification arises from that very limb;
when doubt arises, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.
In contact with one of lower caste, [the penance] increases respectively by two, three, or four times;

in contact with one of higher caste, the one of lower caste should perform half of that. During the period of birth-impurity (sūtaka), one should practice meditation on the Lord (Īśvara) as far as possible.
At the conclusion of that, having consumed the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should worship Śiva without weariness.
Having touched a human bone that is still moist with fat, one should bathe and recite the *ghora* mantra a hundred times;
if it is touched when not moist with fat, one should bathe, sip water, and look at the sun.

In this world, one should bathe upon touching a corpse, remembering it, or being touched by those in a cremation ground, by the impure after a death, by those carrying a corpse, by those who cremate it, or by those bearing other sectarian marks;
likewise, upon touching a Pañcarātrika, a Kālarātri, a Kāpālika, or a Kaulika, one must bathe.

Having performed a bath with the *bakāra* mantras and the "Heart of Soma" mantras, along with those of the Buddhists, the Agnis, and the naked ascetics (*nagnambara*), one becomes pure by being clean after the third [contact] while wearing one's clothes;
however, upon the fourth contact, a Brahmin should perform a bath with his clothes on.
Having touched all the intermediate spaces, perform the two ablutions;
one should perform the bath near Karmāra and Ṛṣika on the anniversaries of the Yugas.
In the vicinity of a butcher, a fisherman, a hunter, a fowler, a washerman, or two staff-bearers,
one should go beyond half a *daṇḍa*; likewise in the vicinity of a woman in childbirth,
upon touching a heron, a dog, a donkey, a horse, or a camel, and similarly in other such cases.
That indeed was filled with domestic pigs and cocks that had been trained to remember their tasks.
One who eats the remains of offerings (*nirmālya*) should perform a bath upon being touched by kings,
jackals, monitor lizards, *divābhīta* insects, or *kuraṇṭaka* plants.
In the event of contact with an outcaste dog-eater (śvapāka), one should perform the Vāruṇa penance.
The same applies upon contact with a Divākīrti, a funeral pyre, a place of smoke, a Niṣāda, or likewise a woman who has recently given birth.
Having touched a twice-born person who is standing on a crossroads, or having touched Lokāyatikas and nihilists,
or likewise having touched a sacred tree (caityavṛkṣa), one should enter the water with one's clothes on. Furthermore,
when a Caṇḍāla or similar person has climbed upon a single tree, [one must do the same].
A Brahmin dwelling there attains purity through bathing.
Upon contact with white feces or urine above the navel—excluding the hands—one should perform a bath;
likewise, one should bathe after shaving, vomiting, or touching someone who is untouchable.

Whatever parts [of the body] are above the navel are pure in every respect; those below it, as well as the excretions from the body such as filth and the like, are impure. When the body has come into contact with impurity, it is purified by seven applications of earth.
And in the event of an injury to the head, one should perform a bath with water.

After cleansing the lower part of the body with earth in the case of dogs and the like, or the defilement by feces, or from birds such as crows and others, one becomes pure once the purification has been performed.
In all cases involving the head, however, there is no bathing with water;
instead, the wise man should perform the penance of recitation by chanting the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times.

If one touches the leavings of food after having performed purification according to the rules, one attains purity by bathing; however, [for touching] three hundred times more than that, [one must perform penance]. In the case of urinating while speaking untruth, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on.
Having touched the circle of the face with handfuls of white feces, urine, and filth.

Earth and cow dung are purified by smearing; [a vessel] is purified by the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). Human bone, fat, feces, or blood, as well as urine and semen, [are likewise purified].
Having touched marrow or blood, one should bathe after performing the ritual sipping of water;
for by bathing after touching a woman in her courses or water, one becomes pure.

One who has been touched by such a person while in an impure state becomes pure simply by bathing. Bathing during the day is praised when joined with the rays of the sun; that same bathing is also recommended at night, except when there is the sight of Rāhu [i.e., an eclipse].
Or else, one should perform the bath at night according to the words of the preceptor or others.
One who observes vows should perform the ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*), while a householder should always perform the mantra-bath (*mantrasnāna*).

If one touches another who is impure, he defiles that person of the same caste (*ekavarṇa*). One touched by such a person does not defile others; however, this rule applies to all cases of contact with the remnants of food (*ucchiṣṭa*).
During a procession of the gods, at a wedding, during sacrifices that have been commenced,
and at all festive celebrations, contact with those who are normally untouchable does not cause defilement.

At a sacred ford, at a wedding, on a journey, in battle, upon foreign soil, and in the vicinity of a city or village, touching what has been touched does not cause defilement. A Brahmin who touches another Brahmin while eating does not make that person impure; they do not lead him to a state of sin.
When his beard has grown and he is eating between the teeth, his son [is not considered impure].
In the case of the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), the *soma* sacrifice, water, and the oblations of breath (*prāṇāhuti*),
there is no fault in being "left-over" (*ucchiṣṭa*) for the sacrificer and the drinker, nor when hair is present on the lips.
In the case of betel, fruit, or even a superior food that has been eaten,
as well as when something stuck between the teeth touches [the lips], a person does not become impure by the remains of food.
O twice-born ones, by using lotus petals, roots, and flowers, as well as those made of grass or wood,
and with fragrant substances mixed with honey, one does not become impure through food remnants.
After bathing, drinking, eating, sleeping, or having eaten [something], upon returning from a journey, after sipping water,
or after putting on a garment, one should again rinse the mouth.
Having voided urine or feces, one should touch water with the *vyāna* breath;
having touched anything impure, one becomes pure by sipping water (*ācamana*).
It is likewise prescribed for sneezing, yawning, and upon hearing the speech of an untruthful person.
Likewise after spitting, after anointing the body, and after eating and putting on fresh clothes.
But upon contact with one who has food remnants, as well as from the washing of his feet,
from conversing with one who has food remnants, and until the removal of that impurity;

One should always perform this ritual sipping (upaspṛśet) even without the sacred thread (yajñopavīta). Upon touching a goat, seeing a linga or other such objects, or upon touching the tongues of other horses, one should touch [the tongue] with the tongue itself; likewise, one should touch what is stuck to the teeth.
Having crossed water, one should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana); likewise after [encountering] a deity or an animal;
upon conversing with a woman, a Śūdra, or a hermaphrodite (uṃbaṣṭha); and upon seeing the voiding of excrement—if one desires to propitiate a deity, having already sipped water, one should sip again.
Just as with the teeth, so it is with those things that are toothless, internal, and composed of that [same substance];
one should not sip water for purification over what remains in the rinsing vessel after one has already sipped.

At that time, for the sake of the twilight prayers, for eating, and likewise for ancestral rites, one should not sip water using the hand of a Śūdra; nor should one do so during the recitation of mantras, fire offerings, or worship.
Having touched a woman of one's own caste who has not been initiated, one should perform the "Agnicaya" bath.
"O Agni, I shall [cleanse] you with warm water and cow-dung for the sake of removing the scent and the smear."
Gold and silver are purified by rubbing and heating;
copper is purified by an acidic liquid; and a vessel of bell-metal is purified with ashes.
The mouth is purified in every way by sour substances or ash;
bamboo becomes pure by scrubbing with cow-hair and water,
and an earthen alms-bowl attains purity through [water] associated with Varuṇa.
It is purified by scrubbing with wood-apple (*kapittha*) that has been touched by a woman’s garment;
or else, one should rub it with conch shells, oyster shells, or pearls that have been washed,
or with the husks of wheat or rice.
The purification of garments is declared to be by means of alkaline salt or water;
likewise for cloth, leather, ropes, and similarly for leaves.
By constantly scrubbing with water the vessels used for food and condiments,
and likewise by heating the water-vessels all around with fire.
[The purification] of stone vessels is by means of water;
that of iron [vessels] is by means of acid; and likewise for all water-born [vessels], bamboo [vessels], and those such as bowls, leaves, and baskets used for food.
In this context, purification is prescribed for those items that have been used and are then discarded.
Those [substances] produced from [impurities] such as feces, urine, and phlegm are to be discarded;
however, those originating from all the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) become purified upon contact with fire.

A vessel that has been licked by insects, mice, or cats is purified by seven washings with water and by circling fire around it. However, one should discard a vessel that has been smelled or licked by a donkey, a camel, a dog, or similar animals.

Indeed, we have not abandoned the cow, the form [of the deity], nor the vessel of ghee. However, that ghee which has been licked by families [of outcastes] or touched by their vessels becomes pure through being released from the fire seven times.
Like a vessel, it attains purity through water poured from a ladle;
abundant food that is not smeared by crows and is not devoid of the Mothers.

Upon contact with the remnants of food, one should set aside the food and, having sipped water (ācamana), sprinkle the food and other items with water consecrated by the Astra-mantra. For oily objects, purification is achieved by drying them; for those with stains, by wiping them clean.
Purity from foul odors is achieved by removing the smell;
seats, beds, and vehicles become pure through earth and water.
One should carefully avoid the hands of servants, the hands of artisans, and the three types of merchandise.
When the staff is not defiled by water, one obtains fruits such as birds and the like;
however, by digging into a pure mountain after having stepped upon it, the staff becomes defiled.
The father [forbade him] from eating food that has been brought along a traveled road, or that which is pure yet touched by the rays of the sun;
that which is mixed with flies or hair, or that which has been trampled underfoot;
and that which is covered in dust or inhabited by ants—such food he saw being consumed.
Having extracted just that much, one should sprinkle it with water.
Purification of clarified butter occurs by sprinkling [water] or by the addition of ashes;
however, cooked food exceeding one *droṇa* that has been defiled by crows, dogs, or the like [requires further treatment].
Having extracted a mouthful [of the substance], there should be an equal amount of ghee;
one should sprinkle it with water infused with gold or else with silver water.
One should avoid that which has been licked by crows, dogs, and the like, or that which is less than a *droṇa* in measure.
And that food shall become purified by the Vedic chanting of the Brahmins,
especially at weddings with abundant food, when sacrifices have been performed,
on occasions such as consecrations, and even on the days of initiation festivals.
Food touched by crows or dogs shall become pure through digging,
filling, burning, as well as by scrubbing and smearing.
The ground becomes pure after seven days from the time of the cows' arrival;
likewise for one who has killed a Caṇḍāla, a Śvapaca, or a defiler of Śiva.
If one has been engaged in extremist views, having cast that aside with water and earth,
and having discarded earthen vessels, one should smear [the ground] with cow dung. Then,
by means of Brahmins who have been initiated, along with gold, kuśa grass, and water—
One should sprinkle the entire house with water; then it will undoubtedly become pure.
If a cohabitation occurs, one should prescribe burning and heating. Even if one has stayed for a single night, the waters—though they may themselves be impure—must be abandoned.
Even when step-wells, wells, and tanks have been defiled, purification must be performed;
likewise when they are defiled by bones, hides, donkeys, and the like, or otherwise contaminated.
Having drawn out a hundred jars, one should then pour the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) into small reservoirs,
stagnant bodies of water, or upon the surface of the earth.
Upon contact with impurities such as Caṇḍālas and the like, one should avoid that [place]; likewise,
that which is frequented by children, women, and so forth,
and that which is touched by mosquitoes and flies, does not become pure.
And Mahātalā was a woman with unbroken eyes, born of jewels.
The dwelling of a Brahmin, a temple of the gods,
and likewise the center [of the village], as well as the cow-pen of pure cows— these are always sacred.
Everywhere that which is impure exists through omission—
trees, leaves, flowers, and fruits upon the surface of the earth being of such a nature—
their leaves, flowers, and fruits are not at all defiled.

Actors, dancers, carpenters, leather-workers, and goldsmiths; those who grind sacrificial posts, eunuchs, and prostitutes—these are proclaimed as those whose food should not be eaten. So too are the wife’s paramour, the maker of arrows, and weavers.
A wheelwright, a washerman, a gambler, a thief,
one who lives by insulting others, a Śūdra, a teacher, and a beggar.
One who is a potter, a painter, a usurer, or a seller of leather; one who, knowing a woman is pregnant, approaches her for sexual intercourse;
one who bestows gifts in vain, one who exerts himself in useless labor, and one who causes dissension among the stages of life (āśramas).
