One who is born of a mixed womb, one who is devoid of Śiva-initiation,
one who subsists by the stage [of acting], one who is cruel, one who eats from a camp, and one who is a secret agent.
A physician, a poisoner, a professional actor, a beggar, a butcher, a seller of spirituous liquor, and one who is a hired servant at the commencement of a consecration—
whatever Brāhmaṇa, out of delusion, subsists by these occupations, [is excluded].

Even when the penance has been performed, he remains [an outcaste], for he is indeed [so]. All Caṇḍālas and those born of a Brāhmaṇa woman from a Kila, as well as the father [of such a child], are excluded by the seers of truth; so too is the wandering mendicant (parivrāj).

Those who have attained happiness through the wealth of kings or the wealth of asceticism— whether they wear matted hair (*jaṭin*) or carry the marks of a shaven-headed mendicant (*muṇḍiliṅga*), or are initiated into the Śiva sect (*śivadīkṣita*)— whosoever, having fashioned a *liṅga* or an image (*pratimā*) and the like in a place for digging,

should worship these [deities] as being self-existent (*svāyambhuva*) and so forth; when clearly worshipped with a thousand *ghora* mantras or ten thousand times, and having recited [the mantra] once, one should then perform peace (*śānti*) for oneself.
Indeed, by those desiring that [liberation],
[one should worship] Vīrabhadra, the Teacher (Śiva), Durgā, Kālī, and Reṇukā;
as well as Sthāneśa, Bhūteśa, the Gaṇas, and the heroic devotees.
One who worships [an image] that has its own primary importance is indeed censurable.
A *liṅga*, a *bera* (image), or a painting on a wall that has been mounted by a *śūdra* [is likewise censurable].
One should not, even in one's mind, perform the act of seeing or bowing there [to such an image].
Wherever it has been worshipped by a Śūdra, whether through delusion or even out of ignorance,
that entire life becomes censured as being equal to that of a Śūdra.
If the Lord is worshipped by others, such as the Kāpālikas and so forth, that [image] becomes fixed;
in seeing or saluting it, a great fault arises:
one becomes one-eyed, a cripple, a child, or even deaf, a physician, or a musician.
One who is devoid of worship for one's own sake, as well as one who has sexual union with a Śūdra woman;
even one who is uninitiated, though he may know the four Vedas, should not touch nor worship [the deity].
A Brahmin initiated into the Śaiva tradition should not [follow] the Vaikhānasa Sūtra,
nor the Pañcarātra compendium, out of a desire for wealth for the sake of others.
One should perform the worship of Śiva and Keśava for the duration of a year;
[otherwise], he is called a *devalaka* by all, and his performance of every rite is utterly despised. That fool who bears the conch, the discus, and the *liṅga* upon his body [is likewise condemned].
He should indeed be known as a heretic, excluded from all ritual acts.
When [the deity] has been worshipped with a thousand *ghora* [mantras], one should perform the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*).
Even one who has deformed nails, black teeth, or is afflicted by a great disease [is purified].

A celibate student who has no wife, one who consumes the meat of the middle part [of an animal], or one who possesses either deficient or redundant limbs, as well as a leper, one with variegated skin, or a child; |||
If a mendicant who is afflicted by a great sin (*mahāpātaka*) or is in a state of distress should perform a worship for the sake of another, the king and his kingdom will immediately perish.
To remedy that fault, one should perform a sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) accompanied by pacificatory rites (*śānti*).
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight, on the fourteenth day, under the asterism Ārdrā, and during the month of Caitra—
he who is devoid of fasting shall indeed be censured;
likewise, one who bears the heated seal and the like will suffer from leprosy and skin diseases.
And at the time of propitiating Hara, one should not, even in one's mind, allow the sight or speech of those who are naked or otherwise behave contrary to the rules.

If [the ritual] is performed for the sake of another by one engaged in fierce passion (*raudrāgama*), it is not to be done by one who knows the *siddhānta*; if it is to be done, it must be [performed with materials such as] stable [clay], and so forth.
Having discarded earthenware vessels, one should proceed with the sprinkling of water.

Whether on a seat, in bed, during bathing, or in rites such as the worship of Śiva, if one is accompanied by those spoken of as being of mixed caste (saṅkara), an expiation shall certainly be required. Thus ends the rule for expiation.
[Devoid of the daily ritual.]
If one performs the worship of Śiva at night when it was previously worshipped only once,
one should always perform the worship of the chosen liṅga, the fire-oblation, the act of giving, and the twilight devotions.
Except during a lunar eclipse, and except for rites performed for specific desires such as the *sādhyas*,
[one should perform] purification, sipping water, bathing, and the wearing of sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads.

Sprinkling with water, the Aghamarṣaṇa rite, meditation during the twilight hours, libations, the ritual placement of mantras on the hands and limbs, the recitation of mantras, and circumambulation— (fifth line)—
as well as salutation to the deities of the directions, are declared to be the daily obligatory rites (nityakarman).
Whether through knowledge or even through ignorance, in the case of each individual's anointing.
One should recite the *Ghora* mantra once for the purification of each respective sin.
If, out of negligence, one has enjoyed [forbidden things] at night after worshipping Śiva for the sake of worldly enjoyment,
or has been afflicted by fear of kings or thieves, one becomes pure by bathing once that [food] has been digested.

Having induced vomiting when there is indigestion and bathed, one should recite the Ghorasahasra mantra one hundred and eight times; then, having bathed again according to the rules, one should worship the chosen *liṅga*. He should then mutter the Śiva-mantra one hundred and eight times for each [recitation].
One who desires liberation should at all times perform the worship and meditation of Śambhu.

If one is deficient in the daily worship, or if one is deficient in worship at even a single time, one should recite the *Ghora* mantra a thousand times. If this occurs unintentionally, it is as stated; however, if done intentionally, double the aforementioned number is required.
For one who performs worship at one time, twice a day, or thrice a day,
a third [type of] prescribed expiation should be applied equally to him.
Starting from the second day, one should perform one thousand recitations with the Aghora mantra,
increasing by three hundred each subsequent day.
If the fortnightly worship is omitted here, one must recite twenty thousand *ghora* mantras;
if the monthly worship is omitted, one must recite ten thousand [mantras] of the *bahurūpin*.

For the omission of the worship of Śiva, purification is achieved through an increase of three times ten thousand [repetitions] per month for up to one year; beyond that, purification is attained through initiation (*dīkṣā*). If one’s own chosen *liṅga* has been stolen by thieves, rats, or humans, [the same applies].
If [the linga] is burnt, broken, cut, lost, or carried away by a stream,
one should recite the Aghora mantra one hundred thousand times and install another linga;
this is declared to be the purification for it, and it should be the same for the pedestal (piṇḍikā).
For movable and immovable images and their pedestals, that very same [purification] applies.
Minor impacts from stones and the like are purified by ten thousand recitations (*japa*);
major impacts are purified by double that amount for the Aghora mantra.
If the *liṅga* rolls of its own accord, one should recite the *ghora* mantra a thousand times;
if it rolls twice as much, one should recite it twice as many times; and if it rolls three or four times, one should add [the same number] accordingly.
And when the *liṅga* falls from the *bhrā* [cakra], one should recite the *bahurūpī* mantra one hundred thousand times.
[The falling of the *liṅga*: When the *liṅga* has fallen from the *ādhāra*, one should recite the *tāla* mantra together with the *tāleya*.
But in the case of one without support, it is doubled; and from desire, it is as before.
If the *liṅga* falls from a human being out of desire and with total intent,
and it becomes shattered, no expiation exists for that.
If a linga is broken or its phallus falls away, his sin shall be great;
for purification, he should perform three hundred thousand recitations of the Aghora mantra.
When a linga has been used for sexual desire, there is no atonement.
If the linga is touched by the foot, even when it has been stepped over, [one should perform] twenty thousand [repetitions].
If the linga is touched by water adhering to the foot, for the Ghora [mantra], ten thousand [are required]. In all such cases, the wise should perform a ritual bath of the linga.
When the *liṅga* is touched by phlegm (*śleṣman*) or by water mixed with phlegm,
it is proclaimed that [the sin] of his is threefold or twofold, according to its various forms.
If the linga is sprinkled with urine and water, [the penance] is two tens of thousands (20,000) along with that [fasting].
If it is sprinkled with blood, semen, menstrual blood, or urine, it is five tens of thousands (50,000).
If the linga is touched with water mixed with those [substances], it is reduced by one-quarter of that amount.
If the linga is touched by a person on an inauspicious lunar day (viṣṭi), one should recite the Aghora mantra one hundred thousand times.

Likewise, for a liṅga that has fallen into a pit containing used flower offerings (nirmālya), the penance consists of one hundred thousand [repetitions] plus half of that, performed while standing in water with one foot raised.
For a liṅga that has fallen into a pit of poison, the penance is one hundred thousand [repetitions] plus half of that.
If a Liṅga has been touched by outcaste people, the expiation prescribed there is one, two, or three hundred repetitions of the Ghora-Śambaram mantra.
If a Liṅga has been touched by a Śūdra, one should mutter the Ghora mantra five hundred times.
And when touched by fishermen, actors, and the like, ten thousand [repetitions] are required.
If the *liṅga* is touched by crows or similar creatures, one should recite [the mantra] twenty thousand times;
if the *liṅga* is gazed upon by outcastes (*śvapaca*), one should recite it fifty thousand times.
If that [liṅga] is touched, one should mutter the Ghoraśambara mantra twice as many times;
if a liṅga situated on either the left or right path is touched, one should mutter it ten thousand times.
If the liṅga is moved from its pedestal and remains free from defect,
one should install that very same one there and recite the Aghora mantra one hundred thousand times.
He should abandon that defective linga which has been used by outcastes and the like;
having installed another linga, he attains purification.
One who observes a fast for three nights regarding Nirvana, Īśvara, or the sacrificial fire,
as well as in the case of a ritual act, a religious observance, a gift, or its violation.

One should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times over them; with the Śaiva Gāyatrī, one should recite it one hundred times. If there is worship at the liṅga during the severing of the eight bonds—whether it be even a mere drop in the portion of Hari or in the portion of Brahmā.
When the water reaches the portion of Rudra, a great calamity arises.
At that time, whether the worship is performed once, twice, or thrice, it is declared to be fruitless; there will be misfortune for the king and distress for the kingdom.
It would result in great fault for either the doer or the one who causes it to be done;
or else, it should be performed at that very time, without specifying the month, fortnight, or day.
Having performed the sprinkling with water, thereafter one should perform the *śānti* oblation;
having recited the Aghora mantra more than a hundred thousand times, one should carry out the reconnection (*sandhāna*).
On the day of the sun’s transit (*saṃkrānti*), on the fourteenth, the eighth, and also on the festival days (*parvan*),
if the *harikṣa* is omitted, the merit is increased fourfold due to the omission of the obligatory rite.
When the consecration of the sacred thread (*pavitrāropaṇa*) has been performed during the months beginning with Āṣāḍha...

One should recite the Aghora mantra two hundred thousand times and then perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. Having performed the Pavitraka rite, even if one has departed for another village during the interval of the Cāturmāsya period, provided he is free from the aforementioned improper conduct.
If that vow of purification is performed without the sacred grass (*pavitra*) or without the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance,
and if the offering of *damanaka* flowers and other rites are not performed, one should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times.
If the vessel for the *arghya* offering and other vessels have not been dismissed by *śambara*,
or if they have been overturned or broken, one should recite two hundred of the *ghora* mantras.

When [the thread] has perished there, one attains success (*siddhi*) in the rosary (*akṣamālā*) after five hundred, then five thousand [recitations] in due order; for the *liṅga*, it is said to be half or a quarter [of that]. If the string is broken, one must perform nine thousand recitations of the *ghora* mantra.
While the thread is not yet worn out, one should recite a hundred times the terrible mantra.
Having washed with water those [rosaries] that have fallen to the ground or those that are knotted upon the rosary strings,
and having worshipped them, one should mutter the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times.
When the bell has been silenced, having recited the eight great [mantras] associated with the *liṅga*,
one should perform an expiation regarding the ritual implements for worship and so forth.

If [the food] has been touched by the foot, the mantra practitioner should recite the Aghora mantra two hundred times; for children and others, however, [he should recite it] ten thousand times from the foot [of the deity]. If the food offering is defiled by insects, meat, or other such things, he should purify it.
One should recite the Aghora mantra one hundred times; thereafter, for the fulfillment of desires, ten thousand times.
When an inferior offering is presented, there is always a terrible [result] for two hundred [verses];
when animal-part incense is offered, Sadyojāta is considered to be [the deity] for one hundred [verses].

If one steps on a *liṅga*, touches a Guru, or [touches] the fire of Śiva, purification is achieved through the recitation of the Aghora mantra twice; if this is done intentionally, it must be performed six times more.
For violating the command of the teachers Śivacaṇḍas, one hundred thousand [repetitions] are required;

for one who is deficient in their characteristics, one-quarter less than a hundred thousand is prescribed. For consuming the remains of offerings (nirmālya), purification is said to be achieved by a quarter of a hundred thousand.
And giving is equal to eating, when it is for that purpose and depends upon that.
Or, if one has consumed the remains of an offering unintentionally,
one should become pure by reciting the *Brahmapañcaka* one thousand and five hundred times.
Consuming [the offering] out of desire constitutes the initiation; there is no other atonement.
Upon stepping over the *nirmālya*, one should then recite the mantra ten thousand times with great intensity.
Touching it is equal to stepping over it, and violating it is equal to consuming it.
Of that deity, the first [offering] is considered to be the sixfold *nirmālya*.

Furthermore, the property of the deity, the food offering (*naivedya*) that has been presented, the substance belonging to Caṇḍa, and the remains of the offering (*nirmālya*); their characteristics are now described.
The property of the deity belonging to the city, fields, and so forth; that substance consisting of gold and clothing;
cooked food, perfumes, and other offerings; and the remains of Śiva’s meal that have been presented—these [are not to be taken].
Caṇḍasva and Caṇḍadatta [should be... (*........*). Even when it is discarded, O Lord of Gaurī, the *nirmālya* is not indeed a mere stool.
Of the *nirmālya*, Kravyāyomā would be the primary [deity], not the lowest.
It is held that from eating cow-flesh one's success is lost, and by transgressing [the rules], ruin follows;
from giving a boil [as a gift] one becomes a deer, and from burning [it], one becomes a Caṇḍāla.
A Śabara becomes deformed and his womanhood [is lost] from the touch [of such a person].
Whatever substance has been touched by flower-offerings (nirmālya), even that which is held in the hands— [for that],
one should prescribe the previously mentioned penance, lessened by one-third.
That which has entered the inner sanctum, such as flowers and other offerings, has gone to the human realm.
Its rays shall become her *nirmālya* (offering remains); of this there is no doubt.
And at the time of worship, [it applies] to the incenses, perfumes, flowers, and so forth.
The light of a lamp and the current of rivers are not, indeed, causes of defilement.

Regarding the installation [of an image], there is no "worn-out offering" (*nirmālya*) until the completion of the fourth rite. Food, medicine, flowers, water, leaves, fruits, and the like— *Note: The text provided contains a parenthetical note regarding the term *nirmālya*. In the context of Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava ritual traditions, this refers to the floral offerings made to a deity that have been consumed by it; traditionally, these are considered impure once offered. This passage establishes an exception for the period following consecration.*
The wise man should eat that which remains after Śivā has partaken, as her leftover food.
He who has been initiated by Śiva and possesses devotion toward them may take food that has not been given;
having recited the root mantra one hundred and eight times and having performed worship, he becomes purified.
Whatever food or sustenance is given to one's chosen *liṅga*, there is no doubt that by consuming it,
one obtains the complete fruit of the worship of Śiva.
And during the consecrations (*pratiṣṭhā*) of the gods, as well as for tanks and gardens,
one should mutter five hundred [times] after eating food elsewhere with the fifth [finger]. In the *Svāyambhuva*, *Daivika*, and *Bāṇa* [tantras], no *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings) is offered.
Nor is it the remains of offerings (nirmālya) from any [deity], nor likewise from any sacred seats (pīṭha).
Having eaten food at the *puṃsavana* rite, one should mutter the *vāmadeva* mantra;
likewise, he who eats on the eleventh day, or even on the twelfth day and so forth.
One should recite the Ghoramantra one hundred thousand or even three hundred thousand times;
during the monthly Śiva-śrāddha, one should recite the Ghoramantra three hundred times.
Likewise, [one should avoid] food that ends with the word *gaṇa* or *gaṇikā*, as well as food containing *sahya*.

And having eaten the food of a beggar, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for that. However, when eating at a cooked sacrifice, a wedding, a gift of a cow, the tying of the girdle of Muñja grass, or the tonsure ceremony, those who follow the traditional conduct do not incur sin.
Whichever caste eats raw food without grass,
one should combine the presiding deity of that caste with the presiding deity of one's own caste and recite [the mantra] one hundred times.
One should observe fasts for one, two, or three days in succession;
[these are the lords] of Puruṣa, Aghora, Vāma, and Jyotis, as well as the Brahmins and others.
Thus, O twice-born ones devoted to Śiva, it has been declared that Īśāna belongs exclusively to other castes.
When there is indigestion, a wise man should abandon recitation (*japa*), ritual bathing (*snāna*), worship (*pūjā*), and fire-oblation (*homa*).
Once it has been digested, he should bathe at the conclusion and then recite the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times.
Having touched one who has been initiated (*dīkṣita*), or one who is impure (*samucchiṣṭa*) belonging to his own caste,

the wise man should recite the mantra of the Lord of his own lineage one hundred and eight times. Having touched one who has been initiated, those deities should likewise bathe and then recite it two hundred times.
A Brahmin [should avoid] a Vaiśya and a Śūdra who are impure from remnants of food;
likewise, one who is consecrated for a sacrifice should fast for two nights or three nights while remaining consecrated.

And the lord of that caste, having unified [the mantras] with the lord of the caste, should recite them in sequence. Having touched the remnants of food belonging to a king or a Śūdra, one should fast for two days.
One should recite the mantra by combining the lords of those respective classes with the lord of one’s own class in their proper sequence.
Having touched those who have not been initiated, one should perform twice the previously mentioned penance.
Therefore, a king is purified by [the penance] of a Vaiśya, and a Vaiśya by that of a Śūdra.

A Śūdra, however, attains purification by a fourth part [of that penance]; of this there is no doubt. When one has consumed the leavings of a superior, one should recite the mantra associated with one's own caste; if one consumes the leavings of an inferior, the best [twice-born] should perform twice that very rite.
O dear one, having fasted and remaining pure, he should then consume the five products of the cow;
observing celibacy and sleeping on the ground—this is remembered as the vow to be observed in all cases.
One's own chosen *liṅga*, if it has fallen, as well as great lakes and ponds,
or [property] seized by bandits or monkeys and the like, may be recovered once again.
When that [time] arrives after an interval, how should the twice-born perform the worship?
Having performed a sprinkling with water, he should carry out the *śānti* oblation.
Having recited the Aghora mantra one hundred thousand times, and the root mantra an equal number of times,
one should perform worship at both lingas daily without indolence;
first having worshipped the eastern [linga], thereafter the western one.
This expiation has been declared for householders in due order.
A student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) should perform double the penance, and a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) should perform triple it;
a renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*) should perform quadruple the penance. [Thus ends the rule for penances.
If one fails to worship the gatekeepers, there will be great affliction by obstacles.

Having completed the *saṃhitā-homa* for that purpose, one should worship the gatekeepers. That worship, however, becomes as if not performed if the sequence of seats is omitted; it results in a state of instability if the ten purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) are omitted.
If a person utters [the mantra] incorrectly due to a deficiency in ritual observances,
or if the sequence is broken by hunger, thirst, and the like, they will be pierced.
If there is a failure of knowledge and so forth, confusion arises on the earth;
when the consecrated [substances] are in a state of instability, the Guru should then perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma).
One should perform all rites—whether daily (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), or for specific desires (*kāmya*)—exactly as prescribed.

In this world, if one lacks substances such as water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth, there shall be a deficiency in the corresponding limb [of the ritual]. If that specific substance is destroyed, it results in a loss corresponding to the part of the foot or the sense organ associated with that substance.
Just as there is a loss of speech when one is afflicted by disease, so too is there a loss of the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) when a limb is missing.
The ox will become talkative; then there will be a wound on its head or its body.
If [the bell] is deficient, there will be suffering from swelling; if it is struck when deficient, there will be injury.
Piśācas, rākṣasas, and others are tormented, and calamities arise;
this is known by those dwelling there when [the temple] is devoid of the offering of lamps.
Or, in the event of an omission due to a visual impairment, or when there is no mantra-reciter, [the offering] may consist of a smear of sacrificial oblation (*havis*),
or else of a portion of that [oblation], or even a portion of the food offering (*naivedya*).
If there is a failure to give [the gift], there will be the destruction of crops and the loss of the materials for that [ritual] limb;
in the absence of the offering of betel-leaf, there will be great hunger and thirst.
Or, if the curtain (*kāṇḍapaṭa*) is lacking, the householder will suffer from a disease of the mouth or eyes.
The destruction of the gods' presence occurs when one has worshipped the deity with that substance.
One should cause Śiva to be worshipped with double the usual offerings, and then perform a propitiatory *śānti* oblation;
or else, one should lead the Guru to perform a ritual ablution (*snapana*) when the [required] materials or limbs [of the rite] are deficient.
O Śivā, one should cause twice the amount to be given; the Saṃhitā-homa must be performed, or otherwise, the recitation of the Aghora mantra a hundred times for each of these substances.
Having recited the *ghora-mantra* one hundred and twenty,

four hundred, or six hundred times respectively for the offering of half, a quarter, or half of that [quarter], one should then cause those substances to be given to the deity in double quantity with the *yam-mantra*.
That wealth was not given even to Dantāya Śivaśaṅkara.
Having worshipped the deities, the preceptor should, at the conclusion, give [the offerings] with the *stvam* mantra;
or he should cause the desired bathing to be performed with twice the amount of materials or an equal amount.
If one performs the recitation of the Śatāghora mantra during the obligatory, occasional, or optional rites,
yet omits the triad beginning with water for the feet (pādya), then [one should proceed] from Sadyojāta, Nareśāna, and Īśāna.
The practitioner, having performed the recitation one hundred times, should apply [the substance] starting from the feet in double the amount;

or that substance may be used alone, or with *dūrvā* grass, flowers, and unbroken rice (*akṣata*). When the oil massage (*abhyaṅga*) is being performed, it is considered that the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya-mantra*) should be recited one hundred times.

If the rites of anointing, bathing, and so forth are deficient, one should recite the *hṛdaya-mantra* a hundred times and then cause [the rite] to be performed twice over. Furthermore, if the oil for the limbs (*aṅgataila*) and other such items have not been consecrated,
there shall be an oblation according to the *saṃhitā* during daily, occasional, and optional worship.
When the previously calculated [number] has been subtracted by the arrows and diminished, one should perform the *saṃhitā-homa* and then carry it out doubled; one should act according to this rule.
If the previously prepared fragrant substances are lost, purification is achieved by means of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*);
one should immediately recite [the mantra] a hundred times and then perform oblations with those same materials.
Twice as much, or even the same amount, or when [the offering] is deficient and lacking flowers; conversely, when flowers have been given, one should recite the Lord's mantra a hundred times.
Then one should give double that amount, followed by the terrible incense and the night-rite;
having recited [the mantra] at the end, one should then offer double the gift for the incense and the night-rite.
When the time for the removal of the collyrium has passed and [the lamp] has been extinguished a hundred times,
one should perform the consecration again and have it placed within a row of lamps.
Or, if it has been touched by fire from the mouth of a mouse or similar creature, [one should likewise restore it].
Whether it be a small image of the *liṅga*, the body [of the deity], or the like, even if it has fallen into the hands of non-Buddhists (*vāmaga*),
the king will suffer from disease. Having purified the defilement with fire, one should install the Supreme Lord (*Parameśvara*) together with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*).
Having worshipped the Lord of the gods with coconut water,
one who possesses the measure of the subtle atom (aṇumātra) should perform the fire-oblation of the two [deities] within the fire.
If fire should arise, one should perform pacification rites upon the *liṅga*, the image (*bera*), and so forth.
If the installations and the garments are consumed by fire, then one should act as follows:

When [the house] has been burnt by fire, one should perform the ritual sprinkling (*saṃprokṣaṇa*) as part of the rite; at that time, one should carry out the pacification (*śānti*) and perform the re-consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) of the dwelling.
One should perform the sprinkling of the temple and carry out the ritual bathing for the deity.
(5th line) In the event that the breaking of the sacrificial post or other such incidents occur, one should perform the expiation prescribed for them.
If the *liṅga*, the image (*bera*), and so forth are endowed with the rites of re-consecration (*sandhāna*) and the like by means of fire,
but then assume another color, they should be abandoned if they are of human origin; however,
for those of self-manifested origin (*svāyambhuva*) and the like, there is a rite of counter-action (*pratikriyā*).

One should perform the ritual with the *keti* mantra accompanied by sprinkling (*saṃprokṣaṇa*) and the offering of incense for the vital limbs (*prāṇyaṅga*). One should recite the fifth [mantra] one hundred times; however, in the event of a deficiency of lamps, one should recite the *ghora* [mantra] three hundred times, and subsequently double the number of lamps.

O Lord of gods, one should cause [the recitation] to be given; likewise, even upon the interruption of the protective lamp, one should cause it to be recited twice as much. Having performed the ceremonial bath for the deity to whom the sacrificial food has been offered, one should subsequently cause the twice-born invitees to be fed with sacrificial food.
Then, when the screen-cloth has been removed, one should recite the armor-mantra two hundred times.
[The Expiation for Festivals] Having determined in advance the specific month and lunar day of the pilgrimage site for each year,
those by whom the festival was previously observed on that particular day [must perform the expiation].
Accompanied by nine days and so forth, with the sounding of kettledrums and other instruments;
for that [period] is indeed tripled during the fire [element], or even doubled on those days.
If that [rite] is performed otherwise, it will bring harm to the kingdom and the king;
therefore, having first performed a propitiatory rite (*śānti*), one should carry out the festival as before.
However, it should take place within another month, or perhaps during that very same month.
On the second day, or on that same day, having performed the offerings for the image and the fire-oblations according to the prescribed sequence,
the festival should be conducted according to its rules;
however, it is ordained that the raising of the banner should take place three days prior.
Thus has the procedure been declared; it should be inferred in the same way even for a double [liṅga]. However, if the liṅga is of self-originated (svāyambhuva) origin, this procedure is prescribed.
O twice-born ones, whether it be a human *bāṇaliṅga*, a divine one, or even one made of clay, one should pass a month, a day, or a lunar mansion at a sacred site; otherwise,
on whatever day the festival was previously established by the ancestors, that [observance] bestows the fruit of prosperity.
During a disturbance in the kingdom, in times of famine, and when there is danger from the king and so forth;
If, due to the lack of wealth or other fears, it becomes impossible to perform [the rite] as previously described,
then even in that case, one should first perform a propitiatory rite (śānti).
Or one may perform the festival even with fewer days according to the previous method;
for if all [days] are omitted, the festival is lost on that auspicious day when it has become too brief.
If a total omission of this [rite] occurs, a great fault arises;
one should then perform a rite of pacification (*śānti*), a pacificatory oblation (*śāntihoma*), and an oblation to the image (*mūrtihoma*).
By means of this procedure, [one may perform] the rites concerning mountains, omens, and so forth.
A festival commenced without the propitiation of obstacles and other deities leads to the destruction of the kingdom.
Then one should perform a pacifying homa and carry out the renewal festival once the banner has been raised, following the consecration of the bull.
If the cows perish, one should then perform a propitiatory fire-sacrifice (*śāntihoma*) according to the prescribed rules.
There, one should conquer [the obstacle] by means of the bull-sacrifice (*vṛṣayāga*) at the base of the flagstaff (*dhvajadaṇḍa*).
However, you should mentally perform the placement (*nyāsa*) and other rites upon the flag with the *dhvaja* mantra.
If the hoisting of the banner is omitted, O King, one should predict danger.
Then the minister, having performed a propitiatory rite, should raise the banner again.
If the circumambulation of the banner is omitted, it brings misfortune to the village and other areas.
One should likewise perform a peace-offering (*śāntihoma*) for the cessation of all defects;
whether the altar is devoid of [the usual] features, deficient, or possesses the [proper] characteristics, it bestows auspiciousness.
Then, having performed a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma), one should fashion the Goddess with all her characteristic marks;
even a staff devoid of such marks brings auspiciousness to the principal deity.
Then one should perform either a *mūrtihoma* or a *śāntihoma*.
If [the image] is deficient in its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), it will bring about danger;
therefore, for a defective image, one should then proceed with a *śāntihoma*.

When there occurs a fracture or breakage of the staff, the secondary staff, the shoulder-piece, or other parts, one should then perform a propitiatory fire-sacrifice; if it is broken, one should proceed with another rite of pacification.

If the banner is devoid of auspicious marks, it brings fear to this kingdom; therefore, one should install another banner endowed with the proper marks for the sake of prosperity. One should perform rites of pacification when planting a banner that lacks auspicious characteristics.
In the same way, one should perform atonement for a bull; thus, one who removes the fault shall bring about purification.
If it is upright, variegated, and not deficient, one should recite the mantra of Īśa a hundred times.
If it is downward-pointing and devoid of a staff, it does not lead to any fault whatsoever.
If there is snapping of a rope, there is fear of injury; one should perform a propitiatory fire-offering (*śāntihoma*).
If bitten by a rat or similar creature, one should then perform a propitiatory fire-offering with garments and other materials.
If the banner falls to the ground, it portends the ruin of the kingdom;
having then performed a propitiatory fire-offering (*śānti-homa*) according to the prescribed rule, one should raise the flagstaff again.
When the flagstaff is broken or otherwise damaged, one should then perform a rite of pacification (*śānti-karman*).
O twice-born ones, one should raise another banner within seven days.
O twice-born ones, if each preceding [banner] is auspicious and there is little loss,
then one should perform the *mūrti-homa* or even the *śānti-homa*.
If this banner, while being raised, is overcome by wind or other elements, or if it becomes bent,
one should perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma) for the pacification of the resulting defects.
If the darbha-garland is missing, one should then perform a propitiatory oblation (śānti-homa);
thereafter, one should wrap a staff possessing the proper characteristics with the darbha-garland.
Whether it be a rope or a garland of *darbha* grass, according to the rule of circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa*),
if that [staff] has been joined to the staff, one should recite the *ghora* mantra a thousand times and lead the *darbha* garland and other items from the front in the order of circumambulation.
Even if the staff and the *kūrca* are present, if one recites the Aghora mantra three hundred times,
and if the staff is missing from the banner, the presence of the Bull (*vṛṣabha*) will not occur; therefore,
the preceptor should then cause the Aghora mantra to be repeated three hundred times.
If the bell falls to the ground, one should recite three hundred [times] the mantra of Dakṣiṇa;
for, O Śivā, the Lord of the Staff brings about the desired bond only when he has ascended.
If the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the water-pot (*kumbha*) has not been performed at the time of hoisting the banner,
one should perform the hoisting of the banner by means of the piercing of the bull-pot (*vṛṣakumbhavibheda*).
At the conclusion, having performed the propitiatory oblation (*śāntihoma*) and having consecrated the pots as before, [the rite is complete].
Then, having performed the placement of the mantra (mantranyāsa), [one should contemplate] the stainless [reality] within the lotus of the heart.
At that time, if the consecration with the water from the Varuṇa-pitcher has not been performed,
one should perform a recitation (*japa*) of one hundred repetitions for each [deity] using their respective mantras.
When that banner has been raised and suspended from the ring,
[a delay] of one, two, three, or four mātrās does not constitute a fault.
One should recite the Aghora mantra a hundred times, reaching down as far as the sun; then,
having performed the propitiatory fire-offering (*śānti-homa*) over the banner that has been lowered and subsequently raised, one should perform the worship of the Bull (*vṛṣabha*).
If the drum is struck at an improper time, delusion arises among the people of the world.
Therefore, having first performed a peace-offering (*śānti-homa*), one should then strike the drum.
One should not perform the recitation of the *Bṛhattāla* unless the rite of pacification has been carried out.

Prior to the commencement of the festival, when the invocation of the deity has been performed, that presence of the gods and others remains; however, if the invocation of the deity is omitted, that presence does not exist.

One should perform the *śānti*-oblation as before and carry out the invocation of the deities. When Keśava, Ambā, Skanda, Vighneśa, Bhānu, and Caṇḍeśvara [are present], there is no fault if they are not offered oblations; nor is there any other oblation required in such an emergency.
One should cause the deities to descend into that [image] by means of the hoisting of the banner;
one should perform the striking of the drum in exactly the same manner.
This applies when the drum-skin and so forth, or the gold and other materials, have undergone damage such as a split in the mouth [of the drum].
Having recited the Aghora-weapon mantra a hundred times, one should then strike another drum;
likewise, having taken up another bell, one should perform [the ritual] as before.
Or if the nose falls to the ground, one should recite the Aghora mantra three hundred times;
likewise, if the foot falls to the ground at the time of the *bali* offering.
At that time, one should perform a peace-offering (*śāntihoma*) if the kingdom is brought to a state of distress;
if a kettle-drum falls to the ground, there will be great danger for the king.
Having then performed the peace-offering, one should worship the kettle-drum with devotion from the heart.
Or if the sacrificial hall has been consumed by fire, or if it is deficient in its characteristic features.
Whether it be a celestial chariot, a sacrificial altar, a kingdom, or a state of distress,
one should cause it to be performed correctly, whether during a festival or even when there is no festival.
Every day, from the present until the day of the pilgrimage site (*tīrtha*), there should be a *śānti*-oblation.
Having ascertained that festival and the characteristics of the sacrificial hall (*yāgaśālā*),
one should perform a *śānti* rite for a single day to eliminate those defects.
This procedure is general for consecration and installation,
as well as for bathing, sprinkling, monthly worship, and the like;
for the replacement of threads, for the limbs of festivals, or for other rites such as the restoration of ruins and the laying of bricks.
One should employ [the ritual] here in obligatory, occasional, and optional rites;
likewise in the preparation for sacrifice, but at the conclusion of the journey.
A pacifying oblation (*śāntihoma*) should be performed for one day on both occasions:
at the commencement of the principal rite and upon the loss of any ritual implements.
One should recite two hundred or three hundred times the *Śānti-homa-ghorāṇu* mantra.
If [the ritual] is deficient or if the components of the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) are missing, one should then perform the *Śānti-homa*.
To remedy that defect, one should prepare the sacrificial mound as before.
Just as it would be with the Śiva-pitcher, the Vardhanī, and the covered jars,
so too it should be with the other jars that are part of the festival;
there may be a breakage, a hole, or a crack, according to their specific characteristics.
For the removal of disease, one should perform a peace-offering (*śāntihoma*) and the recitation (*japa*) of the Aghora mantra four hundred and five times,
or three hundred times.

Having brought the nine jars beginning with the *kumbha*, one should perform the installation as previously described. The *vardhanī* and the *āyukumbha*, or the jars presided over by the Lords of the Vidyeśvaras,
may either be devoid of golden lotuses or provided with a small amount of gold.
By reciting the *Aghora* mantra one thousand times, they would cause poverty for the performer;
therefore, to eliminate that fault, one should again bestow what is established by the scriptures.
Furthermore, those who are deprived of their garments from the ritual jar (*kumbha*) onwards will suffer disease.
Having recited the mantra one thousand times for the Ghorā mantra, the Guru should again present a garment;
even in the absence of the five gems and other such items, he should perform the rite in this very same manner.

If the binding of the auspicious thread (*kautukabandha*) is performed on an inferior limb as previously described, that sacrifice is said to be fruitless; therefore, for the pacification of that defect, [the following should be done].
Then one should perform a pacifying *homa* and bind the protective amulet (*kautuka*);
one should then recite the Aghora mantra three hundred times while applying the ointment to the limbs.
In the same way, when that [consecration] has been performed by means of fire, having immediately performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*),

the binding of the *kautuka* (sacred thread) is prescribed for the deity stationed in its former place. Or, having brought [the deity] to the pavilion or similar location, one should mutter the *ghora* mantra fifty times.
In the absence of the *balita*, *lāta*, and other such rhythms (*tāla*), one should recite the *dakṣiṇa* [mantra].
Whether she is wearing sandals or acting as a carrier, the dancer should offer handfuls of flowers;
likewise, in the event of a fall, a lapse in the dance, or the falling of her sandals.
Having performed the ritual bathing three hundred times with the formidable mantra and one thousand times with the *pādukā* [mantra], one should then lead the circumambulation of the *pādukā*.
In the event of the loss of three hundred lamps, one should provide twice as many;
if there is a deficiency of vehicles during a festival, it brings all manner of faults upon men.

One should perform the ceremonial bathing (*snapana*), the propitiatory fire-offering (*śāntihoma*), and the return procession (*pratiyāna*) during times of rain, great winds, national unrest, or great danger.
Circumambulating the village is not desired; rather, circumambulating the sacred abode (*dhāma*) is desired.

Then the best of the twice-born should perform the ritual bathing (*snapana*) and the propitiatory fire-offering (*śāntihoma*). O lords of brahmins, if while a festival for Śiva is underway on a single site, a festival for another deity is held there, it constitutes an encroachment upon the village.
For the sake of averting those defects, one should perform a propitiatory fire-sacrifice (*śāntihoma*);
likewise, one should perform an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for the Mothers and the two *Rasṭāras*.
If both Aṅgāṅgaja and Bali are long, they do not bring about defects;
however, if Vāmabhairava is established [as long], there will be the destruction of the village.

If the *bali* offering is given through negligence, one should perform a propitiatory fire-sacrifice (*śāntihoma*). If the *bali* sacrifice is performed while resorting to a deserted village, then one should know that the destruction of the kingdom has occurred; yet, if a propitiatory rite is performed, [the danger] shall be averted.

O best of the twice-born, [it is auspicious] when there is a strong foundation, or when it is enclosed by a temple; likewise, when it is situated on a site suitable for the limbs of a deity, especially one that is not occupied by another; and similarly, O best of the twice-born, when it is on a site that is well-proportioned and located at a distance [from impurities].
Endowed with various trees and possessed of many kinds of trees, [such a site] is superior to others; the opposite of this brings about misfortune.
The dwelling place of the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas is called the "excellent" (śreṣṭha);
the interior dwelling is distinguished as the "inner site" (antarvāstu), while the exterior site is for the offering of oblations.
In one case, that which is more powerful is designated as "superior.

Indeed, for those who are unable [to follow the primary rule], one should perform it in this way according to the secondary alternative (*anukalpa*). For those who teach the secondary alternative, one should perform a *śānti* oblation.
If the canopy is inferior, one should perform the recitation for a number equal to one hundred times ten million.
Even if the banner is missing, it shall be so through the recitation of the hundredfold *ghora* mantra;
O best of the twice-born, there is no fault at night when the banner is missing.
If the sacrificial offerings (*balidravya*) are lacking, however, affliction by hunger arises for men.
Therefore, having performed the *mūrtihoma*, one should carry the offering (*bali*) at the end of the procession.
When the *bali* offering has been omitted in a temple, one should recite the *ghora-śata* [mantra] one hundred times;
in whichever direction the village or other place lacks the *bali*, there one should perform the *saṃhitā-huti*.
At the time of departure, or at its conclusion, one should offer the oblation (*bali*) while reciting the mantra of the respective directional lord a hundred times. However,
if the oblation is devoid of food, famine arises upon the earth.
Then, having performed the peace-offering (śāntihoma), one should present the bali offering consisting of cooked rice and the liṅga.
In cases such as its cutting, breaking, or falling, one should likewise prescribe an offering (*bali*).
Having made that *liṅga* very firm, one should worship the Weapon (*astra*) deity until it has departed.
Having performed the *saṃhitā-homa* in that place,
he should then lead [the fire] clockwise from the position of the foot of the *ābhyatalliṅga*.
If the food falls, one should discard it and prepare fresh food, honoring it;
having completed [the offering], one should perform the *saṃhitā-homa* as before.
But if the vessel for the *bali* offering falls, one should mutter the *aghora-mantra* a hundred times.
Having taken another [substance] for the breaking [of the seal] and so forth, one should deposit the offering material (bali-dravya).
If the ten weapons or protective shields, having been gathered on the ground, should fall down,
then one should perform a propitiatory fire-offering (*śāntihoma*), for it brings about fever.
If [the implements] consist of wood or other materials, provided they are joined by cutting, splitting, and so forth,
one should prepare them and likewise fashion other [implements] as well;
having consecrated them with their respective mantras, one should perform the specific rites.
Having recited the mantra following the sequence for the iron-born [weapon], one should lead it to its placement at the end.
When the spear-weapon (*śūlāstra*) has fallen, there is danger for the king;
in that case, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) starting from the southeast direction (*dhāma*), accompanied by the worship of the weapon.

O twice-born ones, if cutting, splitting, or other such injuries occur, the rite should be performed as a penance by one who acts in accordance with the rules, or the festival should be performed as before using another weapon.
They should complete their respective tasks according to their specific sequence of rites;
then one should perform the sprinkling (*saṃprokṣaṇa*) by means of the consecration of the King of Weapons (*astrarāja*).
Whether at the time of departure or at any other time, when the image (*bera*) or other [objects] have fallen, [this rite is to be performed].
The king meets with death; he should immediately perform the remedial rites.
When the unmanifest image has fallen, the Lord himself descends from his source.
Whether it be two or three cubits, one should gradually lead it upward from there.
The Saṃhitā-śānti and the homa for peace, as well as the peace-offering personified by the oblation,
the ritual bathing known as the "Thousandfold," and [the rites] performed at every rhythmic beat according to the sequence of ten thousand.
Or one may perform the ceremonial bathing (*snapana*) or the recitation (*japa*) ten thousand times with the *ghorānu-mantra*.
The food offering (*naivedya*) may also be common; one should then carry out the remaining rites of the festival.

In the case of a deficiency in the ancillary rites (*aṅga*), one should perform the remedial rite (*niṣkṛti*) beginning with the reconstitution (*sandhāna*), as prescribed by the rules for subsequent performance.
One should perform the rite of formal acceptance (adhivāsana) and so forth immediately.
Having set aside the consideration of the month, lunar mansion, lunar day, day of the week, and so forth, the preceptor should perform the ablution again,
either five hundred or one hundred times.
Furthermore, having bound the *snapaka* and tied the *kautuka*, one should arrange the festival offerings;
and in the case of those deficient in limbs such as the head, one should perform the rites according to the prescribed procedure for such cases.
There too, the wise preceptor should perform the joining of that [image] with another body and the festival,
accompanied daily by peaceful fire-offerings.
O Lord, when [the deity] has entered another abode, the best of the twice-born should perform [the rite];

in the measurement of the womb-door and so forth, it must be endowed with the eight [proportions], and not otherwise. Then, having prepared the image (bera), one should indeed proceed according to the instructions for the subsequent rites.
And at the conclusion of the installation rite, preceded by the ritual sowing of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa),
O Lord, one should cause a festival to be held for nine days or other such festivals;
O initiates of Śiva, this ritual procedure is the same even for a liṅga.

O twice-born ones, when the protective cord has been tied outside the festival village, if it is then brought inside, misfortune befalls the king; for the sake of pacification [the following should be done].
Then one should perform the *śānti*-oblation as well as the *saṃhitā*-oblation;
if the preceptor does not perform the rite while standing on the ground,
the village is known to lose its stability, or half of it, by the multiformed one.

The mantra-practitioner should recite [the mantra] five hundred times even if [the ritual vessel] falls; indeed, it is exactly the same. If, while the rites for the deity have begun, whether over many days or on a single day, the death of the preceptor should occur due to negligence or by disease and the like—
If the Pavitra priest should die, how indeed should one act in that situation?
One’s brothers or else one’s son should have the rites performed according to the prescribed rule.
If a teacher here loses his brother, he should bind the Sarasvata vow upon his disciple;
having bathed with his clothes on, he should perform that rite according to the prescribed ritual.
If others do not perform [the rite], O supreme gurus, the parents' deed is accomplished;
having bathed right there in that hall, you should sleep near it and partake of food.
Having performed the rites up to the end of the sacrifice according to the rules, whether during a festival or even when it is not,
the disciple— having bound the *pratisara* amulet and bathed while fulfilling his formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*)—
should commence the bull-sacrifice (*vṛṣayāga*) on the right side of the staff.
Facing north, with a focused mind, he worshipped him.
One should recite the *Bṛhattāla* and worship the deities upon the staff;
there, one should offer the *devayāna* oblation at the end of that particular day.
Having performed it twice in number, whether in a village or even in a temple,
one should likewise perform two circumambulations with the staff.
At that time, one should perform within the sacred ford all appropriate rites,
such as bathing and propitiatory ceremonies (*śāntika*), for the sake of removing those defects.
Having had the Vedic ritual performed there, the twice-born should then lead [the deceased] forward.
And likewise at birth or at death, by means of that [bond] which has formed a continuous attachment.
Having consumed the remnants of the oblation (*hutaśeṣa*), the Guru should reside in that very place;
as well as the king, the chief queen, her father, brother, and son.
If the domestic priest or the chief minister dies, there is danger from the king;
at that time, when the one who offers the oblation has fallen, one should mutter the *śaṃsata* mantra a hundred times.

If the bearer of the weapon, the missile, or the image of the Lord falls to the ground, the Guru should mutter the Ghoramantra one hundred times; for the Śaṅkara-weapon, he should mutter it twice that amount.
In the case of the lamp of the fire-offering or the food offering being overturned, [the same penance applies].
The most excellent guru should perform the expiation according to the method previously described,
in the event of the omission of worship at one of the junctions of the day (*sandhyā*) and so forth,
or the neglect of the water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings, as well as the products of the cow (*gavya*), flowers, incense, and lamps.
For if the ritual task is lost, or if the materials for the oblation are lost,
or if the fire has been extinguished— whether it was attended by Śiva or devoid of Śiva— as before;
or if [the sacrificer] is deprived of mounting the chariot, men on earth would become low-born.
Then, having performed the peace-offering (śānti-homa), one should proceed with the mounting of the chariot.
Whether at the time of mounting a chariot, or even at the time of dismounting;
or at the time of bringing a chariot, or if there is the death of a cow or a Brahmin.
The best of the twice-born should perform the *diśāhoma* and the great ablution (*mahāsnāna*) in that very place, even without the death of the king.
If a Kṣatriya dies during the [period] of the Nāgas and so forth, or a Vaiśya or Śūdra during the period of women and so forth,
or even if there is the cutting off of limbs and the like, the king’s sin will be great.
[One should perform] the Diśāhoma, the Mūrtihoma, and the Śāntihoma...
The best of practitioners should perform [the rite] for the destruction of those defects.
If the umbrella falls to the ground or is torn by the wind,
it is a cause for the destruction of the king, the chariot, and the worship.
Then, having performed the oblation to the quarters (*diśāhoma*) and the ceremonial bath (*snapana*) for Parameṣṭhin,
the Guru should procure another parasol and cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited.
Having consecrated the parasol according to the prescribed rite as before, the preceptor should lead it forth;
however, if the banner falls to the ground upon the staff above the fire-altar.
When [the image] has been mounted, there will be fear for the king from Śṛṅgins and other enemies, as well as from men and other kings.
To avoid those evils, one should have a ritual bath performed for Śivā.
When all the parts of the chariot have fallen, one should lead [the body] for the ritual bath;
when the support of the elements has been severed and the parts of the chariot have been cut and cast down.
Furthermore, having performed another [rite], one should use the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and water purified with *kuśa* grass;
at the time of departure, if a breakage of chariots or other vehicles should occur on the ground,
or if such an event happens in that place or dwelling, one should perform [this rite] at the conclusion of the journey for the pacification of the fault.

If one intends to perform the rites of reconnection (*sandhāna*), one should lead [the deity] along the path of the *Rathantara* chant. Having brought either a palanquin or another vehicle and placed Maheśvara upon it,
one should install the Lord of the Gods of gods in his own abode as before.
Then, having had the chariots bathed by Caṇḍālas, Svapacas, and others,
one should perform a propitiatory fire-offering at the conclusion.
If a great quarrel arises at the time of viewing the diversion,
one should then perform a *śānti-homa* and recite the *aghora-mantra*.
Upon seeing the diversion, one should perform the *saṃhitā-homa*.
If the rite of the collyrium-offering (nīrāñjana) is deficient, the expiation is as previously stated.

If the final bath at the end of the vehicle [of initiation] is deficient, or if the propitiatory oblation (*śāntihoma*) is omitted, there is a lack of divine presence; the remedial rite is the oblation to the image (*mūrtihoma*).
One should perform the ritual bathing (*snapana*) and the pacificatory fire-offering (*śāntihoma*) for the sake of achieving the presence (*sannidhi*) [of the deity].
Whether in a region presided over by inferior beings or when the path of the gods has been set in motion,
one should perform an abundant ritual bathing and a most extensive pacificatory fire-offering.
If the image is devoid of oil-anointing, men here will suffer from diseases of the head;
having then performed a propitiatory fire-offering, one should perform the oil-anointing. [If the image is devoid of a dancing form...]
If the festival of the Dancing Form is omitted on the day previously intended, everyone becomes a sinner; therefore, one should perform a propitiatory rite for that purpose.
One should subsequently perform the circumambulation of Naṭeśa at the desired time;
if there is an interruption in the taking up of the machine, that procession would become fruitless.
Having then performed a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma), one should carry out the ritual giving as before.
If there is a deficiency in the king’s hunting expedition, defeat will occur.
Therefore, having performed a propitiatory fire-offering (*śānti-homa*), one should lead [the king] to the desired hunting ground.
If the site is deficient in auspicious features (*kautuka-tīrtha*), there will be no presence of *gambhā* and other such [auspicious elements].
When the rites for the sacred site have been performed before sunrise at the *tīrtha*,
there shall be expiation through the sequential *śānti*-oblation and the *saṃhitā*-oblation.
When this raising of the flag at Kautukatīrtha has been performed,
one should either arrange for the auspicious bath elsewhere or avoid it altogether. If the powder festival (*cūrṇotsava*) or its constituent part is omitted, there will be affliction by disease.
The Śāntihoma should be performed as a subsidiary (aṅga) to the primary rite (aṅgin), and the Saṃhitāhuti should be offered within its constituent parts.
Alternatively, one may perform it when the sacred abode (dhāman) has been desecrated, or during a ritual bath at a holy ford (tīrthasnāna).
When the sequence is deficient, one should perform the Cūrṇotsava and the Saṃhitāhoma.
O twice-born ones, if that great sacred site (*mahātīrtha*) should be desecrated, that sacrifice would become fruitless;
therefore, having performed a rite of pacification (*śānti*) for that purpose, one should then proceed with the rites of the sacred site.
Previously, when [an obstacle] occurred at that place such as a river and so forth,
one should then perform a *śānti* oblation for the sake of pacifying those faults, as follows:
The subsidiary rites for the sacred sites (*tīrtha*) should be performed; the *saṃhitā-homa* bestows what is desired.
If a human being is born within the temple, there will be great fear for the king.
Having cast away the earth and other materials from that location to the outside, [one should proceed].
One should sprinkle with cow-dung water that place where he has passed away;
then one should perform the auspicious sprinkling (*puṇyāha-prokṣaṇa*) for that location.
However, if he has died or given birth there, one should then dig a pit suitable for burial.
Having wiped it clean, one should fill it with pure clay;
then, having washed the nearby sacrificial pit and other vessels, one should smear the ground with cow dung.
One should perform the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) rite there, followed by sprinkling with cow-products (*gavya*), and proceed according to the sequence;
one should also provide a communal meal for the Śaivas and perform the sprinkling of water over the food.
If the ritual bathing (*snapana*) and the peace-offering (*śāntihoma*) are to take place in the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*),
one should perform what is appropriate for the peace-offering in the presence of the half-pavilion (*ardhamaṇḍapaka*).

In the shrine of the image, one should perform the propitiatory fire-sacrifice (*śāntihoma*) and the ritual bathing (*snapana*), even without [the presence of] water; however, if it is within the food-hall (*annasālā*), one should instead employ the sprinkling of water. Therefore, for the deities residing in that hall, there shall be a ritual bathing accompanied by the propitiatory fire-sacrifice.
One should sprinkle the seat and other items with cow-products for the sake of purification. One should discard earthen vessels and wash wooden ones with water.
The kitchen and the exterior should be cleansed by sprinkling, followed by offerings to the quarters.
In places such as a cooking hearth (*pākasthāna*) and when there is the presence of a corpse or moisture,
one should first effect purification as before and then perform the *paryagnikaraṇa* rite.
At that time, one should perform either the *diśāhoma* or the *mūrtihoma*.
One should perform rites for pacification outside the two enclosures;
if mortals die within twelve daṇḍas of the temple, [the following applies].
Then, having abandoned [the village], I shall perform the obligatory, occasional, and optional rites;
if they are performed [here], there would be the destruction of the village, therefore one should lead [the deity] for the sake of that to the ritual bath.

Furthermore, when a person dies in a dwelling, they are reborn here as a beast, a bird, a wild animal, or a serpent at night; such is the miserable condition of men in this world. One should sprinkle cow-dung plaster there and apply the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).

If the ceremonial bathing (*snapana*) takes place in the inner sanctum (*garbhageha*), one should not perform the propitiatory fire-offering (*śāntihoma*). In that case, the bathing alone should be performed, and one should arrange for a half-pavilion (*ardhamaṇṭapa*);
having gone there, one should consecrate with sprinkling (*saṃprokṣya*) the deities situated within the pavilion of the deity.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should perform the *śānti*-oblation;
all of this is common to both festivals and non-festivals.
If even a single drop of blood falls upon the ground from a temple, an assembly hall, or the body of a cow or a Brahmin, the death of the king shall occur.

Then, one should perform a pacifying fire-offering (*śānti-homa*) and feed an incalculable number of Brahmins. At that time, the preceptor (*ācārya*) should receive a turban, an upper garment, a lower robe, or a diamond-threaded cord; or else, his head may be burnt by fire, for he is in a state of great distress.
If there should be an affliction by fever in the village, then for the pacification of that fault,
the preceptor, having bathed and become pure, should perform a propitiatory fire-sacrifice (śānti-homa).
O best of sages, it should be done in this very same manner by the performer and the patron.
When there is the possibility of the theft and so forth of clothing, bedding, seats, and the like,
or when one is bitten by rats and other such creatures, the results are here stated in their respective order.

In the corner or [the intermediate direction], there shall be prosperity; at the edge, it is proclaimed as enmity. During the birth of a son or the acquisition of fame, the period is peaceful in its middle.

If it falls on the edge, it is declared that there will be either disease or death from another cause. Having folded the cloth three times [and offered it] to Brahmā, Indra, Yama, and Agni, a great fault is declared; this fault is not mentioned in any other context.
In this very same way, for those men who have been bathed at that time,
one should cause them to recite a thousand of the *ghora* mantras and then provide them with new garments.
This applies to men who are devotees of Śiva, who have received initiation, and who are dedicated to Śiva.
If clothing and such items belong to a deity, they shall be purified by sprinkling them with cow-products;
one should then perform a *saṃhitā-homa* or likewise recite the *aghora-mantra*.
If uninitiated persons, such as Śūdras and others, have entered the pavilion of the watch (yāmamaṇṭapa),
one should sprinkle it with water while reciting the Astra-mantra and then mutter the Aghora-mantra ten times.
But if the pitcher or other vessels have been touched by that [impurity], one should place another in its stead;
likewise, when dogs or similar animals enter, [the rite] should be preceded by the *saṃhitā-homa* oblation.

One should perform the smearing with cow-dung, the sprinkling on an auspicious day, and so forth, accompanied by the sprinkling of fragrant water; one should avoid even those who act in a contrary manner.
One should place the water-jars and other vessels situated there, even if they have been defiled by birth-impurity or death-impurity;
having smeared them with cow dung, one should perform the rite of circumambulation with fire.
Having performed the *mūrtihoma* at the conclusion, one should install the water-jars (*kumbha*) and other vessels as previously described.
This same expiation is proclaimed for touching dogs and similar animals;
likewise, if a Caṇḍāla or others should enter [the area], having performed this rite in their presence.
O Śambhu, one should cause the installation to be performed and have the Diśā-homa sacrifice performed.
(5th line) If those [images] are touched by them, one should perform the expiation as previously described.
If the sacrificial hall is consumed by fire, there will be danger in the royal palace. (6th line)
Having removed the previous jars and other items, and having consecrated the bull-bannered Lord (Śiva),
one should perform the ritual oblation to the deity's form and, at the conclusion, [reconstruct] the sacrificial pavilion as before.
Having performed the immediate consecration (*adhivāsa*), one should first carry out the festival;
when the water-shed has been consumed by fire, the *saṃhitā-homa* is prescribed.
When the womb-house has been consumed by fire, it becomes respectively like a pavilion, an image,
the interior of a vessel, and what is outside the vessel.
During the *snapana* (ablution), one should perform the *diśā-homa* (offering to the quarters), as well as the *mūrti-homa* (offering to the forms) according to the prescribed rite;
likewise, the *śānti* (pacification), the *śānti-homa*, or even the *saṃhitā-homa*.
However, in the case of the fangs, or regarding the *liṅga* and *bera* (the image), one should apply the specific expiation (*niṣkṛti*) that has been taught for them.
One should construct a pavilion for the image in the attendant's residence as previously described.
Whether during a festival or not, its ritual procedure is common and equal [to that of the main deity].
Upon entering a village or when there is a fire, one should perform the *saṃhitā-homa*.
When a great conflagration occurs in a village, one should perform a propitiatory *śānti-homa*.
If no remedy has been provided,
[one should offer] a garment and an upper cloth (uttarīya) for the Lord of Teachers (*deśikendra*), along with a turban and five ornaments made of gold.
Or even as small as a finger-ring—that action is considered equal.
By reciting the *Aghoraśata* a hundred times from the mouth of a Guru who bestows bliss,
[the practitioners] then destroy the kingdom and its kings when there is a confusion of teachers.
A ritual performed by one preceptor while situated within a single temple should not be performed by another;
for that would constitute a confusion of preceptors.
The sages said:

The fetching of water and so forth, the offering of fragrance, the preparation of flowers and incense, the lamp, the dedication of the food offering (*naivedya*), the daily worship of the deity, whatever constitutes complete propitiation, and the worship of the retinue and other such rites—
(3rd line) Whatever constitutes complete propitiation, and the worship of the retinue and so forth.
There should be constant festivals, including singing and the like, as well as ritual bathing and the application of fragrant perfumes.
The preparation of the materials for the festival and so forth, the invocation of the deities and other rites,
the worship of the primary *liṅga* and others at that time, and the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*).
How can one person perform many deeds that are accomplished by many men?
Those wise ones are virtuous; I shall explain it to you in brief:
whatever action—whether obligatory, occasional, or optional—is situated within a single time-period.
"It must be performed by a single teacher; this has been well stated by me."
The teacher, his son, and his wife are his kinsmen;
likewise, those initiated by him, the local people, and those men afflicted by poison [belong to him].
Those born into the primary Śaiva families— whether Brāhmaṇas,
Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras— are the *anuloma* [castes], such as the Gandharvas, Nartakas, and others.
If the Rudrakanyās and the Maddās are protectors of his mouth,

then the ritual performed by them shall be considered as performed by the preceptor (*deśika*). Just as [an act] performed by a king is [valid], so too is that performed by the leaders of the vassal states.
Whatever has been established as the duty of kings is likewise approved here as well.
Otherwise, when one must die while still existing [in this world], one should practice tranquility therein;
for in that case, the fault of intermixture is equal, and the expiation is likewise equal.

All those established by the scriptures act repeatedly through action; yet one should abandon that very action which is established by the scriptures among those who perform it. Otherwise, if there were something else to be done, it would be declared as being above the king.
A pacification ritual (*śānti*) should be performed, half the size [of the previous], for the removal of that fault.
[This should be done] with materials prescribed by the scriptures... first, which bestows wisdom and happiness;
therefore, one should perform everything according to the rite with every effort.
Regarding the objects of knowledge concerning sound (*nādajñeya*), which two deities are to be honored in the Kali age?
Furthermore, let it be written by me again, consisting of two thousand verses in number.

[Thus ends the procedure for expiation (*prāyaścittavidhi*) in the *Kriyākramadyotikā*, composed by the venerable Aghoraśivācārya, whose supreme name is the Blessed Supreme Lord. May this be offered to the venerable Sāmbasadāśiva. In the auspicious year named Durmati, on the day of Puṣyā, during the dark fortnight.
